paragraphs.text: Covered him: wrapped him with coverings.

David's life was drawing to its close, and he was in his late sixties, for he became king at the age of thirty and died at the age of seventy, that is, he reigned forty years (2 Sam 5:4, 5). He fell ill at the end of his life and could no longer bear the cold of the air; however many heavy garments they put on him and however many coverings they laid over him, he kept feeling cold and shivering. This shows how great David's bodily weakness was and how early his old age had come, which made him unable to manage the kingdom. This encouraged his son Adonijah to try to seize the kingship, but God alerted David, who ordered that his son Solomon be anointed king, as will appear in this chapter.

His servants: those who worked in the royal palace, who were close to the king and cared for his personal affairs. When the attempts of David's servants to warm him did not succeed, they thought of choosing a young virgin to serve him and lie beside him. In this they were imitating what the kings of the surrounding nations did in such circumstances. The young woman would perform this task without being joined to him as a wife, but as a nurse, since King David had become weak, unable to marry, and was suffering from illnesses. This was a Greek remedy that they used to give to the aged in those times, for they thought that a weak body gained energy and vitality when it was joined to a body full of youth and vitality.

The Shunammite: from Shunem, a village lying southeast of Nazareth at a distance of seven miles. David's servants searched throughout the whole kingdom for a beautiful young woman for this purpose, and their choice settled on a beautiful virgin named Abishag from the town of Shunem. They brought her to the king, and she was a nurse to him and served him, but David did not have relations with her as a husband does.

In the end the body of David, the great man of war, grew weak, and he became unable to carry on with life because of his illness. So do not take pride in your strength or your position, because man is weak by nature and God is the source of strength. Thank Him, use your strength for His glory, and do not be arrogant toward others.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah's attempt to seize the kingship

paragraphs.text: Because of his old age David became unable to carry out his duties as king, so it was necessary to anoint a successor to manage the affairs of the kingdom in the last part of his life. Adonijah the son of Haggith sought to take the throne, since he was the eldest of David's sons then living, and so he considered himself the lawful heir to the throne. Adonijah was David's fourth son, but his firstborn Amnon was killed by Absalom (2 Sam 13), and the second, Chileab (2 Sam 3:3), had died, while the third was Absalom, who was killed when he fought against David (2 Sam 18). Adonijah began to plan to take the kingship and gave his movements a royal appearance: he prepared chariots and horsemen and had fifty men run before him. He was handsome and boasted of his beauty, and David, in his weakness, was unable to rebuke him and prevent him from trying to seize the kingship. Beauty was a desirable thing in kings at that time, but bodily beauty has nothing to do with beauty of spirit and good character.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah's attempt to seize the kingship

paragraphs.text: Joab: he was the commander of David's army, and he was harsh and violent.

Abiathar: he was a high priest together with Zadok the priest. Abiathar was the one left of the descendants of Eli the priest after Saul killed the priests (1 Sam 22:20). Abiathar was with the ark of the covenant in Jerusalem after he had shared David's afflictions and his flight from Saul. Zadok, for his part, was in Gibeon with the remaining parts of the tabernacle of meeting in the days of David. That is, there were two high priests at the same time in the days of David, and after Abiathar was removed, Zadok became the only high priest in the days of Solomon. In this the word of God was fulfilled, that the house of Eli the priest would be brought to an end (1 Sam 3:11-14). Adonijah began to fortify himself by drawing military and religious leaders around him. Joab, the commander of David's army, responded to him, and so did Abiathar the priest, and they joined him in his rebellion, seeking personal interests and gains. Perhaps Adonijah had promised them that they would continue as head of the army and of the priesthood. Thus Adonijah was relying on the arm of flesh, disregarding the divine will.

Perhaps Joab chose to support Adonijah, contrary to God's promise (1 Chr 22:9), because Adonijah was weaker than Solomon, so that through Adonijah's reign Joab could control the kingdom. As for Abiathar, his opposition to God's promise and his support of Adonijah were permitted by God, so that through this evil which Abiathar did, the priesthood would come to an end in the house of Eli the priest, as God had ordered long before by the mouth of Samuel; for Abiathar was the last of the priestly line of Eli.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah's attempt to seize the kingship

paragraphs.text: Shimei: a Benjamite, one of David's mighty men, who is the one mentioned in (ch. 4:18) as Shimei the son of Elah, one of Solomon's twelve officers over all Israel.
Rei: he is the same as Ira the Jairite mentioned in (2 Sam 20:26), and he was one of the priests in the days of David.
At the same time, Zadok the priest, Benaiah, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David's mighty men who loved him were not at ease with Adonijah's actions in his effort to inherit the throne.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah's attempt to seize the kingship

paragraphs.text: The stone of Zoheleth: a stone that the Canaanites held sacred, which was one of the landmarks of an area near "En-rogel."
En-rogel: a spring near Jerusalem on the border between Judah and Benjamin, in the Kidron Valley south of Jerusalem.

Adonijah wanted to give his taking of power a religious character and appearance by offering peace offerings, as though he had received authority from God Himself with the witness of the high priest Abiathar. In this he was imitating Absalom when he made himself king in place of David (2 Sam 15). Adonijah held his conspiracy outside Jerusalem at the stone of Zoheleth, which is beside En-rogel, and he invited his brothers - except Solomon - and the men of the royal court, except those such as Nathan the prophet and Benaiah. This confirms that he was doing something against his father's wishes.

So when sin creeps into a person's heart, it blinds him from seeing the truth; he does not accept the divine will and does not turn to wise counsel, but in arrogance relies on his own wisdom and his own opinion. I wish that you would be humble and take refuge in prayer to God, so that you hear His voice and obey Him, and do not oppose Him for the sake of your personal aims.

entries.section: (3) Solomon's mother asks that he be made king

paragraphs.text: Nathan was troubled when he heard that Adonijah had made himself king over the children of Israel after David, because he knew that God had declared to David that Solomon would be his successor. This was when He promised him that his son, who would be called Solomon, would be the one to build a house for God, and not David himself (1 Chr 22:29, 1 Chr 28:5, 6), as appears from (v. 30). So he thought of saving the situation and told Bathsheba what Adonijah had done without the knowledge of King David. Bathsheba was the wife of Uriah the Hittite, whom David married and by whom he had Solomon.

entries.section: (3) Solomon's mother asks that he be made king

paragraphs.text: After Nathan informed Bathsheba of the conspiracy, he invited her to share with him in carrying out a plan opposed to Adonijah's plan, especially since she and her son were in danger of being killed if Adonijah succeeded and took the government, for it is customary that whoever seizes the kingship kills everyone connected with the former king.

entries.section: (3) Solomon's mother asks that he be made king

paragraphs.text: The plan Nathan drew up was as follows: Bathsheba would go in to David and remind him of the oath he had previously sworn to her, to make her son Solomon king after him, and would ask him why he had not fulfilled what he had pledged, and would tell him of Adonijah's reign. Nathan made her understand that he would follow her immediately to complete the explanation of the matter to the king, because David might not believe Bathsheba's words, but when Nathan confirmed them he would understand and be convinced.

entries.section: (3) Solomon's mother asks that he be made king

paragraphs.text: In this condition of weakness and old age David did not leave his chamber, for he was not able to go out. Bathsheba had a special familiarity with King David, so she could go in to him at any time to reassure herself about him and to oversee his nursing and his needs. No one was with David except Abishag the Shunammite.

entries.section: (3) Solomon's mother asks that he be made king

paragraphs.text: Bathsheba went in to the king and showed her great respect by bowing down to the king, so that the king would understand that she was submissive to him, when she reminded him that he had forgotten his promise to make her son Solomon king after him. David sensed that his wife had something she wanted to say, so he encouraged her to speak, saying to her, "What wouldest thou?" It was the custom that no one would enter to the king while he was meeting with one of his wives or one of his counselors, and so Nathan did not enter with Bathsheba until the king called for him.

entries.section: (3) Solomon's mother asks that he be made king

paragraphs.text: She reminded him first - as Nathan had instructed her - of the oath he had sworn to her, that her son Solomon would reign after him and sit upon the throne of the kingdom.

God's promises to you are very many, and you can enjoy them if you hold fast to them and ask Him to give them to you, for He is merciful and tender toward everyone who feels his need and believes in the power of God.

entries.section: (3) Solomon's mother asks that he be made king

paragraphs.text: She told him what Adonijah had done in declaring himself king without his father's knowledge. She also told him of the feast he had held for this occasion, the sacrifices he had offered in great numbers, and how he had invited to this banquet all his brothers, the king's sons, as well as Abiathar the priest and Joab the commander of the army, but had not invited his brother Solomon.

entries.section: (3) Solomon's mother asks that he be made king

paragraphs.text: She also pointed to his responsibility toward all his people, who were waiting, with their eyes upon him, for him to declare to them who would sit on the throne of the kingdom after him, for it is not necessary that the firstborn reign after his father, but whomever the king chooses.

entries.section: (3) Solomon's mother asks that he be made king

paragraphs.text: She made clear to him that after his departure from this world, if Solomon were not declared king, she and her son would be put to death at the hand of Adonijah.

entries.section: (4) Nathan the prophet tells David of Adonijah's conspiracy

paragraphs.text: According to the plan Nathan had drawn up, while Bathsheba was speaking, he arrived; they told the king, who permitted him to enter, and Nathan bowed down before him. Thus Nathan had the opportunity to confirm Bathsheba's words, so that the king would be moved to take the decision to install Solomon as king. What encouraged Nathan was that in this he was carrying out the word of God which He had spoken to David.

entries.section: (4) Nathan the prophet tells David of Adonijah's conspiracy

paragraphs.text: Nathan asked David wisely, to alert him to the danger, saying to him, "Hast thou said, Adonijah shall reign?!" For he had declared himself king and held a feast, at which the king's sons, the captains of the army, and Abiathar were now gathered. This was to warn the king that a great matter was taking place without his knowledge, and this was contrary to the word of God and to the law of the kingdom, since David had not given them permission for it. Their cry, "God save king Adonijah," implicitly meant that David had died, and this was something that could not be accepted.

entries.section: (4) Nathan the prophet tells David of Adonijah's conspiracy

paragraphs.text: He also showed him that Adonijah had excluded from this invitation Nathan himself, Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and Solomon the son of David, so that the king would understand who those were who were loyal to him and whom Adonijah feared and avoided.

entries.section: (4) Nathan the prophet tells David of Adonijah's conspiracy

paragraphs.text: Nathan repeated his question to David, whether it was he who had ordered Adonijah to be made king, in order to alert him and urge him to take the opposite decision, that is, to make Solomon king instead of Adonijah. It is understood from this that David was accustomed to making known all his orders to Nathan the prophet, because he represented the presence of God with him.

It is wise to alert others and to invite them gently to make decisions without blaming them, for speaking with humility and gentleness wins hearts, lets God work in them, and helps in making decisions.

Here David realized the seriousness of the situation and sensed with his wisdom that action had to be taken to set matters right. So he immediately called for Bathsheba, who had gone out from the king when Nathan came in to him, and she came in and stood in the presence of the king after Nathan went out.

Once again David renews his oath by the living God, who had redeemed him out of all the distresses that had come upon him, that Solomon would be the one to succeed him in inheriting the throne, assuring Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, that he held fast to his former oath and was renewing it this day also. It is understood from this that God promised David that his son Solomon would reign on his throne (1 Chr 28:5, 6), and that at that time David swore to Bathsheba that he would make Solomon king. This oath is not mentioned in the Holy Bible, and here in this verse he renews his oath.

David renewed his oath despite the challenge of circumstances; we too must hold fast to our spiritual pledges and obligations, and not allow worldly preoccupations and temporary matters to hinder our spiritual journey, trusting in the Lord's support for us, so that we may triumph over all obstacles.

Bathsheba was reassured and bowed down to the king, expressing her thanks for what he had decided concerning her son, that he would inherit the throne, and she prayed that he would live long, so that the king would not understand from her request to make her son king that she wanted his death. In this Bathsheba obtained what she asked for, namely, that her son Solomon be made king and that she and her son be saved from death at the hand of Adonijah, and at the same time Nathan the prophet attained his aim as a prophet, which was to carry out the orders of God, who had promised that Solomon would be made king.

The king went on making the decisions necessary to face the situation and set matters right. He asked his servants to call Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and they all came and stood before the king. He called these particular men because Zadok is the priest who would anoint the king, Nathan is the prophet who represents the presence of God, and Benaiah is a military commander who leads the army and protects the new king.

Gihon: a spring of water in the outskirts of the city of Jerusalem, that is, outside its walls, which the Jebusites dug in the year 2000 BC. David chose a place outside Jerusalem from which to begin the procession of Solomon's enthronement, so that all the people might see him as he passed. It was customary in ancient times to install kings at springs of water, since they symbolize the continuance of the kingship, like the continual flowing of water from the spring.

The king gave them his instructions to take with them the royal guard and those close to the king who were loyal to him, and to set his son Solomon on King David's own mule, which meant that he had become the king, and to go down to Gihon, where Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet were to anoint him with the holy oil as king over Israel, and to blow the trumpets, crying, "God save king Solomon." He sent with the high priest, who was responsible for anointing kings, and with Nathan the prophet, a military force under the command of Benaiah to confront the rebels led by the mighty Joab, should he persist in rebellion. Here we see David's love and humility, for he yielded the kingship to his son while he was still alive, since he felt that it was for the good of the kingdom that his son reign in his place to manage the kingdom with strength and firmness, while it was enough for David to live the remainder of his life in the love of God and the praise of Him.

Zadok's anointing of Solomon was in fulfillment of God's law concerning the setting up of kings. As for Adonijah, the Holy Bible does not mention that Abiathar the priest anointed him, but only that he was with him and shared in the celebration, for God did not allow him to be anointed because He was not pleased with his enthronement as king.

After he is anointed and proclaimed king, you shall bring him in a royal procession, and he shall sit on the throne and be king in my place. This is my charge to everyone, that he shall rule over Judah and Israel.
Benaiah declared his agreement and readiness to carry out the word of King David; indeed, he also declared that this was the word of God, which must be carried out.

Benaiah prayed that the Lord would support the new king Solomon in the affairs of government as He had done with his father, and increase him in exaltation and loftiness, and magnify his throne so that it would reach ranks higher even than those which King David himself had reached. This is a prayer that does not anger David, because it is well known that no one wishes anyone else to be better than himself except his son, for when his son achieves more success than he, that is a cause of happiness for his father.
The Cherethites and the Pelethites: the police and the army.

Those who were loyal to David, namely Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah, together with the police and the army, carried out David's instructions to them. They set Solomon on King David's mule and went with him to Gihon, so that the procession would travel a great distance and the greatest number of the people might see it.
The horn of oil: they used to make vessels for liquids from the horns of animals, especially oils and perfumes, among them the anointing oil used to anoint kings and priests.

Zadok the priest had taken with him the flask of oil from its place in the tent where the ark of the covenant was (2 Sam 6:17), and there at Gihon he anointed Solomon king, and they blew the trumpets, proclaiming life for King Solomon.

All the people responded to the shouts of David's supporters and began to express their joy in the new king by playing on pipes - as was the custom on their occasions of joy - and everyone's joy was overflowing, so that the earth almost split from the force of the echo of their voices.

entries.section: (6) Adonijah's failure and his submission to Solomon

paragraphs.text: The city: what is meant by it is Jerusalem, regarded as a limited city compared with the great capitals of the lands such as Babylon and Nineveh. The word "city" in its original linguistic sense may mean a fortress or a citadel, and this means that what is meant is the fortress of Jerusalem, that is, the city of Jerusalem.

After Adonijah had made himself king and the guests in his house had finished the feast, they heard the sound of the trumpet and the musical instruments coming from far off from Jerusalem. Joab asked why the sound of the trumpet, since it is not blown except at feasts, or in war, or on special occasions such as the installation of kings.

entries.section: (6) Adonijah's failure and his submission to Solomon

paragraphs.text: Anxiety spread among all the guests, and meanwhile Jonathan the son of Abiathar the high priest, who accompanied Adonijah, came in, and Adonijah received him eagerly, expecting from him good news that would calm the anxiety of those gathered. Adonijah said to him, "for thou art a valiant man, and bringest good tidings," because he had informed David of the frustration of the wicked counsel of Ahithophel, so that he might prepare for the attack coming upon him from Absalom (2 Sam 15:27, 36; 17:17).

entries.section: (6) Adonijah's failure and his submission to Solomon

paragraphs.text: Jonathan declared to those gathered that he carried disturbing news for them, namely that David was still holding on to his authority as king, since Jonathan called him "our lord." This shows their error in declaring Adonijah king without David's permission. And also that David had made Solomon king, and this increased the danger of their position and their exposure to harm from Solomon the new king.

entries.section: (6) Adonijah's failure and his submission to Solomon

paragraphs.text: Jonathan related to them the details of the events: that Zadok had anointed Solomon king at Gihon, with Benaiah and Nathan the prophet with him; that they then set him on King David's mule and went with him in a great procession, with the Cherethites and the Pelethites around them; and that they passed through Jerusalem with great joy and loud voices, which is what the guests had heard from afar while they were in their place.

entries.section: (6) Adonijah's failure and his submission to Solomon

paragraphs.text: Then Solomon arrived with his procession at the royal palace and sat on the throne of the kingdom, and the servants of King David came in to congratulate him on having made Solomon king, and they prayed that Solomon would be a greater king than he. David rejoiced greatly and bowed himself upon his bed and blessed God, who had granted him to see his son reign after him according to God's promise to him.

entries.section: (6) Adonijah's failure and his submission to Solomon

paragraphs.text: All the guests at Adonijah's feast were greatly afraid that Solomon the new king would strike them down because of their taking part in this treachery of making another person king without the knowledge of King David, and each one fled his own way to hide from sight, for there was no morality among them; rather each one of them was seeking his own interest and benefit, and now each one was looking for how to save himself even if the others died.

entries.section: (6) Adonijah's failure and his submission to Solomon

paragraphs.text: Adonijah feared exceedingly that Solomon would punish him for his rebellion, so he hastened to the bronze altar in the tabernacle of meeting to lay hold on its horns, to take advantage of the custom prevailing at that time, namely that whoever laid hold of the horns of the altar was not thereby spared from being killed, but only until a just trial was held in which he could defend himself, clearing himself of the charge brought against him.
Adonijah's great fear was a sign of his wickedness, because he had intended to do harm to Solomon and all who followed him, especially since Solomon was known to be strong in character.

Do not be hasty in your decisions, lest you fall into matters that cannot be remedied. Take care to pray to God before every action, and even to consult your father of confession, especially in great decisions.

entries.section: (6) Adonijah's failure and his submission to Solomon

paragraphs.text: If he shew himself a worthy man: that is, loyal to Solomon.

They brought him down from the altar: because the altar was set on a high place, but it had no steps (Ex 20:26). Solomon was told what Adonijah had done in laying hold of the horns of the altar, asking that Solomon swear to him that he would be safe and not order him to be killed. Solomon declared that if he was in the wrong he would be punished, and if he was a worthy man no evil would befall him. Then Solomon sent men, and they brought Adonijah to him, and he bowed down before him, trembling.

Solomon did not want to begin his reign by punishing anyone, so he allowed him to return to his house, and in this he gave him an opportunity for good conduct, and if he erred a second time he would deserve punishment.
David's charge to his son Solomon and the removal of the opponents

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: Before David died he gave his charge to his son Solomon, as fathers do when they feel that their departure from this world is near and give farewell counsels to their sons; and as Christ charged His disciples before His crucifixion and offered a farewell prayer (Jn 13-17). This charge includes a spiritual part (vv. 2-4) and an administrative part (vv. 5-9). David's purpose in these commandments is that his descendants hold to the commandments of God, so that they may secure God's care and remain firm on their thrones.

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: He told his son that he was on his way out of the earth, as every human being before him had departed, and charged him to be strong as a man to face the responsibilities of government, as Moses charged Joshua his disciple, who succeeded him in leading the people, to be strong (Deut 31:7, 23), because fear is the cause of all failure. Solomon's age at that time was about twenty years.

David's words show the calm of his soul and his acceptance of death as a natural matter for all humanity, which transfers him from the earth to a better life with God. Likewise his words "Be strong, and shew thyself a man" call Solomon to faith in God, so that he may become strong like a mature and capable man, because the power of God supports him and works in him.

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: Statutes: the law of God given to Moses.
Ordinances: the acts of worship.
Commandments: what is meant by them is the Ten Commandments.
Judgments: the laws found in the Law.
Testimonies: the sayings of God in general in His law.

David charged his son Solomon to hold fast to the commandments of God and His law which He gave to Moses, with all that it includes of teachings and spiritual worship, and to keep all of this so that he might prosper in his life. This charge resembles God's charge to Joshua after the death of Moses (Josh 1:7, 8). And so that Solomon might secure his people's submission to him, he must first obey the word of God himself.

If you want people to respect your words and esteem and obey you, then you must first become a disciple of the word of God in the Holy Bible, the teachings of the Church, and the guidance of your father of confession, so that you secure the soundness of your thought and its influence on those around you.

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: David reminded his son Solomon that if he held fast to the commandments and law of God, God would fulfill His promise that his descendants would reign forever (2 Sam 7:12-16). God's promise here includes two things:

1- A promise conditional on keeping the commandments, by which God would establish the descendants of David on the throne of the kingdom; but they forsook the commandments of God, and the kingship was taken from them by the Babylonian captivity.

2- An unconditional promise, which is King David's reign forever, and this is through Christ, who comes from the descendants of David. Even if they sinned and the kingdom came to an end and the captivity came, Christ would come and reign over the hearts of the believers forever, and the believers would become spiritual kings in Him.

What David means here is holding fast to the law of God and relying on Him, and not on military strength represented by a multitude of horses, or an alliance with Egypt, and likewise not multiplying marriages on the pretext of increasing offspring (Deut 17:16-20). But sadly Solomon fell into these errors, and God was angry with him.

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: Abner the son of Ner: the cousin of Saul and the commander of his army. He killed Asahel, Joab's brother, in self-defense, and Joab killed him treacherously in revenge for his brother Asahel.

Amasa the son of Jether: he was the son of Abigail, the sister of Zeruiah and of David, and therefore he was the son of Joab's maternal aunt. David appointed him commander of his army in place of Joab, who afterward met him and killed him treacherously with his sword in order to return to his position as commander of the army. That is, Joab acted treacherously and killed Abner and Amasa after they had been reconciled with David, and this is not considered an excuse even if it took place in time of war.
His girdle: what the soldier wears around his waist, hanging down.

After David finished his first, essential charge, he moved on to the judgments that Solomon had to carry out so that his kingdom might be secure. He began with Joab, for whom wisdom required choosing the right time to punish him, so that there would be no murmuring in the army, most of whose men admired their commander. David reminded his son Solomon of Joab's treachery toward both Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, since he shed their blood when they were innocent, which should not have happened, as they were not fighting against him. He dealt treacherously with them, for he pretended to embrace them, and while they were in his embrace he killed them, so that the blood flowed on his girdle and down to his sandals (2 Sam 3, 20). In this he resembles Judas the traitor who delivered Christ with a kiss. Joab was strong, indeed stronger than David, and often disobedient to him, so David could not punish him for killing Abner and Amasa until the right time came, when Solomon had become king and had another strong commander of the army, Jehoiada, and Joab deserved to receive his punishment for these two great crimes against God, David, and all the people, through the loss of two great leaders in war.

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: Joab did not make peace, so he cannot find peace for himself, and Solomon's reign, which is marked by peace and wisdom, cannot contain such persons. Therefore David charged Solomon not to let Joab's life end in peace, but to put him to death as the penalty for the crime he committed against innocent men. David had not killed him before, so that the kingdom would not be disturbed because of his chief role in leading the army, and to give him an opportunity to repent; but since he persisted and disobeyed the commandment of God and supported Adonijah to seize the kingship, he deserved to receive punishment for all his errors, and lest he try again to gain power over Solomon's kingdom. In this David is carrying out the law of God that requires the murderer to be put to death (Num 35:16); if he did not carry it out, David and Solomon would be condemned before God.

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: Barzillai: the head of a tribe living in Gilead east of the Jordan, who showed honor to David and those with him when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.

David moves on to speak of another person who did a special kindness for him and his army and showed courtesy when David was fleeing from Absalom. David wished to reward him in the person of his sons, so he charged Solomon to grant them the right to sit at the king's table because of the faithfulness and sincerity of their father, for Barzillai had excused himself from staying in Jerusalem with David because of his old age, and sent his son Chimham to accompany David (2 Sam 17:27-29; 19:31-39). To sit at the king's table means the greatest honor from the king and great trust on his part. From this we see David's justice, for he charges that wrongdoers be punished and that those who do good be rewarded.

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: Bahurim: a village near the Mount of Olives, that is, next to Jerusalem.
Mahanaim: a city east of the Jordan, north of the river Jabbok.

David mentioned a third person, Shimei the son of Gera the Benjamite, who had earlier shown intense hatred toward David and cursed him when he fled from his son Absalom. When David triumphed and returned to his kingdom, Shimei fell at his feet, pleading with him and asking for pardon and forgiveness, and David promised him that he would not kill him (2 Sam 16:5-8; 19:19-24).

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: Bring his hoar head down to the grave with blood: do not let him die a natural death, but kill him.
The grave: the tomb.

David asked his son Solomon not to hold Shimei guiltless, because he had sworn to him that he would not kill him, but that he should try him as a just judge and issue the judgment he deserved. For this Shimei was a deceitful man and not innocent, and if he were left alone he might plot against the kingdom and the king; that is, his apology to David was out of fear and not repentance, and therefore he could do harm to the kingdom. David does not mean a personal revenge here, but his punishment because he had sinned against the kingdom and against the Lord's anointed, King David; and David's promise to Shimei that he would not be killed was conditional on his obedience, so when he disobeyed King Solomon he deserved his punishment.

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: The city of David: that is, Mount Zion, which is part of the city of Jerusalem (2 Sam 5:7), where David placed the ark of the covenant of God.

David died and was buried on Mount Zion. The total period of David's reign was 40 years. The first capital of the kingdom was the city of Hebron, where he reigned for 7 years, and after he took the city of Jerusalem he moved the capital of his kingdom there, where he reigned 33 years. The custom in ancient times was to place tombs outside the cities, but Jerusalem was an exception to this, and the kings were buried in it, such as David and his descendants.

entries.section: (1) David's charge to Solomon and the death of David

paragraphs.text: The kingship passed quietly from David to Solomon, and matters were settled, and he became ruler of the kingdom without rival. David had labored much in his wars with the surrounding nations until the kingdom became stable, and he handed it over to his son Solomon; indeed he also arranged for him the materials for building the Temple and provided him with much gold.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife

paragraphs.text: From this verse to the end of the chapter, the arrangements of God appear, which give Solomon an opportunity to be rid of the wicked who could oppose him in his kingship. It begins here with the coming of Adonijah, the elder brother of Solomon, who tried to seize the kingship against God's instruction that Solomon be made king, but Solomon forgave him after he became king and gave him an opportunity to repent and behave well. And now Adonijah comes to meet Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, and speaks kindly, declaring that he has come peaceably, because Bathsheba was surprised at his coming and suspected that he had an evil purpose. Adonijah politely asked to speak a word with her, and she gave him permission.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife

paragraphs.text: Adonijah claimed that he had every right of succession to the throne of the kingdom, as the eldest of David's living sons, and that all the people had been expecting this to be fulfilled, but the Lord, who has the right to set up whom He wills, chose Solomon. This is not a true acknowledgment of the will of God and submission to His will; rather he accepted it because he could not do otherwise. Though his words show submission to God and His will, he hid in his heart his resentment toward Solomon and his feeling that the kingship should have remained his, had it not been for God's intervention through David and the making of Solomon king. In appearance, then, he submits to the will of God, but in truth he rejects it.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife

paragraphs.text: Adonijah praised Bathsheba, saying that her words were heard by the king, in order to win her over so that she would agree to intercede with King Solomon, by virtue of her special familiarity with him, that he might allow him to take Abishag the Shunammite as his wife, the one who had been a nurse to his father David. This, of course, is a great error, because he dares to ask to marry his father's wife, thereby violating the Law. His request to marry Abishag means two things:
1- His attraction to her beauty (ch. 1:4), that is, desire moved him toward her.

2- It was the custom of pagan kings that the new king would take possession of all the property of the former king, even his wives and concubines. Perhaps Adonijah wanted, by marrying Abishag, to try to recover the kingship by taking the wife of the former king, David. This is what Absalom did before, by going in to his father's concubines to declare himself king in place of David (2 Sam 16:22). And Abishag, though she was only a nurse to David, was considered his wife, and it was not right for his son to marry her.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife

paragraphs.text: Bathsheba acted simply, and perhaps she did not understand Adonijah's evil intentions, or perhaps she felt that giving him Abishag would make him content and establish peace between him and his brother King Solomon, so she agreed to carry out his request and speak to Solomon.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife

paragraphs.text: When Bathsheba came in to her son King Solomon, he welcomed her and humbled himself greatly before her, for he rose from his throne and bowed down before her, and after this he honored her very much, as he seated her on a seat fitting her station at his right hand. This shows the extent of his love for his mother and his humility. It was a custom among the Jews, the Arabs, and the Greeks to honor the mother of the king by seating her at his right hand.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife

paragraphs.text: Bathsheba felt that her request was small and did not perceive its evil dimensions, so she asked her son King Solomon to grant her petition, and he welcomed her, waiting to hear the request.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife

paragraphs.text: Then she disclosed to him the request of his brother Adonijah, that Abishag the Shunammite be given to him as a wife.

entries.section: (2) Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife

paragraphs.text: With divine wisdom Solomon perceived Adonijah's evil intentions, so he answered his mother with disapproval to alert her to the seriousness of the request, for he said to her, "Why dost thou ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? ask for him the kingdom also." He declared Adonijah's evil, not only in breaking the law of God by asking to marry his father's wife, but also in his feeling that he was the eldest and deserving of the kingship. He revealed to his mother that Abiathar the high priest and Joab the commander of the army in the days of David were the ones who had planned this request with Adonijah, to seize the kingship again, as they had planned before.

Solomon's reply means complete rejection of this dangerous request. Despite his great honor for her and his humility before God, he leads his kingdom with wisdom and firmness, without flattery at the expense of the truth, even if it were to please his mother, for pleasing God is more important than everything. Solomon did not violate his promise to fulfill his mother's request, because he considered that the fulfillment of a promise must be within the bounds of the truth and the commandments of God (v. 20).

entries.section: (2) Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife

paragraphs.text: God do so to me, and more also: an oath meaning the necessity of carrying out what he says, otherwise God will punish him with the punishment he wishes to carry out on another, and even more than it.

If Solomon had forgiven Adonijah when he seized the kingship, now that Adonijah commits a great error like this - as we explained - he deserves death. Solomon asked Benaiah - who had become the commander of his armies - to carry out the sentence of death on Adonijah, who persisted in evil, and Adonijah was killed.

Beware of deceit and lying, for God is long-suffering, and in the end He will judge you to destruction, because you despised God and the others to whom you lied. Be content with what you have, keep away from desires, purify your heart from evil, and trust in the power of God, which will support you, so that you do not need this hateful lying.

entries.section: (3) The expulsion of Abiathar from the priesthood

paragraphs.text: Anathoth: a city lying northwest of Jerusalem at a distance of four miles, and the birthplace of the prophet Jeremiah.

Solomon continued to cleanse his kingdom of his wicked opponents. After killing his brother Adonijah, he faced Abiathar the high priest, who had disobeyed the commandment of God by trying to seize the kingship for Adonijah, and thus deserved death. But in appreciation of Abiathar's labor in serving the ark of the covenant of God in the days of David (2 Sam 15:24-29), Solomon did not order him killed, but only removed him from the head of the priesthood, so that Zadok alone would remain high priest; for, as we mentioned, the headship of the priesthood in the days of David was shared by Zadok and Abiathar.

entries.section: (3) The expulsion of Abiathar from the priesthood

paragraphs.text: By the expulsion of Abiathar the word of God is fulfilled, that the descendants of Eli the priest be removed from the priesthood (1 Sam 2:30-33), for Abiathar was of the descendants of Eli the priest, and thus Zadok became the sole high priest, and he was of the descendants of Eleazar the son of Aaron.

Do not take part in sin and help another to evil, or plan for another the way of evil, lest you lose God's blessings in your life and are exposed to destruction. Be careful, and take care to please God before you please people.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: The next person whose time had come to be called to account was Joab, who had allied himself with Adonijah in his rebellion, although he had previously stood on the side of King David against the rebellion of Absalom (2 Sam 18, 19). When the news reached Joab of Abiathar's expulsion from the priesthood, and he had already learned of what had happened to Adonijah when he asked for Abishag as a wife, he realized that his turn must come, so he fled to the altar of the Lord and laid hold on its horns.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: Solomon had assigned someone to watch Joab's movements, because he knew his ability to overturn conditions given his former authority as commander of the army. So when they told Solomon that Joab was beside the altar, he sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and commanded him to kill Joab.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: Benaiah went to carry out the order, but he did not wish to kill a person in a holy place, so he asked Joab to come out of the place, but he refused, insisting on staying beside the altar and holding its horns. Benaiah did not wish to kill Joab, who clung to the bronze altar, except after returning to Solomon.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: The king ordered him to kill Joab where he was, before the altar, and reminded him of the judgment of the Law which says: "Thine eye shall not pity him, but thou shalt put away the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, that it may go well with thee" (Deut 19:13). Also, Joab's holding fast to the horns of the altar does not clear him of the innocent blood that he shed by killing both Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, since the Scripture says: "But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour, to slay him with guile; thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die" (Ex 21:14). But Solomon ordered that Joab be buried, in appreciation of his labor in leading the army throughout the days of David, and because he was also the son of Solomon's maternal aunt.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: Upon the head of his seed: that is, the punishment will come upon the sons and grandsons of Joab if they walk in the evils of their father, as the second commandment makes clear (Ex 34). This was not revenge by Solomon for himself, but he ordered Joab to be killed in fulfillment of the commandment and of his father's instructions. Solomon also knew that in doing so he was fulfilling the word of Scripture: "Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness" (Prov 25:5). Solomon asks peace for the descendants of King David, meaning not only the throne of Solomon but all the descendants who would come from Solomon. And from the descendants of David comes Christ, who reigns forever, and He is the God of peace, who gives peace to those who believe in Him, over whose hearts He reigns, not in this age only but forever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: So went up: because the tabernacle was on a high place in Jerusalem.

Benaiah obeyed the king's command and went to Joab at the altar and killed him and buried him in his own land in the wilderness, where his house was, which carried with it some honor. He did not leave his body in shame and disgrace, because he had fought the wars of the Lord with King David, so he had this right to honor. The burial of a person in his house is a kind of honor, as happened with the prophet Samuel (1 Sam 25:1).

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: With the removal of Abiathar from the priesthood and the killing of Joab, two important positions in the order became vacant, which led Solomon to issue a decree appointing Benaiah the son of Jehoiada as commander of the army in the place of Joab, and appointing Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar; that is, Zadok alone held the headship of the priesthood and Abiathar no longer shared it with him.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: Because of Shimei the son of Gera's earlier bad conduct toward the kingdom, Solomon summoned him from his town Bahurim and sentenced him to live in Jerusalem under restriction, so that he would be under his close watch and not plan anything against the king, for Shimei was a chief of the tribe of Benjamin, and if he returned to his tribe he could plot against the king.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: The brook Kidron: a valley that extends 2.5 km northwest of Jerusalem to the southeast of it. It lies between the wall of the city on its western side and the Mount of Olives on the eastern side, and extends to the Dead Sea.

Solomon warned Shimei that if he went beyond the boundaries of the city, he would have sentenced himself to death. Therefore he must not leave the city under any circumstances, or he would be put to death.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: Shimei pledged to obey the king's command and remained for a long time living in Jerusalem, not leaving it.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: Gath: one of the five great Philistine cities, lying on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea southwest of Jerusalem.

After three years had passed in this state, two servants of Shimei ran away and took refuge with Achish the son of Maachah, king of Gath. Shimei sent people to search for them everywhere, and they found them there in Gath.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: When Shimei learned that his two servants were in Gath, he hurried himself and brought them from there, forgetting his pledge to King Solomon not to leave Jerusalem, or making light of the king's command, or perhaps thinking that the king would not discover his leaving Jerusalem.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: Solomon learned that Shimei had gone out of Jerusalem and gone to Gath and returned again to Jerusalem.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: Solomon summoned Shimei and reminded him of his former oath, that he would not go out of Jerusalem or be put to death. Solomon asked him why he had broken his oath and violated the commandment which he had charged him with.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: Then Solomon declared the reasons for the sentence on Shimei, namely that he was fully aware of the evil that lay in his heart toward his father David, ever since he cursed him and threw stones at him, and now the Lord returns his evil upon his own head. As for David and his descendants, they receive a blessing, and the throne of David is established before the Lord forever.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Joab and Shimei

paragraphs.text: Solomon commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada to kill Shimei, and he did so.

Thus, by getting rid of those who formed a danger to the continuance of Solomon's reign, namely Adonijah, Abiathar, Joab, and Shimei, peace and stability prevailed in the kingdom, and Solomon was able to control matters without rival.
Be careful in carrying out your promises to God, and obey His commandments also, and you will secure your peace, and even your blessed eternity. Do not be negligent, adding new sins to your sins.
The wisdom of Solomon

entries.section: (1) Solomon allies himself by marriage with Pharaoh and sacrifices on the high places

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh king of Egypt: he is Siamun, one of the kings of the Twenty-first Dynasty, who reigned from the year
The city of David: a part of Jerusalem, and then the name was applied to all of Jerusalem.

The house of the Lord: Solomon began its foundation in the fourth year of his reign and it took seven years, that is, he completed it in the eleventh year of his reign, and after that he began to build his own house, that is, his palaces (ch. 6:1, 38). His own house: Solomon built a group of palaces for himself over a period of 13 years (ch. 7:1), that is, he completed them in the twenty-fourth year of his reign.
The wall of Jerusalem: Solomon built a new wall for the city surrounding the new buildings he had erected, and he also repaired the old wall (ch. 11:27).

Solomon thought, with human wisdom, to ally himself by marriage with Pharaoh king of Egypt, for the sake of the standing and power of Egypt, and in this he broke the Law by marrying a pagan woman (Ex 34:16; Deut 7:3). Indeed, he later married other pagan women who had a role in turning him away from the worship of God, so his marriage alliance with Pharaoh was the beginning of the errors into which he fell. He built her a house outside Jerusalem, in which she lived temporarily until he completed building his palaces inside Jerusalem and also built the house of the Lord and the walls of the city.

Some see that Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter did not draw him to the worship of idols, as proved by the fact that he did not set up statues of the Egyptian gods when he built high places for the gods of his foreign wives (ch. 11:1-8), and perhaps she converted to Judaism after her marriage; but this does not negate Solomon's error in marrying a pagan woman.

entries.section: (1) Solomon allies himself by marriage with Pharaoh and sacrifices on the high places

paragraphs.text: The high places: the mountains or high hills.

The tabernacle of meeting at that time was in Gibeon, and in it was the bronze altar on which the sacrifices and burnt offerings to the Lord were offered. However, the people were not committed to offering sacrifices in one specific place until after the building of the Temple, so until that time they offered their sacrifices on any high place. This was a lack of exactness on their part, although Gideon and Samuel offered sacrifices in places other than the tabernacle of meeting as an exception (Judg 6:26; 1 Sam 9:12). And Solomon himself was not committed to offering sacrifices at the tabernacle of meeting, as the Lord commanded (Deut 12:1-14), as David his father was.

Because the people offered sacrifices so often on the high places, they called the tabernacle of meeting at Gibeon "the great high place" (v. 4), meaning that they offered sacrifices on any high place like the pagans.

entries.section: (1) Solomon allies himself by marriage with Pharaoh and sacrifices on the high places

paragraphs.text: Although Solomon was careful to please the Lord and to do the rites and prayers his father had followed, he shared with the people in sacrificing on the high places. This was a disregard on his part, because God commanded that sacrifices be offered in one place, the tabernacle of meeting, and this later helped lead to offering sacrifices to the idols that Solomon set up, in violation of the law of God, because he was not committed to offering sacrifices only at the tabernacle of meeting like his father David.

entries.section: (1) Solomon allies himself by marriage with Pharaoh and sacrifices on the high places

paragraphs.text: Gibeon: it lies northwest of Jerusalem at a distance of 8 km, and is in the portion of the tribe of Benjamin, and was afterward given to the priests. It gained special fame because David placed the tabernacle of meeting and the bronze altar there (1 Chr 16:39; 21:29; 2 Chr 1:3-6). Before Solomon began to carry out his work in the kingdom, he cared for the worship of God, so he went to the altar of the Lord at Gibeon, where the tabernacle of meeting and the bronze altar were, and there Solomon offered many burnt offerings. The Scripture mentions that he offered a thousand burnt offerings; most likely they were not all offered on one day, because the bronze altar could not accommodate offering this number in one day, but it took several days.
Solomon's offering of a great number of sacrifices shows:
1- The extent of Solomon's love for God and his generosity in giving to Him.
2- The extent of Solomon's wealth.

One of the important things we must hold fast to is to give God the first place in our lives, so that we are not troubled by our daily cares, but lift up our hearts to God before we carry out our daily work, or any new work we undertake. God is the only One able to lead us in the wilderness of this world so that we reach the shore of safety in the bosom of His saints.

In response to Solomon's love, which he showed at Gibeon, the Lord appeared to him in a dream and blessed him for his love and encouraged him, and said to him, "Ask what I shall give thee." For God rejoices in the gifts of His children, and so He repays them with abundant gifts according to the abundance of His riches.
We notice that God cares for man's freedom, so He lets him choose the request he wants from Him: "Ask what I shall give thee."

In His love, God wants to give us generously all that we need, and rejoices that we ask and persist before Him. I wish that you would trust in God's love and ask for your needs, especially the spiritual ones, so that you may be satisfied by Him and abide in Him.
Solomon thanked God for His mercy which He poured out on David his father, because he walked with God, and this mercy grew greater in setting his son as king to sit on his throne.

I know not how to go out or come in: I do not know how to act in the external affairs of the kingdom, in dealing with other peoples, and I do not know how to act in its internal affairs. When Solomon thanked God for making him king, he confessed humbly before Him that he was little. Being at the beginning of his twenties, he did not know how to act in the kingdom and how to manage its affairs, especially since the people of the children of Israel were great in number and so needed wisdom and strength in leading them. Solomon felt that he was a steward over the people of God, and so he says "thy people," for God is the true King.

Because of Solomon's sense of his weakness and the great number of the people, he asked God for wisdom, understanding, and the ability to discern, in order to lead this great people and to act well in all their affairs.

God was pleased because Solomon did not ask for material things and earthly desires such as long life, or riches, or victory over enemies, but asked for wisdom to fulfill his duty in leading the people under God's guidance. Therefore God gave him wisdom more than all men, not only in his own time, but no one before him had attained it, nor would anyone after him. This wisdom is knowledge, understanding, and exceedingly great intelligence, and it is human wisdom; but man must submit with this wisdom to God and His commandments, and so receive spiritual wisdom. Sadly, Solomon did not hold to this, so he broke the Law and multiplied marriages, horses, and chariots, and made idols for his pagan wives.
In addition to what Solomon asked, the Lord promised that he would also receive what he did not ask, riches and honor which no other king among his contemporaries would attain.

God promised Solomon length of days on condition of walking in His way and keeping His commandments as David his father walked and did; but sadly, in spite of Solomon's goodness and his great accomplishments such as building the Temple, he established the worship of idols in Jerusalem, so his life was not prolonged, and he lived only sixty years.
His servants: the chief workers with him.

When Solomon awoke from his dream, he rejoiced greatly at the vision of God and His great promises to him, so he went to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of God and thanked Him, to declare that his kingship and wisdom were from God and not from himself or from the people. He offered many peace offerings and made a feast for his servants so that they might share with him in his joy, since the one who offers peace offerings and his loved ones share in eating of them.

Here we see Solomon as a spiritual leader who takes care to make his helpers, the servants working with him, share in the spiritual joy, for he related to them what had happened in the dream, and they thanked God and submitted to His commandments.

I wish that you would make spiritual requests and ask for God's help to fulfill your responsibilities before you ask for material needs. Your God is able to do all things, but He rejoices when He finds your spiritual desires and your love for Him to be great.

This incident tells us of the first manifestation of Solomon's wisdom which God gave him. Two harlots came to the king, each with a complaint against the other. Of course, this case was first presented to the judges and elders, and they were perplexed about resolving it, so they referred it to Solomon to decide it because of his distinction in wisdom.

One of them began to relate to him the problem between them, which was that she and the other woman lived in one dwelling that no other person shared with them, and both of them had borne a child, with a difference of only three days between them.

The woman continued her story and said that the other woman's son died in the night because she - by an unintentional mistake - lay on him. So what she did was to rise in the night, when she realized what had happened, and slip in to where I was sleeping and exchange the two children, putting her dead son in place of the living son, whom she took from me, and she went to her bed.

The woman completes the story and says that when she woke in the morning and prepared to nurse the child, she found him dead, and when she looked closely at him she realized that he was not her son whom she had borne.

At this point in the story the two women began to cry out in each other's faces. The other woman objects and says that her son is the living one and that this woman's son is the dead one, and this one answers her and says, No, rather your son is the dead one and mine is the living. They kept repeating and restating the same words while in the presence of King Solomon.
The king showed the difficulty of the problem, since each of them declares that her son is the living one ... So what, one wonders, is the solution?!
Here the wisdom with which God had favored the king was manifested, for he asked those around him for a sword, and they brought it to him at once.
In order that Solomon might discover the true mother, he said to them, since you are disputing over this child, let him be cut in two and let each one take half.
Her bowels yearned: the heart of the true mother was inflamed for her son.

The true mother could not bear the killing of her son before her eyes, so she begged the king that they give the child to the other woman, while the other insisted on what the king had declared, that the child be cut in two, and her evil appeared in her attempt to be rid of the son as her own son had died.
From the reaction of the two women to the order to divide the child, Solomon was able to know the true mother, so he issued a judgment to give the child to his true mother and not to kill him.

Here everyone realized the wisdom of the king, after they had wondered at his judgment to divide the child, asking how the king could order the killing of a living child and the depriving of both women of him.

By this judgment Solomon gained the esteem and veneration of the people, for they truly felt from his judgment in this problem that God had given him wisdom, to execute just judgments among the members of his people.
We notice that although the two women were harlots, Solomon did not refuse to arbitrate between them because of their evil, but issued a just judgment.

God is ready to give you discernment and wisdom in all your affairs, with a simplicity and power that astonish those around you. Only rely on Him and seek Him, and He will guide you in all your steps.
The wisdom of Solomon and the greatness of his kingdom
All Israel: because the kingdom expanded in his days to its farthest limits, reaching from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.
Solomon was distinguished in his management of the kingdom, so he appointed officials in every sector to manage the affairs of the kingdom, as mentioned in these verses.

Azariah the son of Zadok the priest: he was the grandson of Zadok and the son of Ahimaaz (1 Chr 6:9). He is attributed as the son of Zadok because of Zadok's fame. He was one of the senior officials in the reign of Solomon. The writer of the book did not mention the post he was entrusted with, but his appearing at the head of the list suggests that he was regarded as the first official, that is, a chief minister or prime minister, in addition to his priestly work. He may have been the priest in Gibeon before the building of the house of the Lord was completed, while Zadok was in Jerusalem.

Elihoreph and Ahiah the sons of Shisha: scribes, that is, they recorded the laws of the state and did secretarial work. Shisha, their father, who is also called Shavsha and Sheva in (2 Sam 20:25) and Seraiah in (2 Sam 8:17), was a scribe to King David and to Solomon after him, and his two sons inherited this post from him.

Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud: he held the post of recorder in the reigns of both David and Solomon, as mentioned in (2 Sam 8:16 and 20:24 and 1 Chr 18:15), and his task was to keep records of contemporary events as a record of history.

Benaiah the son of Jehoiada: one of the commanders of the army from the days of David, famous for his courage (2 Sam 23:20-23). He was a faithful friend to Solomon who stood by his side against Adonijah's rebellion, and after Joab was killed he took his place at the head of the army. He was also responsible for protecting the royal palace and the king, that is, he was like the commander of the royal guard.

Zadok and Abiathar: Zadok is the son of Ahitub, of the descendants of Eleazar the son of Aaron. He was one of the two great priests in the days of David, and Abiathar, who is also called Ahimelech, was the other priest (2 Sam 8:17). When Adonijah wanted to seize the kingship, Zadok remained faithful to David, but Abiathar sided with Adonijah, so Solomon expelled him from the priesthood and Zadok alone remained the great priest.

It is noticed that the name of Abiathar appears as high priest together with Zadok although Solomon had removed him. This is explained by the fact that Solomon prevented him from practicing the priestly work but left him the title without the work, in appreciation of his previous great services in the days of David his father and because he was anointed as a priest.

Azariah the son of Nathan: he is also called Azariah. He is the son of the brother of King Solomon, that is, Solomon was his uncle; Solomon appointed him overseer over the twelve officers who will be mentioned in detail (vv. 7-19). Zabud the son of Nathan: he is the son of Nathan the prophet. He was a close friend of Solomon and so was called a priest, not in the sense that he served as a priest in the Temple of God, but because he was close to the king as the priest is close to God. The same meaning was said before in (2 Sam 8:18) that David's sons were priests, that is, close to the king and his helpers. And it was mentioned that he was a priest and the king's friend, that is, he was an adviser to the king and one of those close to him.

Ahishar: an official in charge of the affairs of Solomon's house, as Joseph was over the house of Potiphar, distinguished in his ordering of the house, so that the queen of Sheba was greatly impressed by the ordering of Solomon's house (ch. 10). Adoniram the son of Abda: he is the same as Adoram mentioned in (2 Sam 20:24), and is also called Hadoram in (2 Chr 10:18). He remained in his post throughout the reign of Solomon and Rehoboam, and he is the one whom Rehoboam king of Judah sent to Israel, and the children of Israel stoned him with stones and he died. He was responsible for putting people to work on state projects by forced labor, that is, without pay, such as the building of the house of the Lord, and then the king's house, and he gave them only their food, so he was hated by the people, and therefore his life ended in death by stoning.

We see that the administrative organization in the reign of Solomon took first place before the military organization, because peace prevailed in his reign, which gave him an opportunity to advance the kingdom, unlike David, in whose days wars were many and the kingdom accordingly expanded at his hands.

Managing any work needs order, so I wish that you would manage your own affairs and your work with order, distributing responsibilities and not interfering in everything yourself, lest you cancel the responsibilities of those around you and become burdened with responsibilities.
They provided food: gathered food, and the word "mira" means food.

The king appointed twelve officers, each over a region of the lands of the children of Israel, to gather food for the king's house. What is meant by the king's house is the households belonging to him and the feasts he gave for his helpers and guests, which were a great deal. These officers gathered it without charge from the people, and the people were content because of the abundance of good things with which God had blessed them in the days of Solomon. Each officer gathered food from his region to supply the needs of the king's house one month of the year, that is, the year was divided among twelve officers. The names of the officers and the districts they were responsible for:
The officer, the district: 10B - the son of Hur, Mount Ephraim 1B. The land of the tribe of Ephraim, extending from Jerusalem to Jezreel. It was later called Samaria.
213B - the son of Deker, Makaz and Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan 2B. Shaalbim or Shaalbin: a city in the tribe of Dan.
Beth-shemesh: a city in the portion of the tribe of Issachar.
Elon-beth-hanan: a town in the portion of the tribe of Dan.
314B - the son of Hesed 3B. Aruboth and Sochoh and all the land of Hepher, which is in the plain of Sharon, and these are lands west of the Jordan, southwest of Jerusalem.

415B - the son of Abinadab, all the region of Dor 4B. Son-in-law of the king, he married the daughter of Solomon. Dor: a city on the Mediterranean Sea, 13 km north of Caesarea, and its name is "Tafah"; it was given to the tribe of Manasseh.

Solomon used to encourage marriages between his assistants and his daughters, because this ensures the political stability of the kingdom. 516B - Baana the son of Ahilud, Taanach and Megiddo and all Beth-shean, which is beside Zarethan, below Jezreel 5B. He is also the brother of Jehoshaphat. From Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the place beyond Jokneam.
The recorder. Taanach: the mound of Taanach, which lies on the southern edge of the plain of Jezreel, that is, in the middle of Israel.
Megiddo: it lies 30 km southeast of Haifa in the tribe of Issachar.
Beth-shean: a city 8 km west of the Jordan River, attached to the tribe of Manasseh.
Zarethan: a village east of Jezreel in the land of the tribe of Manasseh.
Jezreel: a triangular plain in the middle of the land of the children of Israel.
Abel-meholah: in the Jordan valley.
The place beyond Jokneam: a city adjacent to the Jordan River on its western bank.
617B - the son of Geber 6B. Ramoth-gilead, the towns of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, and the region of Argob, which is in Bashan: threescore great cities with walls and brasen bars.
Ramoth-gilead: that is, the heights of Gilead, a city of the tribe of Gad east of the Jordan.
The towns of Jair the son of Manasseh: a group of villages in the northwestern part of Bashan.
Gilead: a mountainous region east of the Jordan (half of Mount Gilead was given to Reuben and Gad and the rest of Gilead to the half tribe of Manasseh.

Argob: a region in Bashan that included 60 fortified cities (Deut 3:4), which Jair the son of Manasseh took, so the place was called Havoth-jair, that is, the village of Jair or the villages of the sons of Manasseh.
718B - Ahinadab the son of Iddo 7B. Mahanaim, a city east of the Jordan, half of it belonging to Gad and the other half to Manasseh, north of the river Jabbok.
819B - Ahimaaz, Naphtali 8B, the son of Zadok the high priest. The lands of the tribe of Naphtali.
In the days of David, he used to inform him of the plans of Absalom.
He married "Basmath" the daughter of Solomon"
920B - Baanah the son of Hushai 9B. Asher and Aloth: he is the son of Hushai the Archite. Aloth: a place in the portion of Asher.
The wise and faithful counselor of David who scattered the counsel of Ahithophel.
1021B - Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, Issachar 10B. 1122B - Shimei the son of Elah, Benjamin 11B. A Benjamite, one of David's mighty men.
1223B - Geber the son of Uri 12B. The southern part of the land of Gilead; the land of Gilead is east of the Jordan and was originally that of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan.

Solomon's wisdom is noticed in placing Geber and his son (vv. 13, 19) as officers over two adjacent districts, to make cooperation between them easy, so that Solomon would reach better results from their work. We also find that nine officers worked west of the Jordan and only three were east of the Jordan, because of the smallness of the area belonging to the people of God there. These three officers are the son of Geber (v. 13), Ahinadab (v. 14), and Geber the son of Uri (v. 19). Over all these officers was one general overseer, Azariah the son of Nathan, as stated in v. 5.

It is recorded of Solomon here, along with his wisdom, his ability to organize the state, for he appointed to each responsibility the person suited to it, so that everything went in right order. We too, along with our submission and our faith in the blessing of the Lord in the ordering of things, must manage the affairs of our life and organize our matters with prudence and wisdom, and then leave the Lord to accomplish every matter according to His will.

It is mentioned here that the people of God were very many, and the tribe of Judah is singled out for mention because it occupied a large area and from it came David, from whose descendants Christ came. Thus God's promise to Abraham of a multitude of descendants was fulfilled (Gen 22:17), and an abundance of good things, so they were in continual joy.
The increase in number in the days of Solomon was a symbol of the increase of the descendants of Abraham who would believe in Christ in the whole world in the New Testament.

The divine promise to the people of God was likewise fulfilled, for Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the great river, that is, the river Euphrates, to the river of Egypt, which lies at its border near El-Arish, and it is a seasonal river of flood waters in Sinai and not the Nile. The compulsory gifts, which were considered as tribute from the people, were a cause of the increase in the state's resources, in addition to the fact that forced labor provided the state with much money.
Measure (cor): a measure equal to 229 liters.
Fine flour: the choice flour.
Harts: plural of hind, a kind of deer.
Fallowdeer: animals of the deer family.
Roebucks: the singular is roebuck, which is the gazelle.

What the palace and those living in it, those granted the honor of sitting at the king's table, and the guests and great invitees required was a large quantity of food and drink in one day, as follows: 30 measures of fine flour, 60 measures of meal, 10 fat oxen, 20 oxen out of the pastures, 100 sheep, and large numbers of harts, animals, and fatted fowl.
This means that Solomon's table sufficed to feed about 4000 persons, and he here is a type of Christ, who satisfied 4000 persons with seven loaves and a few small fishes.
This side the river: the lands lying west of the river Euphrates.
Tiphsah: an anciently known city lying west of the river Euphrates.
Gaza: a well-known city on the Mediterranean Sea near the border of Egypt.
Dan: it lies at the far north of the land of the Jews.
Beersheba: a city lying at the far south of Judea.

In the days of Solomon the promises of the Lord to the fathers were fulfilled, for his authority extended from the river Euphrates in the east to the Mediterranean Sea and the border of Egypt in the west, and from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, and all the kings of the countries surrounding his kingdom submitted to him and made peace with him and gave him gifts and money. So the children of Israel, that is, the tribe of Judah and the rest of the tribes, lived in peace, enjoying the good things of the rich land such as vines and figs. The tribe of Judah is mentioned because of its large number and not because it was divided from the rest of the tribes in the days of Solomon.
The people of God were satisfied and safe in the days of Solomon, and Solomon is a type of the believers in the New Testament over whom Christ reigns, so they enjoy spiritual satisfaction and peace.
Stall: the place set apart for putting the animals' food in.

Solomon's wealth is shown here, for he had forty thousand stalls for feeding his horses, and he also had twelve thousand horsemen to ride these horses. The multiplying of horses is contrary to the Law, because God wanted them to rely on Him and not on their military strength through a multitude of horsemen and horses (Deut 17:16).
Steeds: the good horses.

The officers previously appointed over the twelve districts supplied the needs of the royal palace - as mentioned before - each in his month, so the palace lacked nothing. Those responsible for supplying straw and barley brought it to the officers of the districts to send it to feed the king's horses, according to the times set for it, so that there would be food throughout the year for these animals.

I wish that you would thank God for the good things He prepares for you, so you enjoy them, for they are precious because they are from God, and so rejoice in God's love for you and give to the needy, and then the little that you have becomes much, and you are content, thankful, and loving to give.

God's grace to Solomon was very great, for his wisdom was great beyond all measure and he knew many things in various kinds of knowledge and was ready, with a wide heart, to solve all the problems brought to him, so that he expresses the breadth of his wisdom and heart by the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted; so varied were the knowledge and learning by which he was distinguished.

Long-suffering is a great virtue, so I wish that you would care for it, and so listen well to everyone around you however weak they are in expressing themselves, encouraging them with your smile, giving rest to their hearts, so that they find Christ in you.
The children of the east country: they were distinguished by wisdom, like the friends of Job and the magi and the Chaldeans in the days of Daniel.
The wisdom of Egypt: Egypt was famous for wise men, as it was in the days of Joseph and Moses.
Ethan the Ezrahite: from the clan of Zerah of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 2:6), famous for his wisdom, and he is the writer of the three sons of Mahol:
Heman: the son of Mahol the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, known for his great wisdom, and he is the composer of Psalm 88.

Chalcol: the son of Mahol, who was also among the wisest men of his time (1 Chr 2:6). Darda: the son of Mahol, who was also famous for wisdom (1 Chr 2:6). Of course there were wise men in various parts of the earth, whether among the children of the east or in Egypt, but the wisdom that Solomon enjoyed surpassed the wisdom of all these. His wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all men, among them Ethan the Ezrahite and Heman and Chalcol and Darda the sons of Mahol. And his fame and wisdom spread in all the surrounding nations.

Solomon's wisdom appeared in the many proverbs he uttered, which numbered three thousand proverbs, and in the songs he composed, which numbered a thousand and five. Some of these proverbs and songs were placed in the Book of Proverbs in the Holy Bible. We also know that the Book of Proverbs is not all the work of Solomon, as is written in the book.

Hyssop: a small plant that climbs on rocks and walls, from which bunches are made that are used in Jewish rites to dip in blood and sprinkle with. Some see that it is the thyme plant. Creeping things: reptiles.

His knowledge reached to understanding the properties of the earth and the world of plants, and he described many kinds of them, from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that springs out of the wall, that is, from the greatest trees such as the cedar to the smallest plants such as hyssop.
