God's honoring of the righteous David by giving him Asa, his righteous descendant, shows the standing of the saints with God even after their death. God preserved the kingship for David over the kingdom of Judah for 400 years, and after that He permitted the Babylonian captivity as discipline for them, but from his offspring came Christ, who reigns forever.

The reason for God's honoring David was his uprightness in the worship of God and his keeping away from evils, except on a few occasions, the most important of which was his fall into the sin of adultery with the wife of Uriah the Hittite and then the killing of her husband. But he repented quickly, for he did not persist in his sins and he loved God with all his heart. The mention of his sin here shows the mercies of God, and that every man is exposed to error, but if he repents God lifts his sin from him. God calls us to be careful: if the saints were exposed to falling, how much more the ordinary man! But the important thing is to hold fast to God, as David held fast to Him and rejected the worship of idols.
God opens the door of hope before you, however great your sins, so that you may return to Him quickly, obtain His mercies, regain your life with Him in holy worship and enjoy fellowship with Him.
The First Book of Kings

entries.section: (1) Abijam the son of Rehoboam, king over Judah

paragraphs.text: This verse returns to confirm the bad relations between the two parts of the kingdom, Judah and Israel, for disputes and wars between them began from the time of Rehoboam and Jeroboam, as was mentioned earlier in (ch. 14:30), and the details of these wars are found in (2 Chr 13).

entries.section: (1) Abijam the son of Rehoboam, king over Judah

paragraphs.text: The wars between the kingdoms of Israel and Judah continued not only in the days of Rehoboam but also in the days of his son Abijam (ch. 14:30), but when Abijam took refuge in God, He gave him strength, so he triumphed over Jeroboam and called his people to return to God, as is mentioned in (2 Chr 13), and Jeroboam did not return to fight Abijam after Abijam's victory over him. The rest of the life of Abijam is recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah, which is a book in which the records of the kings were written, other than the book of Chronicles that is in the Holy Bible.

entries.section: (1) Abijam the son of Rehoboam, king over Judah

paragraphs.text: The reign of Abijam was very short, three years, after which he died and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Asa reigned in his place.

After the death of Abijam, his son Asa reigned in his place over the kingdom of Judah, and this was in the twentieth year of the reign of Jeroboam, or the twentieth year of the division of the kingdom. We notice that Abijam reigned three years, from the eighteenth year to the twentieth of the reign of Jeroboam, because part of a year is counted as a year, which means that Abijam reigned less than three years.

God kept the kingship for the offspring of David despite the evil of Rehoboam and his son Abijam, and then came the righteous Asa. In Israel, however, the kingship changed among nine families over two and a half centuries, because all of them fell into evil.

The reign of Asa in Jerusalem was long, for he reigned 41 years, and this was a grace from God because he was righteous, so he was able to carry out many reforms during his long reign, a period longer than the reign of David and Solomon. The name of his grandmother, his father's mother, was Maachah the daughter of Absalom, and as we mentioned in (v. 2), a grandmother is sometimes called the mother, the meaning being the grandmother, and she is mentioned here because her personality was The First Book of Kings strong and dominated Rehoboam her husband and Abijam her son by her evil; but Asa did not submit to her, rather he removed her, as will appear in (v. 13).
The sodomites: those who practice sexual perversion as the passive partner.

The righteousness of Asa appeared in his cleansing his land of the worship of idols, for he removed all the idol worship that his father Abijam and his forefather Rehoboam had made. He also removed all the sins connected with these forms of worship, such as fornication and sexual perversion, so Asa removed the houses set apart for the practice of these sins, which were established beside the temples of the idols. But he was not able to remove all the houses of the sodomites, as is proved by the existence of some of them in the days of his son Jehoshaphat (ch. 22:46); but at least he was much better than his father and his forefather.
An idol in a grove: the grove was a pillar of wood or stone with a statue at its top of the goddess Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians.
The brook Kidron: a valley lying east of the city of Jerusalem, between it and the Mount of Olives, in which there was worship of pagan gods.

Asa was concerned to remove everything that encouraged the worship of idols. Despite the strength of his grandmother Maachah, who encouraged the worship of idols and had set up an idol in a grove for the worship of the goddess Ashtoreth, Asa deposed her, so that she dwelt in a private dwelling far from the palace, in order to nullify her authority and influence. Then he destroyed the wooden idol of the grove, burned it with fire and scattered its ashes in the valley of Kidron, where the pagan gods were worshiped, as a disdain and defilement of this worship.

Asa walked in the worship of God alone and removed the idols from Jerusalem and the places near it, but he did not remove all the high places around Jerusalem, which had begun in the days of Solomon (2 Chr 14:3). On these high places, in his days, the worship of God was offered, although this was an error against the Law, which commanded that worship be offered in the temple of God alone (Deut 12:11), in addition to the fact that in the days of Rehoboam and Abijam they offered worship to idols on the high places. This shows that Asa was righteous in removing the worship of idols, but not completely.

Abijam had triumphed over Jeroboam king of Israel and taken from him much spoil, which he sanctified to the Lord, and he placed in the treasuries of the house of the Lord quantities of gold and silver and the vessels made of them. Likewise his son Asa triumphed over Zerah the Ethiopian (2 Chr 14:9-15) and sanctified, that is, set apart, his spoils of war of gold and silver and placed them in the treasuries of the house of the Lord. This shows his love for the house of the Lord and not for his personal luxury.

Baasha rose up and killed Nadab the son of Jeroboam and all the offspring of Jeroboam, and reigned over Israel, and there were many wars between him and Asa for most of the days of Asa. The land had rest for only ten years (2 Chr 14:1).
Ramah: a small village built on a high plateau near the border of the tribe of Benjamin, ten kilometers north of Jerusalem on the road to Bethel.
Baasha began his preparations to fight the kingdom of Judah by building a village called Ramah very close to Jerusalem, for the following reasons:
1- To make it easy to attack Jerusalem.
2- Ramah was on a main road from Bethel to Jerusalem, and he wanted to prevent any trade with Jerusalem.
The First Book of Kings
3- To prevent the inhabitants of Israel from going to pray and keep the feasts in Jerusalem, lest they be influenced and follow King Asa.
4- To prevent the emigration of those of the inhabitants of Israel who wished to live near Jerusalem.

Ben-hadad: He is Ben-hadad the First, the grandson of Hezion, who may be the same as Rezon who seized Damascus and opposed Solomon (ch. 11:23, 25). There is more than one king of Syria by this name: the second Ben-hadad was in the days of Ahab king of Israel, and the third was in the days of Jehoahaz king of Judah (ch. 20:1-34, 2 Kgs 13:3-13). Syria: present-day Syria.

This was one of the errors of Asa, for he did not turn to the Lord but to Ben-hadad king of Damascus to help him against Baasha. He gathered the gold and silver that were in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and the treasuries of his palace and gave them to the men with whom he sent a message to Ben-hadad. The quantities of gold and silver remaining in the treasuries were small, and they were what Abijam and Asa had gathered as spoil in their wars, because Shishak king of Egypt had taken the gold and silver from the treasuries before that (ch. 14:26). By this Asa gave the sacred things of God to the pagans, and that angered God.

In his message Asa reminded him of the alliance existing between them as it had existed between their fathers, and he presented him with gifts of silver and gold, asking him to break his covenant with Baasha king of Israel so that the latter would withdraw from fighting him. This, of course, was an error on the part of Asa. For instead of praying and relying on God, he asked Ben-hadad, a mighty king neighboring the two kingdoms, to support him, and he sent him gifts. Hanani the seer rebuked Asa for this conduct (2 Chr 16:7-10).

Whatever the threats or difficult circumstances you meet, do not take refuge in the world and its powers, but in God, for He alone is your helper, and let not your heart be troubled, because God who is with you is stronger than all. Pray first, and God will guide you to what you can use of the material things around you.
Ijon: a city in the northern part of the land of the children of Israel.
Abel-beth-maachah: a fortified city in Naphtali.

Cinneroth: a fortified city in Naphtali, known as the plain of Gennesaret (Mt 14:34). Ben-hadad heeded the call of King Asa and commanded his armies, and they attacked the cities of Israel and destroyed the cities of Ijon, Dan and Abel-beth-maachah and all the region of Cinneroth and all the land of Naphtali.

When Ben-hadad attacked the kingdom of Israel and seized some of its cities, Baasha was afraid and stopped building the city of Ramah, because he felt that Ben-hadad had broken the covenant with him and allied himself with Asa, and he feared that Ben-hadad would continue to overrun the cities of Israel. He could not fight two adversaries at the same time, Syria and Judah, so he withdrew and dwelt in his capital Tirzah.
None was exempted: he exempted no one from coming and taking part in the building.
Geba of Benjamin: a city in Benjamin on the northern edge of the kingdom of Judah. Today there is a village of the same name 6.5 km northeast of Jerusalem and close to Ramah.
Mizpah: a city in Benjamin that Asa fortified. The prophet Samuel used to live in it (1 Sam 7:16, 17). It is near Ramah, about 1.5 km away, and about 13 km from Jerusalem.

The First Book of Kings King Asa summoned all the men of the people and exempted no one from coming, to gather what Baasha had left of the stones and timber that he had intended to use in building Ramah, and King Asa used them to build the two cities "Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah."

The writer of the book teaches us that there are other details of the reign of Asa recorded in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah," and he also tells us that Asa was afflicted with a disease in his feet in the time of his old age. Details about the life of Asa are found in (2 Chr 14, 15, 16).
Asa died and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Jehoshaphat succeeded him on the throne of Judah.

entries.section: (3) Nadab and Baasha reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: In the second year of Asa king of Judah, Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel, and his reign was very short, for he reigned only two years, which in reality is less than two years, that is, one year and some months, because he began to reign in the second year of Asa and Baasha succeeded him in the third year of Asa.

entries.section: (3) Nadab and Baasha reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: Nadab walked in the way of his father Jeroboam, in the worship of the two golden calves, and he prevented the people from going to Jerusalem and worshiping in the temple of the Lord.

entries.section: (3) Nadab and Baasha reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: Gibbethon: the name of a town in the portion of Dan. It lies directly east of Ekron, near the Mediterranean Sea, in the south of the land of the children of Israel.
Nadab was besieging Gibbethon, trying to recover it from the Philistines, because the Philistines had taken it from the children of Israel, and Baasha plotted against him and killed him there.

entries.section: (3) Nadab and Baasha reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: Nadab was killed in the third year of Asa king of Judah, and Baasha reigned in his place. Here begins the series of assassinations in the kingdom of Israel, which occurred nine times, and all of them were wicked and tried to seize the kingship from one another.

V. 29: The first thing Baasha did when he took the kingship was to kill all the offspring of Jeroboam and destroy his house completely, so the prophecy that Ahijah the Shilonite prophesied was fulfilled (ch. 14:10, 11). The First Book of Kings

entries.section: (3) Nadab and Baasha reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: That was a punishment for the sins of Jeroboam and for his driving his people into the same errors, when they worshiped pagan gods, forsaking the Lord their true God; by that they brought the wrath of the Lord upon themselves.

entries.section: (3) Nadab and Baasha reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: The writer of the book mentions that there is a civil history of the period of Nadab's reign written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel," in which other details about the life of Nadab are mentioned.

entries.section: (3) Nadab and Baasha reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: As we saw in the preceding verses, there were wars between Asa king of Judah and Baasha king of Israel throughout the days of their reign; the era of peace had ended in the wake of Solomon's reign, and there were many wars between the kings of Judah and the kings of Israel, because of the two peoples' departure from God. The war meant is not only a great war, for the great war was in the sixteenth year of the reign of Asa, and the rest of the time there were skirmishes, and of course these wars weakened the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, which helped the surrounding nations to prevail over them. Perhaps the kingdom of Israel, despite its large size, felt its weakness because the temple of God was not in it, and therefore it feared the small kingdom of Judah and tried to attack it from time to time.

God was long-suffering with Jeroboam, but in the end the divine punishment had to be carried out by the destruction of his offspring who persisted in evil. Do not despise the long-suffering of God, but turn back from your sin, for He is merciful and ready to forgive it, however great or repeated it may be, and learn from the errors of others so as to keep away from them, and you will live in assurance.

entries.section: (3) Nadab and Baasha reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: In the third year of the reign of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over the kingdom of Israel, and the capital of his kingdom was "Tirzah," and he remained king for 24 years.

entries.section: (3) Nadab and Baasha reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: Baasha walked in the way of evil as Jeroboam walked, and he did not depart from the sin of the worship of idols which Jeroboam had devised, but he led his people Israel after him in the same crooked way. The kings of Israel from Baasha to Ahab

Jehu the son of Hanani: He is the son of Hanani the seer who rebuked Asa (2 Chr 16:7) and dwelt in Jerusalem. He probably rebuked Baasha at the end of his reign, and also rebuked Jehoshaphat king of Judah for supporting the wicked King Ahab (2 Chr 19:2, 3). The prophet Jehu came before Baasha king of Israel with all boldness to rebuke him for his evil, hoping he would repent. This was at the end of Baasha's life, after he had worshiped idols and led the people astray for many years. God showed Baasha His favor to him in raising him out of the dust, for he was of the common people, and God granted him to reign over Israel. God makes clear to him that his reigning was by His permission and not by Baasha's own strength, but sadly after he became king he did not submit to God, who had given him the grace of kingship; rather he angered Him by the worship of the idols that Jeroboam had set up, and he led the people astray after him, and they provoked God and defied Him. Yet God still says "My people" despite their sins, because He is a tender and merciful Father.

The divine judgment on the sins of Baasha was to take away and destroy his offspring, as God destroyed the offspring of Jeroboam by the hand of Baasha, and their corpses would be cast out in the city, to be eaten by the dogs, and in the fields, to be eaten by the birds of prey. This is a disgrace to these kings and their offspring, because they angered God. Baasha killed the offspring of Jeroboam out of hatred for Jeroboam and not out of obedience to God; therefore God disciplines him by destroying his offspring also, just as Babylon disciplined the kingdom of Judah, but God afterward punished Babylon by means of the Medes and Persians, because it did not discipline Judah in obedience to God but out of greed and evil.
All this rebuke shows:
1- The boldness of the prophet Jehu.
2- His purpose, which was to call Baasha and his offspring to repentance.

3- Lifting their eyes to eternity: although they would reign, they would die in a shameful manner, so that perhaps they would take heed during their reign and regain their eternity by returning to God.

4- Reminding Baasha that the judgment that was passed on Jeroboam and his offspring, and that Baasha carried out by destroying them and treating their corpses with contempt (ch. 14:1-16), is the very same judgment passed on him, so that perhaps he would take heed and repent.

5- God's fatherhood and tenderness toward His people, whom the wicked kings of Israel had led astray, still remain, and He calls them "My people," so that perhaps they would take heed, return to Him and leave the worship of idols.

Be attentive to what happens in your life and to the words of God that you read in the Holy Bible, for they are personal messages to you, calling you to return to God, so that you may live with Him and save yourself from many troubles on earth, and then have a place in heaven.
All the acts of Baasha are written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel."
Tirzah: It was the center of the kingdom of the ten tribes of Israel for about fifty years. It is ten kilometers northeast of the city of Shechem, that is, Nablus.
Baasha died after a reign of twenty-four years, as mentioned in (ch. 15:23), and was buried in "Tirzah," the capital of his kingdom, and his son Elah succeeded him on the throne.

Here He confirms the punishment of God that He announced by the hand of the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani in (vv. 2, 3), as a result of the sins of Baasha and of his son Elah, who reigned after him for only two years, for the following reasons:
1- The worship of the idols that Jeroboam set up.

2- His violence and cruelty in killing the offspring of Jeroboam; and when this verse speaks of his killing Jeroboam, it means his killing his offspring. Although God had permitted this as a punishment for Jeroboam, Baasha did all this in order to have the kingship to himself, so that no one of the offspring of Jeroboam would oppose him, and he was very cruel in destroying them.
3- He committed many evils, motivated by selfishness and various lusts.
For this reason God permitted the destruction of all the offspring of Baasha, exactly as Baasha did to Jeroboam; so it was done to him.

entries.section: (2) Elah the son of Baasha, king of Israel

paragraphs.text: Elah succeeded his father Baasha on the throne of Israel, and this was in the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah. The capital of his kingdom was "Tirzah," and his reign was short, for he reigned only two years, and in truth he did not complete two years, because it is mentioned that Zimri, who killed him, reigned after him in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of Asa (v. 15), and part of a year is counted as a year.

entries.section: (2) Elah the son of Baasha, king of Israel

paragraphs.text: Conspired: plotted and rose in revolt against him.
Zimri his servant: those who worked for the king were called his servants, whatever their positions.

One of the commanders of his army conspired against him, Zimri, captain of half his chariots. When Elah was in "Tirzah," drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, his steward who was appointed over his house, Zimri broke into the house and killed him, and this was in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and Zimri took the throne.

This shows the extent of the corruption that had spread in the kingdom of Israel: the king was occupied with his own pleasures and immersed in drinking wine, while at the same time treachery spread. So Zimri, who was trained for war, being a senior officer in the army and commander of half the chariots, attacked the king and killed him while he was drunk. Instead of the king being a leader of his army, which was fighting the Philistines (v. 15), he was absorbed in his pleasures. Perhaps the killing of King Elah was a plot agreed upon between Zimri and Arza, for there was a party among the people that followed Zimri, and perhaps Arza was one of its members, as will appear in the following verses that this party would stand against the party of Omri.

Do not be absorbed in the pleasures of the world and its evil lusts and be deceived by them, for their end is destruction. Beware of Satan, who puts poison in honey, and keep away from everything that leads you to sin and seek God, and you will delight in fellowship with Him and be always happy.

entries.section: (2) Elah the son of Baasha, king of Israel

paragraphs.text: His kinsfolk: his relatives and friends and everyone who could avenge his death.
Him that pisseth against a wall: every male of his offspring.

God had sent the prophet Jehu to warn Baasha, but he paid no heed to the words of the Lord, so the time of divine punishment came, and as soon as Zimri sat on the throne he set about destroying all the relatives, friends and kinsfolk of Baasha, leaving him no relative or friend to avenge his blood, and thus the word of the Lord which He had spoken was fulfilled. The destruction of the offspring of Baasha was the natural result of his sins and of his leading astray the people of the kingdom of Israel, exactly as Jeroboam led Israel astray by the worship of idols, so God permitted the destruction of his offspring, and this shows:
1- The cruelty and violence of Zimri in destroying the offspring of Baasha.
2- The justice and vengeance of God: as Baasha did to the offspring of Jeroboam, so Zimri did to his offspring.
3- The certainty that the word of God will be carried out: He is long-suffering, but His word must be fulfilled, as He announced to Baasha by the mouth of the prophet Jehu.

entries.section: (2) Elah the son of Baasha, king of Israel

paragraphs.text: The rest of the acts of Elah are written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel," which is a civil book, other than the books of Chronicles that are in the Holy Bible.

In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned in "Tirzah," but his reign lasted only one week. The army of Israel at that time was besieging "Gibbethon," which the Philistines had seized, and it seems that the dispute over Gibbethon continued for many years, for here it is mentioned that it was under siege, and also 26 years earlier, in (ch. 15:27), it was under siege in the days of Nadab the son of Jeroboam.

With the killing of Elah the second dynasty that reigned over Israel came to an end; the first dynasty was the dynasty of Jeroboam and the second was the dynasty of Baasha, and then Zimri reigned, who continued in the kingship only a few days. (See the list of the kings of Judah and Israel at the end of the book.)

The soldiers of the kingdom of Israel encamped against Gibbethon heard that Zimri had revolted against King Elah and killed him. It seems that Zimri was not loved by the whole army, so the soldiers besieging Gibbethon, who belonged to Omri, were angry at Zimri's killing of Elah, because Elah was peaceable even though he did not care for the kingdom. So they rose to avenge his blood and made Omri king over them, and they left Gibbethon and moved toward Tirzah, the capital of the kingdom, and besieged it. Tirzah was a beautiful city but unfortified, and they intended to seize Zimri and kill him after they had made Omri king, for it was in their plan to kill Zimri after enthroning Omri. Perhaps when Omri saw Zimri killing the servants and officers of King Elah, he feared for himself that Zimri would kill him, so he led the army to put an end to him.

When King Zimri saw that his capital Tirzah was under siege, since the city was unfortified and easy to storm, he was certain that Omri would seize him and even make a public spectacle of him for killing King Elah, who had preceded him. Therefore he set fire to the palace in which he dwelt, and he took his own life, and the great palace burned. Perhaps he wished that Omri should not enjoy this magnificent palace.
Thus we see that the result of the treachery and killing which Zimri committed came quickly upon his head, and he died a hard death, that is, burned in fire.

Do not be dazzled by positions and possessions so that you walk in evil to reach them. God is just, and He sees your deeds and will punish you for them, and if He is long-suffering for a time, the punishment will be harder. Be sure that evil never gives rest or happiness, but being with God and walking in His commandments is the only thing that gives you stability, assurance and happiness.

The death of Zimri in this terrible manner was a divine punishment for his sins of the worship of idols, violence and injustice, not only in his earlier life but after he became king over Israel, and by this he led the people astray and encouraged them to worship idols and do every evil. It is remarkable that this happened in only seven days, which shows that he was very wicked and began evil from the first day of his reign, so he provoked the Lord by his sins.
The details of the life of Zimri and the conspiracy that he led against Elah are written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel."

The people were divided into two parties, one party supporting Omri, who rose against Zimri, and the other party supporting Tibni, who had backed Zimri and opposed Omri's movement and his stirring up of the army against Zimri. The division continued for four years or a little more (vv. 15, 23), from the twenty-seventh year to the thirty-first of Asa, during which civil wars arose between the two parties, in which the strength of Omri and his army appeared over the other party, which had followed Zimri and was now led by Tibni. With time this party grew weak and Tibni died, either in one of the wars or from grief at what had become of him, and by this Omri was able to reign alone over Israel, for the army was with him, and it was of course stronger than the people who supported Tibni.

In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri reigned over Israel, and his reign lasted twelve years, and "Tirzah" was the capital of his kingdom in the first six years of his reign. These six years after the death of Zimri include the four years in which the struggle with Tibni and his party was intense (vv. 21, 22), and they are in truth less than six years by some months, since they began from the twenty-seventh year of King Asa until the thirty-second.
Two talents of silver: a talent of silver has several weights, ranging between 17 and 40 kg.

Samaria: It lies north of Jerusalem at a distance of 56 km, and Omri built it in the year 924 BC, and it continued until the captivity of Israel, when the Assyrians destroyed it in the year 722 BC; its place is now the city of Sebastia. It stood on a hill and so was easy to fortify, and it was suitable as a capital.

Omri bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer, who owned it, and built on it the city of Samaria, named after Shemer, and made it the capital of his kingdom. Thus the capital moved from Shechem, which had been the seat of the kingdom, to Tirzah, and then to Samaria.

Omri surpassed all who were before him in his deviation, and that of his people, from the way of the Lord. He walked in the way of Jeroboam and led the people to pagan worship, which angered the Lord, and perhaps the evil of Omri lay in pressing the people to worship the golden calves that Jeroboam had set up, which increased the people's error.

The acts of Omri were recorded as history in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel." History declares that Omri was a politically and militarily successful leader, but sadly he was far from God by his worship of idols.

Omri died and was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab succeeded him on the throne of Israel. Thus began the dynasty of Omri, which reigned a long time over Israel and was the most wicked of dynasties in the worship of idols and injustice (Mic 6:16).

Omri used the kingship to do evil more than all who were before him, so God punished him by destroying him and his offspring after a time. Be careful to use your abilities, your position and your circumstances to glorify God, to be joined to Him and to draw others to Him, and you will save yourself and those around you and have a place in heaven.

entries.section: (5) Ahab the son of Omri, king over Israel

paragraphs.text: In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria, and his reign lasted twenty-two years.

entries.section: (5) Ahab the son of Omri, king over Israel

paragraphs.text: Ahab did much evil, and the evils and sins that he committed during his reign exceeded the evils of all who sat on the throne of Israel before him and after him. Thus we find evil increasing: Omri did evil more than all who were before him, and his son Ahab learned from him and became more wicked than his father, and his pagan wife Jezebel, the daughter of the king of Sidon, helped him in that. What shows the enormity of Ahab's sins is that in his days the voice of God was clear by the mouth of the mighty Elijah, but he rejected the word of Elijah and persecuted him and tried to kill him, as will appear in the next chapter.

Beware, for the sins you commit affect your children, since you are an example. Therefore care for your relationship with God and for your repentance, and you will lead your children in the way of God.

entries.section: (5) Ahab the son of Omri, king over Israel

paragraphs.text: The Zidonians: the inhabitants of Sidon, a rich coastal city famous for trade and fishing, lying in present-day Lebanon.

Ahab was not content with following the way of Jeroboam in the worship of the two golden calves, but added to that by marrying "Jezebel," the daughter of "Ethbaal" king of Sidon, and it was she who drew him to the worship of Baal, her god, and to bow down to him. He built a house for Baal in Samaria and set up an altar, which he placed in it; that is, he spread the worship of Baal and encouraged it, and the worship of the two calves that Jeroboam had set up became open pagan worship and not a symbol of the worship of God. He persecuted the prophets and the believers and killed many of them (ch. 18:4). Ahab and Jezebel became a source of evil not only in the kingdom of Israel but in Judah also, because the daughter of Ahab, Athaliah, was married to the king of Judah, and she even took the kingship alone afterward.

entries.section: (5) Ahab the son of Omri, king over Israel

paragraphs.text: Ahab set up many groves for the worship of idols, so the Lord was angry with him because he increased in their worship more than all the kings of Israel who were before him.

entries.section: (5) Ahab the son of Omri, king over Israel

paragraphs.text: In his days Hiel the Bethelite built Jericho. There was a curse on whoever would build the city of Jericho, spoken by the mouth of Joshua the son of Nun, and everyone knew of this curse, but the fear of God was no longer before the children of Israel, so they despised the threats of God as they had despised His promises. More than 500 years had passed since the word of the Lord by the mouth of Joshua, but the Lord had not forgotten His word, so Abiram the firstborn son of Hiel died when he laid the foundations of the city, and his youngest son Segub died when he set up its gates, and probably the rest of his sons died afterward. Jericho had already been built as dwellings, as mentioned in (Josh 16:1, 7, 18:12), but what is meant here is its being built as a fortified city.
Elijah, the famine and the raising of the widow's son

entries.section: (1) Elijah withholds the rain and the ravens feed him

paragraphs.text: Elijah: a name meaning "My God is Jehovah."

Ahab went to the furthest extent in the worship of idols. He was not content with the worship of the golden calves that Jeroboam had made, but worshiped Baal abundantly, to the degree that he had 850 prophets of Baal and of the groves. His pagan wife Jezebel helped and encouraged him in that, so he was in truth the most wicked of the kings of Israel, and by this he drew his people away from the worship of God. So God was compelled to discipline them in deed and not by mere warning, and the prophet Elijah appeared, after Ahab had killed the prophets of God and the rest had hidden for fear of him. Obadiah, who worked with the king, had hidden some of them and was feeding them. Elijah was one of the dwellers of the village of Tishbe in the region of Gilead, lying east of the Jordan, where there are many wildernesses, so he lived as an ascetic man who spent most of his life in the wilderness, which helped him to be courageous and to have a strong relationship with God, for he felt the presence of God, which kept him far from sin and gave him boldness in his service. The Holy Bible does not mention his father or his clan, so that some of the Jews thought that he was an angel, but the Apostle James affirms that he was a man like us (Jas 5:17). He was an apostle from God to proclaim His voice among the wicked people, like John the Baptist, who also lived in the wilderness and then appeared to prepare the way of Christ.

Elijah stood among the people before the wicked King Ahab in his capital Samaria and announced God's discipline of the whole people, for he commanded the heavens not to rain or give dew, and it continued for three years and six months (Jas 5:17), and this means:
1- A community in the whole land.
2- The authority of the children of God over nature.

This divine discipline shows the helplessness of the pagan gods on whom Ahab relied, chief among them Baal, for they could not lift the famine even if Ahab claimed that they were the source of goodness and fertility. Thus God brought them into an affliction unto death by hunger, that perhaps they would repent and return to Him.
It is understood from the epistle of James that Elijah prayed and then commanded the heavens and they obeyed him, so by prayer he drew on the power of God, who is able to do all things.
Elijah's saying "As the Lord lives, before whom I stand" means the following:
1- That God is living, while the idols have no life in them.
2- Elijah's constant feeling that he is before God, and this gives him fear of God, purity and strength.

Do not be afraid to proclaim the voice of God however much the obstinate stand before you, but be concerned to pray first, so that the words may be from God and you may keep your humility when you speak.

entries.section: (1) Elijah withholds the rain and the ravens feed him

paragraphs.text: The brook Cherith: a watercourse opposite the Jordan that flows into it from the east.

It was the divine plan that Elijah should hide so that the king would not know his place until the period of discipline ended, in order to give the people an opportunity to repent. So the Lord asked him to leave Samaria and go east of the Jordan to hide by the brook Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan. In the midst of the drought God provided him water from the stream of the brook Cherith and sent him food by the ravens.

Thus Elijah went far from Ahab and walked a long distance from Samaria and crossed the Jordan to live in the wilderness and complete his solitude and his worship of God. There, when the famine came and spread over all the land of the children of Israel, God did not forget His prophet Elijah, but sent the ravens to feed him. We notice several things in the ravens' feeding of Elijah:
1- God's authority over the birds: He turns the birds that snatch food from men into birds that bring it to them.
2- Ravens fear man, but here they approach quietly and serve him because God commanded them to do so.
3- From where did the ravens bring this delicious, prepared food! Only from God.

4- Ravens were among the unclean birds for the Jews, as the Law prescribes, but God turns them to the service of men, to declare that He is the Lord of the Law, who uses it or changes it according to the need of His children, and that the birds are clean in His sight, as will appear in the New Testament; in the Old Testament, however, He taught them some spiritual teachings, as a transitional stage to the New Testament, the covenant of grace.
5- The regularity of the ravens' coming at fixed times for many days declares God's perfect care for His children.
If God turned the unclean raven into a servant of His prophet, He is able to turn you, however great your evil, into a clean person, and even a servant in the Church, to care for His children.

entries.section: (1) Elijah withholds the rain and the ravens feed him

paragraphs.text: Elijah obeyed the word of God and went to the brook Cherith, and there he experienced the love of God and His care. He drank from the brook and the ravens fed him twice a day, morning and evening, with delicious food of bread and meat. It was delicious food because it was from God, so in his solitude he enjoyed God's care more than the prophets of Baal enjoyed the table of Jezebel, filled with luxurious foods every day (ch. 18:19). Thus God provided for Elijah with water from a small brook, Cherith, and not the great river Jordan, for God can care for the needs of His children even from small sources, as He afterward fed him by means of a poor widow.

Elijah lived in seclusion with God at the brook, and for most of the days of his life, so he had an opportunity for prayer and contemplation and a strong relationship with God, which helped him to stand courageously before the wicked King Ahab.

In proportion to your concern for your prayers, your readings and your meditations on the word of God, you are able to face the problems of life, serve God and proclaim His voice, whatever afflictions you meet, because God will support you and work through you, and you will always be strong.

entries.section: (1) Elijah withholds the rain and the ravens feed him

paragraphs.text: It came to pass after a period of time that the brook dried up, because the heavens had not rained at all during this period.

entries.section: (2) The widow of Zarephath of Sidon feeds Elijah

paragraphs.text: Zarephath: a small village lying on the Mediterranean Sea south of the city of Sidon, eight miles from it, on the road to Tyre.

After the famine increased because the waters of the rivers dried up, God commanded Elijah to leave the brook Cherith, which lies near his homeland Gilead east of the Jordan, and go to the village of Zarephath of Sidon, so he crossed the river Jordan and headed toward the Mediterranean Sea. This shows:
1- That God is able to provide for His prophet near his homeland, or in any country far from it, that is, in every place.

2- It also shows Elijah's obedience to God, for he went to the homeland of the wicked Jezebel, the daughter of the king of Sidon, and was not afraid of her violence, because God is able to protect him.
3- Likewise God declares that He is the God of all peoples, so He used the Gentiles to provide for His prophet, as He used the Jews.

4- There can be believers among the Gentiles better than all the people of the Jews who worshiped Baal; the woman of Zarephath of Sidon believed the word of the man of God Elijah, so God chose her out of all the women of the children of Israel to feed Elijah in the famine (Lk 4:26), for she was better in her faith than all the Jewish women.
5- God did not send Elijah to a king or a great ruler, but to a poor widow to feed him, because it is God who provides through men, for they are instruments in His hand.
This widow is a type of the Church, which is in an appearance of weakness, but God works in her because of her faith in Him, and she gathers the Gentiles as well as the Jews.

Elijah is a type of Christ, who goes to the Gentiles and asks them for His needs and blesses them, as Christ went to the Samaritan woman and asked her for water, and preached in Galilee of the Gentiles because His own rejected Him, as the people of God rejected Elijah and worshiped Baal (Jn 4).

entries.section: (2) The widow of Zarephath of Sidon feeds Elijah

paragraphs.text: At the entrance of the city he saw a woman gathering sticks, so he turned to her and asked her for a little water in a vessel to drink.

entries.section: (2) The widow of Zarephath of Sidon feeds Elijah

paragraphs.text: A morsel of bread: any kind of food, even a little. As she was going to fetch him water, as he had asked, he called to her, saying: Bring me, I pray thee, a morsel of bread in thine hand.

entries.section: (2) The widow of Zarephath of Sidon feeds Elijah

paragraphs.text: The barrel: a vessel in which flour is kept.

As the Lord thy God liveth: This Gentile widow had probably learned that Elijah was a Jew, or a prophet, from his language or his clothing, so she believed in his God that He is a great God, even though she had not rejected her pagan gods. The famine had spread to Tyre and Sidon, so the woman told him that she had no cake, or any bread, or food, but all she had was a little flour in a vessel and a little oil in a cruse, and that she was gathering a few sticks to cook on her fire, to make for herself and her son what they might eat, and thus what she had of food would be finished, and she and her son would be exposed to death by hunger.

The widow's words were a statement of the facts and not a complaint or grumbling, for she was calm, as is proved by her faith in the God of Elijah, which would appear in her obedience to his word and her great generosity, for she would give him out of her want, that is, the little she had, despite the spread of the famine.
Thus, as Abraham was a cause of blessing to all the earth, the wicked Ahab was a cause of curse and of the spread of famine in his land and in all the lands around him.

In proportion as you please God, He blesses your life and blesses those around you, and they love you for the sake of the blessing of God that has come upon them because of your being with them. Be confident in your God and rely on Him, for He keeps you, satisfies you and blesses you in every place.

entries.section: (2) The widow of Zarephath of Sidon feeds Elijah

paragraphs.text: Elijah reassured her and told her not to fear anything, and asked her to prepare for herself and her son what she had resolved, on condition that she first make him a little cake and bring it to him, and afterward make for herself and her son.

We ought to put God first, giving the firstfruits and the tithes, and trust that the blessing of God will bless the rest, so that it suffices and overflows, however difficult our material circumstances.

entries.section: (2) The widow of Zarephath of Sidon feeds Elijah

paragraphs.text: In the spirit of prophecy Elijah gave her a promise from God that the barrel of flour would not be emptied nor the cruse of oil fail until the drought ended and the rain fell. Thus we find Elijah witnessing for God and working a miracle among the Gentiles, and even near the homeland of Queen Jezebel, the wicked daughter of the king of Sidon, and this shows his courage and faithfulness in his service.

entries.section: (2) The widow of Zarephath of Sidon feeds Elijah

paragraphs.text: The woman did not doubt for a moment what Elijah had told her, and she relied on the promise of God and on the generosity and love of giving that characterized her, so she went and did as the prophet had told her, and food was supplied to her, so that she and her son ate for a long time, without the barrel of flour being emptied or the cruse of oil failing, exactly as the Lord had said by the mouth of Elijah. These days were about two years, that is, until the end of the famine.

Thus we see that the woman's giving out of her want made her receive a blessing and generous giving from God, which satisfied her and her son throughout the famine, and perhaps she also invited her relatives to eat with her, so that she was by this a preacher of God among her Gentile relatives.

entries.section: (3) Elijah raises the widow's son from the dead

paragraphs.text: After those events her only son was struck by a sudden illness, and the severity of the illness increased moment by moment until he died.

entries.section: (3) Elijah raises the widow's son from the dead

paragraphs.text: When the widow's son died she did not grumble, but this led her to repentance. For if the famine had come upon the earth and the rain had not fallen because of the sins of men, then the death of her son could be because of her sins. She felt that Elijah was a prophet, so she called him a man of God, and she also felt that he was righteous and she a sinner, not worthy of his presence in her house, so she confessed that she was a sinner and that the death of her son was a reminder to her of her sins so that she might repent. Thus we see how this widow was distinguished in her faith and repentance above all the people of God, for God sent Elijah to this woman and not to any other woman of the children of Israel, and worked this miracle of blessing the oil and the flour in her house, because of her distinction in faith in God. Although she was a Gentile, her repentance preceded the repentance of the people of God, for Ahab was still persisting in evil and the people of Israel were following him.

entries.section: (3) Elijah raises the widow's son from the dead

paragraphs.text: Elijah asked her to give him her son, so he took him from her arms and carried him up into a chamber on the roof, where he was staying, and laid the child on his bed. We understand from this the generosity of the widow, for she had given him a separate chamber on the roof in which to live in his freedom and continue his worship of God. We also see the faith of Elijah, who was not troubled by the death of the widow's son, but carried him in faith to the upper room and laid him on his bed to pray there, confident of God's power to raise this boy. Although he had not heard of a dead person being raised before this, he believed in the power of God, and perhaps the Holy Spirit guided him and encouraged him to pray that he might raise the boy from death.
Do not be troubled if adverse things or severe trials happen in your life, but take refuge in God by prayer and be confident that He will hear you and will not leave you.

entries.section: (3) Elijah raises the widow's son from the dead

paragraphs.text: Elijah prayed to God, reproaching Him with boldness, and said to Him: why have You done evil to this woman by killing her son, when she is a woman great in her faith, her obedience, her generosity, and then her repentance? Elijah was not troubled; on the contrary he spoke with boldness, confident that God hears him and will intervene.

entries.section: (3) Elijah raises the widow's son from the dead

paragraphs.text: The prophet stretched himself upon the child three times and cried out, calling upon the Lord, praying to Him, entreating that the soul of this child might come into him again.

He stretched himself upon him because he believed in the power of God that was in him and in God's ability to transfer this power to the boy so that he would live. He stretched himself three times in the name of the Holy Trinity, who is able to do all things, and his stretching himself three times also shows his perseverance in prayer.

From here we see the importance of the blessing of the saints and of touching anything connected with them, such as their relics, or the incense placed upon them on their feast days, for the blessing is a grace with which God distinguishes His children, so that they become a blessing to all around them. God supported Elijah with extraordinary miracles, for he was the first to bless food so that it became abundant and the first to raise a dead person, though he differs from Christ in that he prayed and the dead person rose, whereas Christ commanded with authority and then the dead person rose. All this divine support was because evil had spread intensely in the days of Elijah and most of the people of God had worshiped idols and there was no one to witness for God, so Elijah witnessed for Him with powerful miracles, he and Elisha after him.

entries.section: (3) Elijah raises the widow's son from the dead

paragraphs.text: The Lord heard the prayer of Elijah, and the soul of the child came into him again, and he lived.

Thus the affliction turned into a blessing; that is, the death of the boy was a blessing in the working of a great miracle for the first time in the history of mankind, namely the raising of a dead person, just as the want of bread in the widow's house turned into a blessing that never ended.

entries.section: (3) Elijah raises the widow's son from the dead

paragraphs.text: Elijah took the child and brought him down from the roof of the house into the house and delivered him to his mother, saying: See, thy son liveth.
Since it was a surprise to the woman to see her son standing on his feet, Elijah alerted her and encouraged her to rejoice and believe that her son had regained life.

entries.section: (3) Elijah raises the widow's son from the dead

paragraphs.text: Before this miracle that was accomplished by the hands of Elijah, the woman was certain that he was a man of God and that what he uttered of the words of the Lord was true, and she declared her faith in God.
The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: The drought continued three years until the word of the Lord came to Elijah, charging him to appear to Ahab, who had kept searching for Elijah while he was hidden throughout those years, and God promised him that He would end the period of drought and give rain. God commanded Elijah to meet Ahab, because Ahab was the king and responsible for all the people, and through him the prophets of Baal and all the people could be summoned, as will appear in the rest of this chapter. For despite the drought that had occurred, Ahab did not return to himself and repent, so the Lord's call came to Elijah to appear, in order to offer Ahab another opportunity for repentance in the story of the priests of Baal, as will come.

The New Testament mentions in (Lk 4:25, Jas 5:17) that the duration of the drought was three years and six months, while here it says three years. The difference is that Elijah's first meeting with Ahab was in the spring season, in which no rain falls until the beginning of the next month, about six months, which the New Testament included, while here the duration is counted from the beginning of the winter following the spring.

God had withheld the rain because of the people's departure from the worship of God and their worship of Baal under the leadership of Jezebel and Ahab, who also killed the prophets of God. Despite the hardness of the hearts of Ahab and Jezebel, the people were affected by the famine and began to return to God, or became ready to repent and reject the worship of idols; therefore God told Elijah that He would send rain. This shows that God permits affliction to draw His people to repentance, but He is full of tenderness, so that when they begin to respond He overflows upon them with His blessings.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: Elijah carried out the divine command at once and went to meet Ahab in Samaria. There he noticed the suffering of the people because of the famine.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: Ahab had appointed Obadiah as steward of the affairs of his palace, and he trusted him and entrusted his palace to him. This Obadiah was a godly man who feared the Lord. Thus we find that the wicked Ahab entrusted his house to no one but a godly man who worshiped God, because the godly are the faithful ones in whom all trust, even the wicked.

Hold fast to the commandments of God, and you will please Him and obtain His blessing, and He will give you favor in the eyes of all, and you will even be a preacher of God among the wicked, to bring them back to God.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: Cut off: killed.

When Jezebel was hunting the prophets of the Lord to destroy them, Obadiah worked to rescue them from her hand by taking 100 prophets from the school of the prophets and placing fifty of them in each cave, and he used to bring them bread and water to keep them alive in the time of the drought, that is, he fed them throughout the famine, and from this we conclude the following:

1- The persecution by Ahab and Jezebel of the prophets of God and the killing of many of them, since she felt the weakness of her gods to bring down rain, so she ascribed the drought to the men of God and tried to kill them, especially since Elijah had escaped from her hand into the wildernesses.

2- The courage of Obadiah, his faith and his generosity in caring to provide for 100 prophets from the school of the prophets, and so we find mention of the school of the prophets after the age of Ahab, as in (2 Kgs 2:1, 2, 4).

3- The prophets of God were in isolation from the people, living a life of solitude to pray for the people. It is understood from this that Jezebel was not able to cut off all the prophets of God, as is proved by:
1- Obadiah was able to hide a hundred prophets of God.
2- The existence of schools of the prophets in the days of Elisha, as we mentioned.
3- The existence of seven thousand knees that had not bowed to Baal, as God told Elijah (ch. 19:18), and there may be among them a number of prophets of God.

And because Jezebel encouraged the worship of idols, she did not kill the prophets who served the golden calves that Jeroboam had set up in Bethel and Dan, nor did she kill those who offered sacrifices to the idols on the high places in Israel; four hundred of these prophets are mentioned in (ch. 22:6).

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: What occupied Ahab's mind in the time of the drought was not the life of his people but the life of his animals, horses and mules. Here he asks Obadiah, who was in charge of them, to go out with him to search for springs of water or valleys, so as to keep alive as many of his beasts as he could. He certainly imported food from the surrounding countries, such as Egypt, for himself and those with him, and left his people to die of hunger. And despite all that the drought did in the land, Ahab and Jezebel did not repent and return to God, confessing their sins, which were the cause of the drought.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: He decided that each of them should go in a different direction from the other, so that they could search for water over the largest possible area of the land, and this shows that the drought was severe and the rivers had dried up, so they tried to search for any springs in which there was still water.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: While Obadiah was carrying out the mission that the king had given him, he met Elijah face to face and bowed down before him, and although he knew him personally he asked Elijah to confirm that it was he. Of course Elijah's meeting with Obadiah was by God's arrangement, and Obadiah was astonished at Elijah's appearance, since Ahab was searching for him to kill him, but he certainly rejoiced in the blessing of the meeting, because Elijah represented the voice of God in the wicked kingdom that had departed from God and attached itself to the worship of idols.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: Elijah assured him that it was he, and charged him to go back to his lord Ahab and tell him that he had found him.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: Obadiah told Elijah that this message which Elijah had given him to carry exposed him to the danger of death, for the following reasons:
1- Because Ahab would be angry with him for not seizing Elijah, and might kill him.

2- Ahab had sent and searched for Elijah in every place in the kingdom and the surrounding kingdoms and made them swear, that is, charged them strictly, to seize Elijah so that he might come and pray and lift the drought, and all were unable to find Elijah.

3- If he told Ahab that he had found Elijah, and asked him to come with him to meet him at the appointed place, and after he had brought him he might not find Elijah, for the Spirit of God would carry him, as was customary, to some other place, then Ahab would feel that Obadiah was mocking him and would order him killed. Obadiah believed that God protects His prophet Elijah from the hand of Ahab, who wanted to kill him, and carries him to any place and hides him there, as He had rescued him throughout the previous three and a half years and rescued him from the hand of Ahab.
In the end Obadiah begged Elijah not to let him die, because he feared God and did not worship Baal as Ahab and the rest of the people did.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: Obadiah mentioned to Elijah that he had cared to provide for a hundred of the sons of the prophets, so that this might intercede for him and Elijah would not expose him to the danger of death by making him carry this message to Ahab. Obadiah was one of the best of the godly who lived in the days of Ahab, who worshiped God and did not worship Baal, but secretly, lest Ahab kill them; he also cared for the prophets of God, but also secretly. He did not have the strength of Elijah to proclaim the truth even if he were exposed to death, but this does not cancel his piety and his love for God.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: Elijah, who felt the presence of God at every moment, which he had become accustomed to in his seclusion in the wilderness, pledged and assured Obadiah that he would meet Ahab on this very day, that he might be reassured. Elijah mentioned the Lord of hosts as a title of God in order to assure Obadiah of two things:
1- That he pledges before the mighty God who is able to do all things, so his pledge is sure.
2- To reassure Obadiah, so that he would not fear the power of Ahab, since it is nothing before the power of God.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: Then Obadiah was reassured, confident of Elijah's truthfulness, so he went back to where he found Ahab and told him that he had found Elijah, and Ahab went to meet Elijah, and this of course was more important than finding springs of water and grass. Here appears the weakness of Ahab before the power of God that was in Elijah, for the king went to Elijah, in whose hand was the life of all the people and of Ahab himself. For God gives His children awe and a power that subdues the wicked to them.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: When Ahab reached Elijah, the evil of Ahab appeared, who had not repented until now of his sins despite the severity of the drought, so he accused Elijah of being the cause of the severe affliction that had come upon the kingdom of Israel, by his withholding the rain, so that this great famine occurred. Perhaps by this he wanted to stir up the people who were with him against Elijah.

entries.section: (1) The drought and the search for Elijah

paragraphs.text: Baalim: the plural of Baal, since the name of Baal was applied to many cities and places, so Elijah means every Baal they worship; the introduction of the worship of Baal into Israel was at the hand of Ahab and Jezebel his wife. With all strength and courage the prophet denied the accusation directed at him, and with all boldness the prophet turned the accusation back upon the king and the house of his father, showing him that the cause of the wrath that had come upon the land, by the withholding of water, was the neglect of the commandments of the Lord and the worship of idols, in which Ahab and all his house had walked.

And whoever troubles the people of God deserves stoning and death, as happened with Achan the son of Carmi in the days of Joshua (Josh 7:25). Elijah's saying to Ahab "in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the Lord" means all the people, whom Ahab leads, but he also said to Ahab "thou hast followed Baalim," that is, in the singular, because the one who introduced the worship of the Baalim into Israel was Ahab.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: Mount Carmel: a mountain extending from the east of Palestine to near the Mediterranean Sea, a distance of about thirteen miles, and the river Kishon extends south of the mountain from the east and heads northwest until it flows into the Mediterranean Sea at a place south of the city of Haifa. At the top of its summit is an area called the Burnt Offering (al-Muhraqa), where Elijah offered his sacrifice; it is a huge flat area on the mountain with an elevation of about one thousand seven hundred feet above sea level, and it lies in its eastern part.
The prophets of Baal: they claimed to be prophets while they were liars, so they were called prophets, and Baal is the sun-god, whom Ahab worshiped.
The prophets of the groves: groves were set up, that is, wooden pillars, for the worship of the goddess Ashtoreth, who is the moon-goddess, whom Jezebel worshiped.
Which eat at Jezebel's table: Jezebel fed them and cared for their needs.

Ahab was in great need of the falling of rain because of the intensity of the hunger, so when Elijah spoke to him with authority and commanded him to gather all Israel, that is, the heads of all the people, and also to bring the prophets of Baal, who numbered four hundred and fifty, and the prophets of the groves, whom Jezebel cared for, who numbered four hundred, Ahab obeyed in submission and carried out the command quickly, and he was like a child before a great master, because the power of God was in Elijah. Perhaps he was reassured that the number of his prophets was very large and Elijah was one person, so he did not fear the confrontation, and perhaps he thought that Elijah wanted to show his authority by bringing down rain before all the heads and officials of the kingdom and did not imagine anything else.
Elijah chose Mount Carmel and the place that he specified, which was afterward called the Burnt Offering, for the following reasons:
1- There was in this place an old altar that Elijah repaired (v. 30), and perhaps it was from the days of the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so it was a holy place in the eyes of the people.
2- Because of the height of the mountain, the fire upon it can be seen from a great distance, so Jezebel and very many of the people would see it.
3- The mountain is in a central place between the dwelling places of the tribes, so the largest number of the people could see what happened on it.
4- Because of the height of the mountain, one can also see from it the sky and the clouds, which foretell the coming of rain.

5- The Canaanites considered this mountain a dwelling of their gods, so it was an opportunity for Elijah to proclaim the power of God, which is above all gods, because of the sanctity of this place, especially after what Elijah did on it; it became a holy place in the eyes of the people, and so the prophet Elisha made a dwelling for himself on it (2 Kgs 4:25). It appears that Jezebel was more fearful than Ahab, so she prevented the prophets of the groves from going to this confrontation, to which none went but the prophets of Baal (v. 22); perhaps she feared to show the weakness of her gods before the power of God, or that any harm would befall her prophets.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: Before the power of the word of God on the mouth of Elijah the king obeyed at once and sent and gathered the heads of the people, that is, the heads of the tribes and clans, and all the prophets of Baal, because the king was in great weakness through the intensity of the famine, and he thought that Elijah was commanding the gathering of all these to show his authority in bringing down rain.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: Halt between two opinions: the lame person, because of the weakness of his legs, leans to the right and then to the left and cannot walk straight with steady steps.

The people were surprised that Elijah did not pray for the rain to come down, but confronted them with the cause of the problems they were suffering from, that is, the famine, namely their departure from God and their mixing His worship with the worship of idols. They had seen in God the power and authority over all things, as He had done with their fathers from of old, and they saw in the worship of Baal a pleasing of the king and a satisfaction of their evil lusts that accompany pagan worship. And here in Elijah's question he demands that they choose whom they will worship, either God or Baal, because the two kinds of worship cannot be mixed, for this does not please God. Before this plain question the heads of the people were silent, because they realized their error, and perhaps they still wanted to hold to both forms of worship, because they could not leave God, the true God, while at the same time they still feared the king and wanted to satisfy their lusts, and therefore they needed a power to shake them and restore their faith in God, and this is what Elijah would do in the following verses. They found nothing with which to answer Elijah. It is noticed that Elijah did not ask the king or the prophets of Baal, because they were wicked, attached to the worship of idols and rejecting God.

God wants all your heart, your soul, your mind and your strength, so let not your heart be occupied with both God and the world, because the love of the world is enmity with God. God also gave you Himself on the cross and gives you His Body and Blood on the altar every day, so the least response is to give Him your life, as He gave you His life; then you will be filled with satisfaction and strength and live in assurance and with good things that cannot be expressed.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: Elijah continued his speech with the heads of the people and said to them, "I, even I only, remain a prophet of the Lord," who proclaims His name in all the kingdom; for although there were other prophets, such as those whom Obadiah was feeding (v. 13), they were all hidden for fear of the violence of Ahab. He also said that there were now four hundred and fifty pagan prophets who worshiped Baal, so he was one against four hundred and fifty, yet he speaks with faith and authority and does not fear the great number before him, nor their loud voices, nor the king's support of them. It is noticed that the prophets of the groves, who numbered four hundred, whom Jezebel cared for and fed, did not attend this meeting, although Elijah had asked Ahab to summon them; perhaps Jezebel feared for them from the power of Elijah and his God, and this shows that Jezebel and Ahab, despite their evil, feared Elijah, but they did not submit to the fear of God and persisted in the worship of idols.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: Elijah added and said to the people, so that you may know who is the true God: let them give us two bullocks, and let the prophets of Baal come forward and choose one bullock, and slay it and cut it in pieces and offer it as a sacrifice to their god Baal, and let us see whether he will bring down fire from heaven to consume the sacrifice, or not. And I will offer the other bullock as a sacrifice, and we shall see whether God will bring down fire from heaven to consume it, or not. The people approved this proposal, since Elijah was able to influence their hearts and arouse in them the love of the one God as they had learned from their fathers, and because the power of God was with him, the Spirit of God was able to influence hearts, and they submitted to Elijah's proposal and even approved it, so that the prophets of Baal could not afterward refuse Elijah's challenge to them, and perhaps they were hoping that Baal could bring down fire from heaven, because he had authority over fire, as they claim.

It is noticed that Baal is the sun-god, who is known to his followers to have authority over fire and rain, so here Elijah exposes Baal, because when he is unable to bring down fire this shows his weakness before the people, and therefore his inability also to lift the famine by bringing down rain.

Elijah's call was strange to the minds of the people, because he asked them to worship either God or Baal, and the fire would come down from heaven from God or Baal to declare the acceptance of the sacrifice; it is not possible to worship the two together, at the time when the worshipers of Baal welcomed the worship of any other god beside their god, such as the goddess Ashtoreth, for whom they had set up the groves. So the idol worshipers seem to be courteous and tolerant and to accept other forms of worship, and Elijah to be the rigid one who has no love, since he wants the worship of God alone; but all this did not weaken Elijah, and he proclaimed his faith and his challenge to the pagan god Baal.

Hold fast to your faith, and do not accept ideas foreign to the Church under the pretext of tolerance and love, even if some accuse you of rigidity and of limiting entry into heaven to yourself and those who believe the faith of your Church. Be strong like Elijah and pray for all, but do not give up your faith for which the martyrs died.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: After Elijah had spoken to the people as above, he directed his words to the prophets of Baal and said to them, begin by offering your bullock as a sacrifice and put no fire under it, and ask your god to bring down fire and accept your sacrifice. He told them to begin because they were greater in number, and this was wisdom on his part, for after they fail to have their sacrifice accepted and no fire comes down, he comes forward and succeeds in bringing down the fire, and it appears that his God is the true God. For if he had begun first and the fire had come down on his sacrifice, they might have said, we too can, and there might have been confusion and their inability would not have appeared; but their beginning to offer the sacrifice and their failure shows clearly the weakness of their god Baal and that what they claim of his authority over fire is a lie. Elijah left to the prophets of Baal to choose the bullock they wanted, lest they say that Elijah had chosen a good bullock and left them a bullock with defects that their gods, that is, the Baalim, the plural of Baal, would reject.

It is noticed from all this that Elijah delayed the bringing down of rain in order to treat the cause of the problems, which was the weakness of their faith in God and their worship of idols, so that they might repent and return to God, and then He would give them rain as a divine gift from Him to His obedient children.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: The prophets of Baal came forward and set up an altar, or repaired an old altar of Baal that was in this place, and offered their sacrifice on it, that is, they cut it up and laid it on it, then raised their prayers to Baal that he would accept their sacrifice, and they continued a long time in prayer, from the morning until noon, and they danced around the altar, because they believed that Baal was pleased with them by dancing, as they also believed in many mistaken practices such as fornication, for they satisfied their lusts, or Satan moved them to that, so that the pagan gods would be pleased with them; but all their prayers and dancing were of no use and no fire came down from heaven, so they were in great embarrassment and distress before the people. Perhaps the prophets of Baal believed that the power of their god, who is the sun-god, appears clearly when its heat intensifies at noon, so they cried out and danced until noon, but nothing happened.

We see here that the prophets of Baal and Elijah present the same form of worship, which is a sacrifice, so that the gods may be pleased with them, but there is a vast difference between the worship of God and the worship of idols. Satan was and still is imitating the form of true worship but with foreign ideas, to lead men astray from the true worship of God, and whoever does not examine carefully may think that all forms of worship are one and be deceived and go astray, so he leaves his Church and departs from God. So be careful, do not listen to ideas foreign to your Church, or be drawn to any worship that differs from your Church.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: After the prayers and dancing of the prophets of Baal for a long time until noon, Elijah said to them, cry aloud to your god, for a god in his greatness may need a loud voice, and by this he mocks them, because God sees and hears everything, even if it is in a low voice. Then he said to them, perhaps your god is absorbed in some particular thought and not attentive to what you say, and of course logically this is wrong, for how could a god not watch over his followers, when he is spirit and not man, so how could he be absorbed in a thought that prevents him from hearing the prayers of his followers? He also said to them, perhaps your god is in seclusion, and this the mind does not accept, because he is not a man who withdraws from people and goes into seclusion, but a spirit who does not need seclusion, so he belittles their god. Elijah also added the possibility that he is on a journey, and of course distances mean nothing to spirits, for they are able to hear from afar. By all this he warns the people that the pagan gods are not gods and have no existence, that perhaps they would take heed and return to God, the true God, in whom there are none of all these weaknesses. Then he said to them finally, perhaps their god is asleep, and of course a spirit does not sleep.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: It is remarkable that the prophets of Baal believed what Elijah said, who was mocking them, for they thought that their god Baal was in seclusion, or asleep, and so on, and they cried out with loud voices, and in their hands were swords with which they began to cut themselves until their blood gushed out. This was a custom of theirs in their prayers, so that perhaps when their god saw their blood flowing he would take pity on them and answer them. Thus they lived in superstitions that Satan made them imagine.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: Noon: the sixth hour for the Jews, which corresponds to twelve noon in our time.
They prophesied: they prayed and called upon their god and cried out to him.
At the offering of the oblation: that is, the ninth hour for the Jews, which corresponds to three in the afternoon, when the evening burnt offering was offered.

The prophets of Baal continued crying out from the morning until noon, and then until three in the afternoon, but their god Baal did not answer them with anything and no fire came down from heaven, so they were in great failure and despair. Why did the prophets of Baal fail to bring down fire? And how was Satan unable to bring down fire? And how did Elijah challenge the prophets of Baal to offer a sacrifice to see who could bring down fire, God or Baal? All this goes back to Elijah's faith in the power of God, and the presence of Elijah as a prophet of God proclaims the presence of God, and in the presence of God every satanic work fails; that is, it was impossible for them to bring down fire in the presence of Elijah, because the power of God that was in him stops the work of Satan, as the inability of the magicians appeared in the days of Moses when they turned their rods into serpents and the serpent of Moses' rod swallowed them up (Ex 7:12).

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: When the third hour after noon came, there was no more time for Elijah to wait, because the evening was near, so he came forward and called all the heads of the people to see the work of God and His acceptance of his sacrifice, and he repaired an old altar of God that was probably in this region from the days of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: Elijah used in the repair of the altar twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, who is Israel, for despite the division of the kingdom he believes that they are one people and that the tribes must return to be one people, and this is what happened after the captivity.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: Elijah built an altar in the name of the Lord, that is, it is different from the altar of Baal and all pagan altars, and on it the miracle and the divine revelation would take place.

After he built the altar he dug around it a deep trench as great as would contain two measures of seed, and probably what is meant is not the volume of two measures, since a measure equals twelve cups, that is, about eight and a half liters, but that the depth of the trench was the height of a sack or bag holding two measures; in sum, it was a deep trench.
