He made this trench because in some pagan forms of worship they would dig a trench and put fire in it, and it would come out from under the altar and consume the sacrifice, whereas here he would put water in the trench, that the people might be sure that there was no fire on the ground and around the altar.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: After Elijah built the altar he arranged the wood upon it in order, because our God is a God of order and so that the power of the miracle might appear, for Elijah hides nothing among the wood, as there could be if it were placed in heaps. Then he laid the bullock on the arranged wood, after he had cut it into pieces, and then commanded his helpers to fill four barrels with water and pour it on the bullock and the wood and the altar, so everything was drenched with water and it ran down from the altar and fell into the trench dug around it. Then he asked them to pour four barrels a second time, and four barrels a third time, until the water covered everything and filled the deep trench surrounding the altar, so that any doubt might be removed that there was a source of fire hidden in the altar and around it, as some pagans used to do. This shows the extent of Elijah's confidence in God, who would bring down a mighty fire from heaven that could devour the sacrifice however soaked with water it was.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: At the time of the offering of the oblation: the time of the evening burnt offering which the Law commanded to be made, and which was offered daily on behalf of the people before God that He might be pleased with them, and which is a symbol of the sacrifice of Christ on the cross, by which He pleased the Father.

After Elijah had arranged and built the altar, the burnt offering and the wood, and put the water on them, he waited until the time came for offering the evening sacrifice, that is, from three o'clock to five in the evening, in order to declare that God rejoices when worship is offered to Him at its appointed times, and reveals Himself to His children at this time and confirms their faith. At this time Elijah stood and prayed to God, and his prayer contained the following:
1- He reminded God of His promises that He gave to the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Israel, and he substituted the word Israel for Jacob, in whom the prophecies were fulfilled.
2- The proclamation of the power of God, which surpasses all the pagan gods, that the people of God might believe in Him and that He might appear before all the nations.

3- Showing that Elijah is the servant of God who carries out His commands, for it is God who commanded the withholding of the rain and the occurrence of the famine, that the people might repent and believe that He is the only God, especially when He accepts the sacrifice by fire from heaven.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: Thou hast turned their heart back again: they began to return to God by faith and repentance from the worship of idols.

Elijah asked God urgently to answer his prayer, for his faith in God does not cancel importunity, since this shows the extent of his faith and his clinging to God, and he told God that he asked His answer by bringing down the fire to consume the sacrifice for two reasons, which are:
1- To show clearly that God is the only God and all the pagan gods are nothing.

2- If He had stirred the feelings of the people to believe in Him and repent, when Elijah confronted them with the question to choose whether to worship either God or Baal, since it is not possible to combine them (v. 21), and then when the inability of the prophets of Baal to bring down fire to consume their sacrifice appeared, now he asks that the faith and repentance of the people be completed when the fire comes down to consume his sacrifice, and this shows that a man's repentance and faith do not come in a moment but come in steps until they are complete.

If you have a petition before God, wait on Him and press Him, and declare to Him that you will not leave Him and that you trust in His ability to solve your problem, for God rejoices in your faith and your importunity.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: After Elijah's deep, powerful prayer, full of importunity, God showed His glory before all the people and fire came down from heaven and consumed the sacrifice and the wood under it and the stones under the wood that formed the altar and the dust under the altar, and by the power of the fire it was even able to touch the much water that was around the altar, so the whole place became burned with fire.
This fire certainly came down from heaven, as is proved by the following:
1- There was no lightning or rain or the possibility of fire coming down from natural phenomena.

2- The fire consumed the sacrifice, then the wood and after it the stones and below them the dust and the water, that is, it came down from above to below and not like the nature of fire, which rises from below to above.
3- The touching of the fire to the water confirms that there was no fire hidden beneath the altar, as the pagans used to do in their worship.
4- In the case of ordinary fire, it kindles the wood, which burns the sacrifice, but in this case the fire burned the sacrifice before the wood caught fire.

The drenching of the sacrifice with water is a symbol of the sacrament of Baptism, in which a man is immersed in water, and the heavenly fire is a symbol of the work of the Holy Spirit in the sacrament, who came down at the prayer of Elijah, who is a symbol of the priest. The burning by fire of the twelve stones, which represent the people of God with its twelve tribes, is a symbol of God's calling His people to offer their lives as a sacrifice of love, that they may enjoy the overflow of His love and mercy.

The people were far from God, attached to the worship of idols, and so deserved to be burned by the fire of divine wrath, but only the sacrifice was burned instead of all the people, and it is a symbol of Christ, who died for mankind and redeemed it.

God is ready to work powerful miracles if the matter requires, so trust in that; He is able to solve your problems in quiet ways that people do not notice, except you, or by a great work visible to all, but in every case believe in Him and press Him, for He will surely intervene and solve your problem.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: As a result of this divine miracle of the coming down of fire from heaven, the following occurred:
1- The people declared their submission to God alone by their bowing down before Him and their readiness to obey His commandments and orders.

2- They declared strongly that the Lord is the God alone and repeated that, confirming their faith, and by this God answered the petition of Elijah (v. 37) and supported him and was glorified before all His people.

entries.section: (2) The acceptance of Elijah's sacrifice and the killing of the prophets of Baal

paragraphs.text: Elijah commanded the people to seize all the prophets of Baal and let none of them escape and to bring them down to the river Kishon, and there he commanded that they be slain, and by this he fulfills two things:
1- Confirming their faith in God, by cutting off the evil from among them and removing it.
2- Their taking part in the purification of the land so as to regain their confidence in themselves as children of God.
Elijah's slaying of the prophets of Baal was not cruelty on his part, as is proved by the following:
1- This was the carrying out of the Law of God, which commands the killing of whoever incites another to the worship of idols (Deut 13:6-9).
2- The slaying of the priests was a command from God to Elijah, as appears from (v. 36).
3- Had Elijah been lax and left the prophets of Baal alive, and most of them were probably Jews and not foreigners, they would have worked again to mislead the people and their worship of idols.
Thus Elijah removed the prophets of Baal at the river Kishon, which is still called the river of the slaughter, where the heads of these wicked men were cut off.
A sound: a loud noise.

After Elijah killed the prophets of Baal, he looked at King Ahab, who had been fasting because of his agitation over the expected event of Elijah's confrontation with the prophets of Baal and the heads of the people, and he had been watching what those prophets did in their prayers and their cutting of themselves with swords, and then the coming down of the fire to consume Elijah's sacrifice. Perhaps he wanted to know the truth, who is the greater God, the God of Elijah or Baal? All this made him unwilling to eat; and after the king saw the killing of his prophets he was not troubled, because he began to feel with the rest of the people that God is the true God; therefore Elijah said to him: go up from the river Kishon to the high place on Mount Carmel where tents had been set up for the king and a table for him to eat, because the time had passed four or five in the afternoon.
Elijah told Ahab that he heard the sound of an abundance of rain, though it was not a sound heard by the ears of Ahab and all who stood by, but Elijah heard it by the spirit of prophecy.

Probably at this time the heads of the people began to depart after this long day with its powerful events, and Elijah is blamed for not making use of the opportunity of the gathering of the heads of the people from all regions of the kingdom, their being moved by what had happened and their declaring their faith in God, to lead them in specific steps to begin the new life with God, such as returning to God by daily prayer, holding fast to His commandments and His Law and getting rid of the statues of Baal set up in their various lands. This is the natural completion that he should have done, because he knows that men are moved and then forget what they felt and return to their former wicked life after a period. His being occupied with bringing down the rain, which was the people's first demand, if he had delayed an hour to preach to the people, would have been better; but Elijah, despite his greatness, was also a man with his weaknesses.

On the other hand, we see God's response to the need of His people, for after they declared their faith in Him God intervened by His power to lift the famine, and He announced to Elijah that the rain would come down in power, and he in turn announced it to the king and all who stood around him.

The king obeyed the word of Elijah, since he was convinced of the power of God and of His prophet Elijah, and he did not care about the death of his prophets, because he knew that they were deceivers, in addition to his need for food, so he went up to where a table had been prepared for him on the high place near the place where Elijah's sacrifice was accepted.

Elijah, however, went up from the river Kishon to a high place on Mount Carmel from which he could see the sea, and only his servant followed him. There on the top of the mountain Elijah bowed down on the earth and began to pray that God would have compassion on His people and send the rain and lift the famine, and probably his prayers first included thanksgiving to God, because He had intervened and revealed Himself through the fire coming down from heaven, and by this He supported His prophet Elijah before all the people and brought them back to His worship. So words of thanksgiving mingled with supplication to God to complete His work and have mercy on His people and give them rain. This bowing down and the prayers accompanying it confirm Elijah's humility and faith in God, who is able to do all things, and also his lowliness, for in his prostration he put his head to the ground with his face between his knees, and so he proclaims his weakness and his need of God.

Although God had called Elijah to meet Ahab and tell him that the rain would come (v. 1), he prayed much for the rain to come down. The promises of God do not make us slack in prayer, fasting and every act of worship; on the contrary, they draw us to increase them, so that we may enjoy the fulfillment of these promises and our love and attachment to God may increase, for the promises have no effect if we do not pray and press God to bestow them on us.

We also see that Elijah was not occupied with his glory after the coming down of the fire, for he did not stand to receive the praise of the people, but hurried to complete his work of solving the problem by bringing down the rain.

After Elijah prayed, he sent his servant to a higher place on the mountain, to see the sea clearly from there, where the clouds begin to appear from afar, then move until they come to the middle of the sky, and after that the rains come down. The servant went and saw nothing, so he returned and told Elijah so.

Elijah continued his prayers with more lowliness and supplication before God, then returned and sent his servant to look at the sea from afar, but he found nothing and returned and told Elijah so. Elijah continued in his prayers and in sending his servant, so that he sent him seven times. These prayers show Elijah's faith and his importunity at the same time and his supplication for the sake of all the people; the heads of the people should have continued with him in prayer, but they departed because of their weakness, while he, as a representative of them, continued to pray.

God did not send the rain quickly in order to show the greatness of Elijah's faith, his humility and his clinging to prayer, so that he might be an example for this people, that they might return to God and hold fast to prayer.

When you see some sins and weaknesses in those around you, do not judge them, but ask God for them, and according to their need offer prayers, fasts and prostrations (metanoias); by this you will be a true servant and one who loves those around you.

The seventh time, Elijah's servant saw a little cloud, which he saw with difficulty because it was like the size of a man's hand, rising out of the sea, that is, from the farthest part of the sky, so he rejoiced and hurried to tell Elijah that there was hope of clouds appearing and rain coming down. Elijah, however, understood that this little cloud was the beginning of very many clouds that would cover the sky and bring down heavy rains; therefore he commanded his servant to hurry to the king, who was on the high place above Mount Carmel, and tell him to hurry to go to his palace in Jezreel, so that the heavy rain would not hinder him from that. From this we understand that we should not despise any divine blessing, even if it appears small, because it may be the beginning of abundant blessings; as the Incarnation of Christ as a little child in a manger was the beginning of the redemption of mankind on the cross, which all generations awaited.

Quickly the clouds filled the sky and a stormy wind blew and heavy rain poured down, and Ahab hurried in his chariot toward Jezreel, where Ahab had a palace other than his palace in Samaria, the capital of his kingdom.

Elijah was from a city like those in the mountain of Gilead east of the river Jordan, and the inhabitants of this mountainous region were distinguished by tall stature and physical strength, in addition to the fact that Elijah lived in the wildernesses most of his life, so his ability to walk and run was great; but it is unreasonable that he should outrun the chariot of King Ahab, drawn by horses, from Mount Carmel to Jezreel, where the king had a palace in which he spent the winter season, in addition to his great palace in his capital Samaria. The distance from Carmel to Jezreel was about fifteen miles, but the verse here mentions that the hand of the Lord was on Elijah, so it is understood from this that the Spirit of God carried him part of this distance, but he was running, perhaps at the beginning of the way, before the king's chariot, and then after this he reached Jezreel before the royal chariot. In this running we sense two things:

1- Support for King Ahab, for he ran before him, that is, he was one of his followers accompanying him, and this encourages him to stand firm in faith in God and rejection of Baal and repentance from pagan worship, so that he would not waver when he met the wicked Jezebel, the pagan, attached to idols and strong in personality, who used to influence him. Perhaps when he saw Elijah running quickly, then the Spirit of God carrying him, then his outrunning him to Jezreel, he would be certain of the power of God that was in him and hold fast to the faith that Elijah proclaimed.

2- To be in Jezreel to receive the message of the wicked Jezebel, which she would send to him, as we shall see. From what has gone before we see Elijah's activity and his use of time: he had assembled from the morning with the king and the prophets of Baal and the heads of the people, and waited until noon for the prophets of Baal to pray, then repaired the altar, prepared his sacrifice and offered it at three in the afternoon, and after that God accepted it by fire from heaven and the people declared their faith in Him, then he seized the prophets of Baal and led them to the river Kishon and slew them there, and this took time until four-thirty; then he spent about an hour in prayer until the rain came down, and after that he ran before the chariot until he reached Jezreel, and this took half an hour or more, so that he reached Jezreel at the end of the day. This is an example of the true servant, who works always, and God supports him with power.
God appears to Elijah the fugitive

Ahab reached his palace and met his wife, the wicked Jezebel, who nurtured and supported idol worship in the kingdom. He told her what had happened on Carmel: how the prophets of Baal failed to bring down fire from heaven, while for Elijah a great fire came down and consumed his sacrifice, so the people believed, and he seized all the prophets of Baal and slaughtered them at the brook Kishon. He did not mention to her the power of God that brought down the fire, or the inability of Baal to do so, and naturally he did not tell her how the rains poured down, because she had felt them herself, since they filled the whole kingdom. But why did Ahab not tell Jezebel about the power of God? This goes back to the following:
1- His faith in God was very weak, in addition to his being affected by the killing of the prophets of Baal who were his followers.
2- His fear of Jezebel, who nurtured idol worship, lest she become angry with him, especially since her personality was stronger than his.

3- He may have come back to his senses after the uprising of the people when the fire came down and the prophets of Baal were killed, and begun to think that he had lost four hundred and fifty priests of Baal, and wanted revenge on Elijah and left that to his wicked wife; that is, he provoked her to take vengeance on Elijah when she heard of his harshness in killing the prophets of Baal.
4- Perhaps he feared that Elijah would become a person of great standing, as Moses and Samuel were, so that the people would follow him and Ahab's position as king would be weakened.

Jezebel was greatly enraged when she heard of the slaughter of the prophets of Baal, and she expressed her anger by sending a messenger to Elijah, who was in Jezreel, telling him that she had sworn by the gods that she would kill him by this time tomorrow. This message means the following:
1- That she was very angry and wanted to kill him, as she said.

2- That she could not kill him because she feared the people would rise against her, especially after they had returned to God and come to know that He is the true God. But by this threat she wanted to frighten Elijah so that he would flee, leaving the field clear for her, and she could by her schemes bring the people back to the worship of her idols. This is the more likely meaning.

When Elijah heard Jezebel's threat, he sadly carried out her plan, or rather the plan of Satan, and fled quickly from Jezreel southward to Beersheba, which lies in the south of the kingdom of Judah, about one hundred and fifty kilometers from Jezreel. When he arrived there, he was in great distress and despair, so that he could not even bear to be with his servant; he left him there and went on southward into the wilderness to be alone.

Elijah's flight was the opposite of what God wanted, for the people had become ready for life with God, and he ought to have remained in their midst and encouraged them to hold fast to God's commandments and law so that they would be established in the faith. But his flight gave Jezebel the opportunity to bring them back to their old life of mixing the worship of God with idols. And the state of despair Elijah was in kept him from going to Jehoshaphat, king of the kingdom of Judah, in Jerusalem, to which Beersheba belonged, because in his fear he trusted no one with himself, not even the righteous Jehoshaphat, since he had become related by marriage to Ahab.

When Elijah looked at himself, he was afraid. If only he had looked to God, He would have taken the fear away from him, even though when he was with God he had not been afraid of King Ahab or of all the prophets of Baal who were with him. He is like Peter, who took his eyes off Christ when he was walking on the water, and began to sink.

You are mighty as long as you look to God, and demons tremble before you. But if you give in to your weakness, Satan will trouble you with his thoughts, and even draw you away from God and bring you into despair. Repeat a short prayer throughout the day so that you remember that God is always with you.

Juniper tree: a kind of wormwood-type tree that grows in the desert and gives abundant shade. Elijah left his servant at Beersheba and went southward on the road through the wilderness of Sinai, a day's journey. A day's journey means seven hours that a person walks in a day, resting during them, and in these seven hours he covers twenty miles. Feelings of sorrow had overcome Elijah for the following reasons:

1- Bodily exhaustion as a result of what had happened two days earlier, when he offered the sacrifice, killed the prophets of Baal, and prayed a fervent prayer until the rain came; then he ran before Ahab's chariot until he reached Jezreel, on the day after that; then how he traveled a great distance from Jezreel to Beersheba; and finally on this day he walked seven hours until he arrived and rested under the juniper tree. This bodily weariness therefore also affected his state of mind, because of the difficulty of the events he had passed through.

2- His fear of Jezebel's threat to cut off his head. Despite his faith and courage in confronting Ahab and killing the prophets of Baal, he weakened and feared Jezebel and fled, and some fear still remained within him that she would send a messenger after him who would kill him.

3- His despair over the usefulness of his ministry. After he had succeeded in bringing the people back to faith in God on Mount Carmel, he was not able to lead them in the new life with God, because Jezebel had threatened him with death, so he fled, surrendering to despair and losing the sense of God's support for him.
4- His sense of loneliness, that is, that he was the only one who still worshiped God, while all the people were behind Jezebel in idol worship.

5- Perhaps he had become proud when God accepted his sacrifice by fire and he was able to kill the prophets of Baal, that is, he had achieved what no one else had achieved, so the devil afterward fought him with pride, which turned, after Jezebel's threat to him, into fear and despair. God allowed him this weakness so that he would be humbled and review himself in the quiet of the wilderness, but the merciful God would not leave him, as we shall see in the following verses.

He expressed his despair by asking for death, that he might be gathered to his fathers, and perhaps he then remembered the troubles that the earlier prophets such as Moses and David had met with, and forgot the power that had supported him.

After the toil of a long day, when Elijah felt weariness, distress and despair, he slept under the juniper tree. But God's tenderness could not leave him, because he was His son, even if he was in spiritual weakness. So He sent him an angel who touched him tenderly and woke him, and it was evening. The angel told him to eat, for he had prepared a table before him, that he might eat and be comforted and that it might bring him out of his sorrowful feelings. We notice here that God cares for Elijah's food in a wonderful and amazing way: when the famine began He sent him the raven to feed him with bread and meat, then He fed him at the widow of Zarephath of Sidon, and now He feeds him by means of the angel.

In the hour of distress, be sure that God is able to intervene in ways beyond understanding to rescue and sustain you. So be at peace, rely on Him, and seek Him with faith, whatever the troubles around you, for He will surely intervene.

Cake baked on the coals: a kind of large bread made by placing flattened dough on a stone made very hot by the sun, or heated by fire, so that the bread is cooked within minutes. This bread is well known and loved in the Arab regions full of deserts. This bread is also called the bread of the baked cake (Gen 18:6), which Abraham made for his three guests.

Elijah rejoiced greatly and was comforted by the sight of the angel and his tender touches. He looked and found that the angel had prepared the table by his head, consisting of a large cake baked on the coals and beside it a large jar filled with water. This bread tastes delicious, and it is a beloved table: hot food and plenty of water comfort a person sleeping alone in the wilderness, without food or drink. So he rose and ate much of this large cake and drank as much water as he wanted, then slept in peace in the hands of the angel who guarded him and cared for him, especially after his stomach was filled with food and drink and he was satisfied.

After Elijah had slept long enough under the angel's guard, which was probably the whole night, the angel touched him tenderly in the early morning for the second time (which means that he was under the angel's guard and care throughout the night), and woke him. After he had rested and the food he had eaten was digested, the angel told him to rise and eat a second time, because he would walk a long distance to reach the place he was heading for. For God, in His foreknowledge, knew that he would walk a long way in the wilderness until he reached Mount Horeb inside the wilderness of Sinai. This is a divine tenderness that surpasses understanding and surpasses a mother's care for her infant, because He cares for His prophet despite his sin and weakness, for he is His son before everything else, especially since Elijah had become alone, isolated from everyone, and found God with him, compensating him for everything. God showed man's psychological need for someone to share with him when angels came to minister to Christ after He had fasted forty days and forty nights (Mt 4:2, 11).

Horeb: a mountain in the wilderness of Sinai on which God appeared in His glory before His people, and to which Moses went up and received the commandments and the Law and the pattern of the tabernacle of meeting.

Elijah arose, ate of the bread and drank of the water while in the hands of the angel. We notice that God gave him the food that suited him, because he had grown accustomed to life in the wilderness and austerity; so He gave him bread and water only, although years before He had given him bread and meat, and afterward He gave him unleavened cake at the widow of Zarephath of Sidon, and now He gives him bread, because he had become accustomed to the ascetic life.

After that Elijah arose refreshed and strong, to walk a long distance in the desert until he reached Mount Horeb, which the Holy Bible calls the mountain of God. It is a holy place, indeed the holiest place in the wilderness of Sinai and its surroundings, and the Holy Bible does not mention that anyone visited it after Moses except Elijah; it is the place where the saints meet with God. The distance to Mount Horeb is about one hundred and sixty miles, and Elijah covered it in forty days, walking about four miles each day, which is roughly a third of the distance a person can walk daily. Perhaps he did this because he was in no hurry to reach the mountain, because he had forgotten fleeing from Jezebel and walked with God, because he was encouraged by the appearance of the angel to him. He may also have walked some days longer distances than four miles and rested on other days from walking.
And who made Elijah go to Horeb? There are two possibilities:
1- That God guided him by the angel to go to this holy place, so that he might be strengthened and receive a spiritual and psychological blessing.
2- That, since hope had begun to stir in his heart after seeing the angel, he longed to go to this holy place where God gave man the commandments and the Law.
But why did Elijah spend forty days fasting until he reached Horeb, when he could have reached it in about a week, or more, if he had walked a longer distance each day?

1- It was God's opportunity to develop hope within Elijah and establish him through the quiet of the wilderness, the striving of the walk, and the remembrance of God's dealings with Elijah in the previous years.
2- So that Jezebel's pursuit of him might be completely forgotten, and he might be occupied with his life with God in the quiet of the wilderness.

3- So that he might fast the longest period a person can endure, which is forty days, as Moses fasted on the mountain. During a long fast a person forgets his own strength and rises spiritually, to feel God.

4- So that he might remember how God preserved Moses and prepared him to meet Him on the mountain, and how the people came to Him in the wilderness for forty years so that they would forget the idols of Egypt and know God; that is, to remember that God alone is his helper, his refuge and his satisfaction.
5- So that he might see how God sustains him for forty days without food as he walks in the wilderness, enjoying fellowship with Him.

When Elijah reached Mount Horeb, he found the cave into which Moses had entered when he asked to see God, and God hid him in it and passed by before him (Ex 33:22). The text says "the cave" with the definite article to confirm this meaning, and does not say "a cave", that is, any cave in the mountain.

After Elijah had slept in the cave and woken, he felt peace on this holy mountain, and he became strong and ready for God to speak to him and rebuke him. So He said to him, "What doest thou here, Elijah?", meaning by this several things:
1- Why did you leave your work as spiritual leader of the people after they declared their faith? They need your guidance and encouragement so that they may remain firm in the faith.
2- Why did you fear Jezebel, although I supported you before the wicked Ahab and you did not fear to confront him? Why have you fled now and come here?

3- Elijah was accustomed to being led by God. It was He who sent him to the brook Cherith, where the ravens fed him (ch. 17:3-6), then sent him to Zarephath of Sidon to be sustained by the widow (ch. 17:9), and after three and a half years sent him to meet Ahab (ch. 18:1) and brought him to Mount Carmel. But here God did not command him to come to Sinai.

Elijah rejoiced at meeting God, with whose fellowship in the wilderness he had become familiar, and he hurried to speak to Him, to pour out all the pressures stored up in his heart and all his feelings of distress and despair, for He was his God and his only refuge. So he expressed everything within him and his weaknesses, and told God that he had been jealous for God's glory, because the people, led by the king, had turned away from God, and their wickedness appeared in the following:

1- They forsook their covenant with God (to live as a people of His own), which they had made with God on Mount Horeb with Moses long ago. Now they forsook it and associated idol worship with Him, which God had forbidden in His covenant with them.

2- They threw down and broke down the altars that the people of Israel had built on the high places for the worship of God, because they were far from God's altar in Jerusalem. Building these altars was a mistake, since the only altar ought to be in Jerusalem, but it was of course better than worshiping idols. So when Jezebel stirred up war against those who believed in God, she demolished these altars that these believers had built.
3- The hand of the wicked Jezebel stretched out to kill God's prophets, who opposed the worship of idols.

Then in despair he said to God, "I, even I only, am left", although he knew that there were a hundred prophets whom Obadiah was sustaining, but they were hiding for fear of Jezebel. So he felt their inability to serve, and now here he joins them in despair and hides from the face of Jezebel. Perhaps he felt his failure to bring back even one person of the people to God, although this was not true, as we shall see from God's following words, in addition to the effect on many, whose faith would be completed with time.

In all this Elijah overlooked and forgot that God is the One working in his ministry, and not Elijah by his own strength, and that every step that takes place is used by God to complete His kingdom over the hearts of His children. By himself he despairs, but by relying on God he is strengthened and continues his ministry, even if the fruits do not appear quickly.

We also notice that Elijah, in his distress and agitation, did not answer God's question but poured out his suppressed feelings, and God listened to him in His fatherly love to give him rest. But it would have been better for Elijah to answer the question by declaring his repentance for his sins, saying: I have grown weak, my God, and feared Jezebel and fled here, and God in His tenderness would have forgiven him and guided him as to what to do. There was no need for the excuses that Elijah offered for his flight. He reminds us of Adam when God called him in the garden: he did not declare his repentance before Him, but offered an excuse, that he was naked, and then that the woman gave him and he ate. From God's meeting and speaking with Elijah, God's wonderful love appears in the following:

1- God's steadfastness in His love, however man changes. It was He who called him to stop the rain, and sustained him by the ravens, then at the widow of Zarephath of Sidon, and supported him and accepted his sacrifice on Mount Carmel, and still has compassion on him in his despair at Mount Horeb. God is truly the Father who never changes in His love.

2- God's love appears even more when man grows weak. He had sent him the ravens to feed him, then the poor widow in Zarephath of Sidon, but now for the first time an angel appears to him to feed him, because he is in greater weakness than before, so God's mercies toward him increased in order to rescue him, just as Christ after His resurrection sent a special message to Peter who denied Him, letting him know that He had risen, and likewise took him apart at the Sea of Tiberias after His resurrection and rebuked him to restore him to his first rank (Mk 16:7, Jn 21:

3- God's longsuffering appears in the angel waking him while he was under the juniper tree, then waking him a second time and feeding him again, and after that in His being longsuffering toward him for forty days to encourage him and renew his hope, and finally in appearing to him on holy Mount Horeb, to begin rebuking him and restore him to his former strength.

4- God's love appears in not rebuking the prophet Elijah when he fled from Jezebel, but letting him arrive in peace at Beersheba, then leave his servant and reach the juniper tree, and there feeding him twice by the hand of the angel, then caring for him until he reached Horeb, although God did not approve of his flight from Jezebel. But God's fatherhood has compassion on His children even during sin, and at the proper time rebukes them and brings them back to Him. God's love surpasses understanding, for He loves us while we are in sin, and not only after we repent, and He cares for us, so that perhaps His mercies may lead us to faith and repentance.

Look at God's love in your past life and how He cared for you, especially in troubles and above all when you were negligent toward Him, so that you may be ashamed and return and be bound to Him more, and thank Him at all times.

God commanded Elijah to go out of the cave to see God. For despite Elijah's lack of repentance and his mistaken excuses, God was not angry with him, but tenderly brought him out of the cave to appear to him and rebuke him and make him understand everything. It is a wonderful longsuffering with which God treats His children.

Elijah waited to see God, whom he expected to pass before him in one of the mighty forms that show His glory, such as the withholding of rain and drought, or the coming down of fire from heaven to consume his sacrifice. For Elijah had imagined, in the face of the evils of Ahab and Jezebel, that only mighty divine work that shakes the world was fit for the occasion. And as he was waiting, he felt a strong wind that rent the mountains, that is, a storm that shattered the rocks and moved them from their place, and he thought this was an angelic act announcing the nearness of God's coming, but God did not speak after that.
Elijah continued waiting for God, and an earthquake occurred that shook the whole place, and Elijah said to himself that this was a prelude to God's presence, but he heard nothing from God.
And after this he saw a great, strong fire appear before him, and he said to himself that our God is a consuming fire and will speak now, but he heard nothing.

We notice that these three phenomena are those by which God appeared to His people on the mountain in the days of Moses, when He gave him the commandments and the Law (Ex 19:16, 18). So Elijah imagined that these were the preludes to God's appearing, and because Elijah was zealous and fiery, he expected God's appearing always to be in a mighty, miraculous form. Finally Elijah heard a still voice, which perhaps he did not at first take notice of, but afterward he heard the voice of God, as we shall see in the following verses, so that God might confirm to him that spectacular works are not the only form of working, but God can work quietly and draw many to Himself. For Christ worked quietly and went about doing good everywhere, and He covered the sins of sinners, unlike Elijah, who is troubled and complains of the sins of the wicked king and people (v. 10). And in quiet work even unto death Christ gave us a perfect redemption. Indeed Elijah himself had quiet works that influenced those around him without his knowing it, for his life in the wilderness was an example to his generation and to the generations to come, in the love of solitude and virginity, for he is an early image of monasticism. And Elijah's steadfastness in his faith was a support to the hidden prophets and the seven thousand knees that still believed in God. God works in every way, so let us submit to Him and accept His ordering.

God appeared with a still voice that Elijah did not expect as a prelude to God's appearing, and God appears in our lives in many forms to which we pay no attention, because we imagine God according to our own desires. We have a clear example in Christ: when He became incarnate, only a few believed in Him, while the rest doubted and thought Him an ordinary man and not God. So in proportion to our reliance on God and our submission to Him we can discern His speaking to us through our daily life.

When you see problems in your home, or in the Church, or in any place, do not always think that the solution is a mighty divine intervention that troubles the wicked and shows your right. God may see that the solution is quiet work, even if your position seems weak, or you are accused by others. Do not hasten the fruits, for they will come, even after a while. Continue in quiet work and trust that God is with you and will never leave you.

Elijah finally realized that he was in the presence of God, so he hurried to cover his face, indeed to wrap it in his mantle, because he was in the presence of the great and awesome God, just as the angels cover their faces with their wings from the brightness of His glory. Then he heard God repeat to him the same question as before: "What doest thou here, Elijah?" And this means the following:
1- That Elijah's first answer was not sound.
2- The longsuffering of God, which gives His children many opportunities so that they may repent.

Elijah gave the same answer as before (v. 10), that is, his heart had not yet been moved to repentance, and he was still troubled, and thoughts of self and despair were fighting him, and he had not submitted completely to God.
The wilderness of Damascus: a desert lying between the region of Bashan and the city of Damascus.

Hazael: he was one of the officials close to King Ben-hadad, king of Aram (present-day Syria), and he killed his lord the king and reigned in his place, and attacked God's people and afflicted them greatly.

Jehu the son of Nimshi: he was a military commander in the kingdom of Israel, and he killed Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah and Jezebel and all the descendants of Ahab, and his descendants remained on the throne of Israel until the fourth generation.

Elisha the son of Shaphat: he was a farmer, and his father was a rich man from the city of Abel-meholah, which lies north-east of Shechem, and he was of the tribe of Issachar, and he took over the spiritual leadership of the people after Elijah was taken up to heaven.

God's love appeared in restoring Elijah to his ministry, for He said to him, "Go, return on thy way", and asked him to anoint Hazael king over Aram, and Jehu king over Israel, and Elisha prophet in his place. These three matters were only a calling and appointment from God and were not actually carried out until after Elijah's ascension, for the one who appointed Hazael and anointed Jehu was Elisha, because Hazael, being a pagan king, is not anointed with oil, whereas Jehu is from God and is anointed with oil. But these words of God mean restoring Elijah to his work as a prophet, though for a limited period, and Elisha would arise after him; for Elijah had made a great mistake by fleeing from God's work, just as Moses made a mistake and doubted God, so He barred him from entering the Promised Land, and as King Saul overstepped and offered a sacrifice in place of Samuel, so God rejected him and anointed David in his place.

God appointed three officials to protect His people from the wicked, for through the afflictions that would come upon God's people they would return to Him. So it is understood that Hazael would persecute God's people and kill many, that the rest might return to God; then Jehu would arise as king over Israel, and he would also kill the descendants of Ahab and the worshipers of Baal and his priests and many of the wicked, so that those who remained might repent. And if, after this, there were still a number of the wicked, the sword of Elisha would kill them, that is, the strong words of God that are in his mouth, for God works in various ways to bring His people back to faith and repentance. And these three are completely different from one another: the first, Hazael, is the head of a pagan state neighboring God's people, namely Aram; the second, Jehu, would be king over God's people Israel; and the third would be a prophet calling in God's name. So God works through the head of a foreign state from outside and through the head of His people from within, and the prophet was the voice of God in the kingdom of Israel, in which there is no temple of God, which is in the kingdom of Judah.

And these three did different kinds of work: Hazael was from the royal court, Jehu was a commander in the army, and Elisha was a farmer. That is, God can use all capacities for His service and for the repentance of His people. And by these words God reassures Elijah that He will remove evil, but not by his hands, but by means of others, these three; that is, he should not be hasty in carrying out God's judgments. So God distributed the service that Elijah ought to have performed among three. If Elijah had not fled, God would have used him, but God declares His pleasure with him by restoring him to anoint these men so that they may bear his responsibilities for him.

God reassured Elijah that he was not alone in worshiping God, but that there were seven thousand persons who worshiped God and had not bowed to Baal nor kissed his images, as was the custom of the pagans in their worship, bowing to the idol and kissing it. And this number includes the hidden prophets and other believers. God loves these, cares for them and knows them by name, although they were weak and hid in fear of Jezebel's persecution, while Elijah alone was the one who openly declared before the king that he worshiped God and proclaimed His name. So God has compassion on all and makes excuses for them, whether Elijah or the hidden believers. And the word "I have left" means that it was God who preserved these believers, even if some of them were weak and all that distinguished them was not bowing to the pagan gods. Elijah did not know them, since they were not distinguished, nor servants, nor helpers, and were not evident disciples of his, but they believed and lived a pure life in secret for fear of persecution.

By this God encourages Elijah that his ministry bore fruit in these seven thousand, so that he might be comforted and continue his ministry. And the number of seven thousand is of course a very small proportion compared with the total number of God's people, yet God cares for them and knows them one by one, and this encourages believers to stand firm in their faith, however many around them are far from the faith.
Yoke of oxen: a pair of oxen pulling a plow, able to plow an acre in about a day.
His mantle: a rectangular piece of cloth more than two meters long and less than two meters wide, resembling a cloak, which belonged to the prophets and was made of wool or hair.

Elijah's quick obedience to God appeared, who led him by the Spirit to the place where Elisha lived, so he went from the wilderness of Damascus, crossed the Jordan River and reached the city of Abel-meholah, which lies west of the Jordan River in the tribe of Issachar, and he saw Elisha. He probably knew him before, as one of the sons of the prophets or one of the pious young men who believed in God, so he did not need to get to know him. And he found him in his father's fields, overseeing the workers who were plowing the land, and his father owned twelve plows, pulled by twelve pairs of oxen, and this shows us how rich his father Shaphat was, because in one day he plows twelve acres, and of course he owned many times this number, that is, no less than a hundred acres, or perhaps more.

Elisha was careful to oversee the work in his father's fields, for his father had entrusted him with this work, and he was watching the last, twelfth plow in its plowing of the land to see that it was done well, so that the land would be fit for sowing afterward. He is meticulous and bears responsibility however great. And Elisha was probably a young man in his twenties, so that he could oversee this large work.

When Elijah saw Elisha he went to him and cast his mantle upon him. Casting the mantle meant Elisha's call to follow Elijah and be a disciple at his hands, to bear the responsibility of prophecy after him, just as when a man casts the mantle over a woman it means asking for her in marriage and taking her into his house, as in the case of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 3:9). Both of them are under the same mantle, that is, they become as one body in respect of work and responsibility. And so Elijah humbled himself and passed the prophetic work and the leadership of the people to Elisha, and since he humbled himself in this way he received a glory that no one else received, for after some years he went up to heaven in a chariot of fire. For when he was a shining star who withheld the rains and brought down fire from heaven, he was fought with pride and despair, so he fled; but when God rebuked him and he was disciplined in the wilderness, he became humble, so he received the greatest glory, and even appeared with Christ and with Moses on the Mount of Transfiguration (Mt 17:3).

Elisha rejoiced at Elijah's call to him to follow him and devote himself to the prophetic work and leave the management of his father's lands, and this shows how much Elisha loved God and his readiness to leave everything for His sake, for he ran after Elijah, that is, he carried out the divine call immediately.

But he asked Elijah's permission to kiss his father and his mother goodbye. Perhaps he was an only son with no brothers, since his brothers are not mentioned, and this makes it harder for the parents, that their only son would be consecrated to the service of God, in addition to their being rich. Yet they did not object to his consecration and did not hinder him. This shows that they were parents who cared for the spiritual life of their son and were submissive to God, and did not think of their love for their son in a selfish way that hinders the work of God, as some now object to the consecration of their children.

Elijah allowed him to return to bid his parents farewell and said to him, "What have I done to thee?", that is, it is God who called you and not I, and you have the right to bid your parents farewell, and you also have the right not to respond to the call. Perhaps by this he warned him not to be delayed by the customs of that time, in which they would spend days and weeks in farewells and their celebrations, lest he fall into the sin of postponement, which might weaken his desire for consecration, as Christ warned the one who wanted to follow Him but asked permission first to bury his father (Lk 9:59-61). And so Elisha left all his father's wealth for the sake of God, as Moses earlier left Pharaoh's palace for the sake of God, and as the disciples afterward left their work and followed Christ, and in the same way the saints did, such as St. Anthony and St. Paul, who left their wealth out of love for God and consecration to Him.

After Elisha rejoiced at God's call to him to follow Elijah and consecrate himself to God's service by means of the mantle that Elijah cast upon him, he wanted to express his joy at the consecration and his cutting himself off from the affairs of life. So he took a yoke of oxen, which was pulling one of his father's plows (probably he asked his father's permission for this), and slew them and made a feast for his loved ones and acquaintances, and used the wood of the plow to kindle the fire to cook the meat. Here it resembled a peace offering presented to God, that is, a sacrifice of thanks to God for choosing him and for his ministry. By this he announced to all that he was bidding them farewell to be consecrated in God's service, so that even thoughts of doubt, or the difficulty of the service, could not shake him and make him return to his former life, for this announcement was a cutting off and leaving of the old life to go on a new road that he would not leave. Then Elisha bade his parents farewell, and it seems that this farewell took only a little time, so he went and followed Elijah to be his disciple and serve him, as it is mentioned that he used to pour water on his hands (2 Kgs 3:11). And so Elisha began his consecration and discipleship at the hands of Elijah, and perhaps Elijah told him that he would be his successor in leading the people after a period of time, which increased Elisha's attachment to him and his care for discipleship at his hands, which lasted about sixteen years until Elijah was taken up to heaven, and Elisha took over the leadership of the people.

If God calls you to any spiritual work or service, do not be hindered by the affairs of life, and remember that Christ gave you His life on the cross, so whatever you offer Him is a small expression and a simple response to His love.
Ahab's victory over Ben-hadad and the pardon granted to him
Ben-hadad: a common name for the kings of Aram.

Aram: they are the origin of the present Syrian people, and they lived between the mountains of Lebanon and the region between the two rivers, that is, Iraq. Many states were named Aram according to the region in which the Arameans lived, so there were Aram of Damascus, Aram of Zobah and Aram of the two rivers; that is, the Arameans lived in a huge region that was divided into many states.

For political or economic reasons Ben-hadad king of Aram thought of seizing Samaria and the lands of Israel that belonged to it. So he gathered thirty-two kings who were subject to him, allied with him, and neighboring his country, and set out with a huge army of horses, horsemen and chariots, and besieged Samaria and began to war against it, that is, to aim his weapons at it and hurl his missiles upon it. The city of Samaria was so well fortified that the king of Assyria later had to besiege it for three years until he brought it down and carried the kingdom of Israel into captivity (2 Kgs 17:5).

In pride Ben-hadad, who was besieging Samaria, sent messengers to King Ahab, who lived in Samaria, demanding that he hand over all the silver and gold he had, as well as his wives and his children. This means that Ben-hadad had become king over Samaria and what belonged to it. Perhaps Ben-hadad meant by these demands to provoke Ahab to refuse, so that he would have a pretext to attack Samaria and seize it. This shows how confident Ben-hadad was in his huge military power.

In humiliation and fear Ahab agreed to all of Ben-hadad's demands. This shows how sin humbled Ahab, and the weakness of Baal, whom he worshiped and relied on, appeared; whereas David the prophet, by the power of God, triumphed over the Arameans and subdued them. Ahab did not remember this, so as to repent and return to God and imitate David. Nor did he remember what Elijah did with him when God's power and Baal's weakness appeared (ch. 18), for his heart was still stony and far from God.

Sin humbles man, but when God reigns over the heart, He strengthens man and raises him in glory and splendor. So do not be lax with sin, lest it humble you; and if you sin, the door of repentance is open, that you may regain your sonship and your glory, and Satan will not be able to dominate you.

Ben-hadad's messengers returned to him and informed him of Ahab's agreement to his demands, so Ben-hadad grew in pride and greed. He sent his messengers a second time to Ahab, declaring to him that Ben-hadad was not content with his first demands but wanted to send his servants to search the king's palaces and the houses of his servants and subjects, to take from them not only everything precious or whatever Ben-hadad found pleasing, but also everything desirable and great in the eyes of Ahab and his servants, such as the idols they worshiped. He wanted not only the material things Ahab possessed but also to humiliate him. And so we see in Ben-hadad an image of Satan, who cannot be appeased; if we yield to him partially, he goes further to crush and humiliate us.

Ahab felt the humiliation increasing upon him, so he called the leaders of the people and its elders and told them how great an evil Ben-hadad wanted to do to him and to them, because he had agreed to his first demands, so Ben-hadad grew in greed and in humiliating him with his second demands. In all this Ahab did not seek God but sought help from people, because he had forgotten God; and on the other hand he did not turn to Baal, because he was sure of his weakness, as appeared in his meeting with Elijah (ch. 18). Ahab called the elders of the people for the following reasons:
1- Because Ben-hadad's demands were not limited to his palace but extended to the houses of the people and its leaders as well.
2- He felt fear at soldiers entering every place in Samaria, and at his being exposed, with all his people, to humiliation and death.

The leaders of the people felt how great the humiliation would be that would come upon them all when Ben-hadad's soldiers entered their houses, and they might overstep and kill whomever they wished of them. So they declared to the king their rejection of Ben-hadad's demands, since they preferred death to this humiliation, or they felt that in either case they were exposed to death. Perhaps they relied on the fortification of their city and not on their military strength, because Ben-hadad's power was very great.
Ahab answered the messengers who came to him with the second message that he could not accept it, and in humiliation and fear he told them two things:
1- "I am a servant to Ben-hadad", for he said, "Tell my lord Ben-hadad".
2- He confirmed his agreement to the first demands, that he himself would hand over his possessions, his wives and his children, but that no one would search the palaces of Samaria.
Perhaps Ahab was encouraged by the opinion of the elders of the people, and so he declared his refusal of the second demands.

Ben-hadad was greatly enraged when his messengers returned to him bearing Ahab's refusal of his second demands, so he sent his messengers a third time bearing an extremely violent message of threat, in which he swore by his gods that he would destroy Samaria and make it rubble and dust, and that because of the multitude of his army Samaria would be small before his might, so that if each soldier took a handful of the dust resulting from the destruction of the city, this dust would be less than the number of his soldiers. This shows:
1- His complete confidence in his gods.
2- His extreme pride.
3- His contempt for Samaria and its God and all who were in it.

And in his oath by the gods his great confidence in them appears, for he said: if I do not destroy Samaria, as I have declared, may the gods destroy my country and add to its ruin beyond what I wish to do to Samaria. He was completely confident that he would destroy Samaria, and of course the gods did not destroy his country, because they are nothing.

He that girdeth on: the soldier who puts on his weapons and binds them to his body, such as armor and helmet. He that putteth it off: the soldier who has won the victory and returned to his homeland and taken off his weapons.

Since Ahab was strengthened by the encouragement of the leaders of the people, he replied to Ben-hadad's third message, saying: do not boast that you have secured victory over Samaria, for you have not fought and have not won, and you do not know the future, and any unexpected things may happen that hinder your seizing Samaria. In all this Ahab did not return to God, but thought with his own mind and the words of his elders.

When Ahab's reply to Ben-hadad's third message arrived, Ben-hadad was immersed in his pleasures, drinking wine with the kings allied with him in this war, and this shows how reckless he and those with him were; they were not attentive with concentration and ready for this war. It also shows that Ben-hadad was given to pleasure, and this is what would lead to his defeat and that of those with him, and it reminds us of King Belshazzar, king of Babylon, who was immersed in drinking wine and his pleasures in the days of Daniel, and how he and those with him died and Babylon fell on that very night (Dan 5). In pride Ben-hadad commanded his army to get ready and take position to attack Samaria, while Ben-hadad himself kept drinking wine with the vassal kings, immersed in his pleasures, which had taken control of him.

God's wonderful tenderness toward all mankind, even toward those who disobey Him and defy Him, appears in that He looked upon Ahab, who persisted in idol worship and was humiliated before Ben-hadad, and yet did not return to God. God had compassion on him and sent him a prophet from among the prophets who had been hiding for fear of Ahab and Jezebel, and now he appeared by God's command and relying on God's power, to bring Ahab the good news of what he could not have expected, namely that God would be with him and give him victory over this very great army of Ben-hadad's. Thus God's overwhelming power would be shown, defeating this mighty army by means of the very small army with Ahab, since his military strength had become very weak, only seven thousand soldiers (v. 15). By this good news God intended several things:
1- That Ahab would repent and believe in God and reject the pagan gods that were unable to rescue him from Ben-hadad, and that God alone would rescue him.

2- That the people, led by their elders, would believe in God when they saw Him give them victory and deliver them from Ben-hadad. For if they had not lived by the faith they declared before Elijah when the fire accepted his sacrifice, God would appear in power a second time when He delivers them from Ben-hadad.
3- The breaking of the pride of Ben-hadad and all the kings with him, that God's power might appear above all the pagan gods whom Ben-hadad and those with him worship.
4- That He might show His seeking love toward man who does not seek Him, just as He became incarnate to redeem us, and they crucified Him, then He rose to raise all who believe in Him.
God is seeking you and calling you to Him every day, so do not neglect His voice, but thank Him and obey Him, and you will live and rejoice in fellowship with Him.

Ahab was strengthened by the good news of this prophet, because he no longer had any support or help except from God, so he submitted to Him and asked the prophet for the details of how this victory would be accomplished. He said to him, "By whom?", that is, who will fight the Arameans; and, strangely, God said to him through the prophet's mouth: "By the young men of the princes of the provinces". For the kingdom of Israel was divided into provinces, that is, governorates or districts, and each province had an administrative head with a special guard, and these were these young men, whose work was guarding and who were not trained to fight against enemies. But God's power is displayed when He works through the weak, so that the power may be God's. And Ahab obeyed because of his weakness and helplessness.

Then he asked the prophet a second question: "Who shall order the battle?" Will Israel, or will he wait until the Arameans attack? And God's answer was that Ahab himself should lead the young men of the princes of the provinces and begin by attacking the Arameans, in order to test Ahab's obedience to God and his faith, and to establish this faith when he is victorious, so that perhaps after this he might live with God. But sadly, after the victory he left God and offered Him not even one thank offering, nor did all the people, and he returned to his former life of idol worship.

Ahab numbered the young men of the princes of the provinces, and they were two hundred and thirty-two, a very small number to face tens of thousands of the Aramean army. He also numbered the army of the kingdom of Israel that was in Samaria, and they were seven thousand, who would follow the young men of the princes of the provinces. All this was so that God's power might be displayed with His weak people, and when He gives them victory over the Arameans the glory is God's alone.

The army of the children of Israel went out, led by the young men of the princes of the provinces, and King Ahab himself led the army. This was at noon, when the army of Aram did not expect war, since war usually begins in the morning. Ben-hadad and the vassal kings were immersed in their pleasures, drinking wine, for Ben-hadad in pride had despised the children of Israel, and this increased his immersion in his pleasures.

Ben-hadad learned from his watchmen of the going out of soldiers from Samaria, and perhaps he heard the noise of their going out, so he sent messengers to make sure and learn the truth about those going out from Samaria. His messengers informed him that there were a few soldiers, about three hundred, who had come out of the city and were advancing on the camp of the Arameans. In all pride he commanded that they be taken alive, whether they had come out surrendering to Ben-hadad or had come out for war. This shows:
1- Ben-hadad's pride and his confidence in the strength of his armies, that he could easily take alive any number of the children of Israel and had no need to kill them.

2- His confidence in the weakness of the children of Israel before him, so he would seize those coming out against him, to kill them whenever he wished. Perhaps he wanted to torture them before killing them, to be an example to the people of Israel, to frighten them so that they would surrender to him easily.
3- Ben-hadad wanted to take them alive in order to obtain from them information that would help him in seizing the city.

The young men of the princes of the provinces went out from the city of Samaria, followed by the army of the children of Israel, the seven thousand, and God gave them faith and strength, so they attacked the army of the Arameans and each of them killed the man before him. The army of the Arameans was afraid of this sudden attack and the falling of some of them, so the Aramean army fled, and the army of Israel pursued them and killed some of them, and their fear and flight increased, so that their king Ben-hadad was very afraid and shocked at what had happened, and he had no choice but to flee on a horse among the horsemen, in disguise, leaving his royal chariot, to save himself.

Then Ahab went out with the seven thousand to pursue those fleeing from the army of Aram, killing as many of them as he could and smashing their chariots, so God made a great slaughter in the army of the Arameans. In this victory we see the following:
1- God gave strength and psychological support to the young men of the princes of the provinces, who were untrained for war, so they attacked with force and killed all whom they met.
2- God put terror in the hearts of the Arameans, so they were afraid and fled at once.
3- Ben-hadad's immersion in drinking wine made him unable to face the situation, so he fled in humiliation and helplessness.
4- This great, unexpected victory ought to have led Ahab to faith in God and to the removal of idol worship, but sadly he did not return to God.

Ahab did not send to the prophet of God who had given him the good news of victory, to thank him, but the tender God took the initiative a second time and sent this prophet to Ahab, informing him that Ben-hadad would return to fight him at the turn of the year, probably meaning the summer, when conditions are suitable, since the day is long and there is no rain. So God here warns Ahab to prepare his armies and weapons for war months before it begins. He did not tell him this the first time, because Ben-hadad had already besieged Samaria and there was no time to prepare.

Ben-hadad is a type of Satan, who does not cease to fight us however much we triumph over him. Therefore be always ready and do not slacken if you achieve any victory over him and reject his sins. Hold fast to God's commandments, set a guard over your senses, and keep away from what makes you stumble, and you will live victorious all your life.

The counselors of the king of Aram thought that the gods of the children of Israel were gods of the hills, which is why they were able to defeat Aram in the hills surrounding Samaria. This was counsel from them that the king had not asked for, but they were eager to offer it for the good of the kingdom.

In ancient times they believed that there were gods of the mountains, gods of the valleys and gods of the seas. Because they believed that the children of Israel were like the other peoples and had gods like the gods of the peoples, they thought that the gods of the children of Israel were gods of the hills whose power appeared only on the hills. They thought this belief for the following reasons:
1- The abundance of mountains in the land of the children of Israel.
2- The children of Israel did not use chariots, because they are not fit for war except in the valleys.
3- The people of Israel used to offer their sacrifices on the hills, meaning of course the pagan gods into whose worship the inhabitants of the kingdom of Israel had fallen.

4- Perhaps the Arameans knew that the children of Israel sang to their God psalms that showed that He was a god of hills, as David says, "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills" (Ps 121:1) and "His foundation is in the holy mountains"
(Ps 87:1). In addition to this, the huge size of the Aramean army shows in the valleys and not on the hills, and so they would terrify the army of Israel.
The counselors gave Ben-hadad counsel for victory over the children of Israel, and their plan included a set of proposals:
1- To fight them in the plain, where there are no hills, so that victory over them would be easy, because of their belief that the gods of Israel were gods of the hills only.
2- To remove the thirty-two kings subject to Ben-hadad and appoint military commanders in their place so that they could lead their armies.

3- To prepare a great army like the first one that besieged Samaria, with the same number of horsemen, soldiers, horses and chariots, that is, in great multitude that would guarantee victory. The king agreed to their counsel and began to carry it out, and this shows the ignorance into which the followers of idol worship fall, for they do not know that there is one God for the whole universe, and He is able to do all things and protects His people Israel.
And all the items of the plan show Ben-hadad's pride and his reliance on the multitude of his armies and plans, for he was not humbled even after his defeat.
Aphek: a city lying east of the Sea of Galilee, about five kilometers away, in a plain that is higher than the city of Damascus.

Ben-hadad carried out the counsel of his servants. At the turn of the year after his attack on Israel he prepared an army like the first and moved toward the city of Aphek, where there was a wide plain, to fight Israel, and he went up to Aphek because Damascus, where Ben-hadad lived, is lower than Aphek.

When Israel learned of the movement of the armies of the Arameans and their arrival at Aphek, their army got ready and they took the provisions they needed, because the place was far from Samaria and their cities, since Aphek is considered to be in the north of the land of the Jews. The number of the army of the children of Israel was very small compared with the huge army of the Arameans, and Israel divided its army into two companies, so they looked like two little flocks of kids before the hosts of the Aramean army, for flocks of goats are always small in number. But their reliance was on God's power that supported them, as the prophet had given them the good news (v. 22).

To encourage His people Israel, God sent them His prophet for the third time, and called him a man of God, because he is God's voice to His people. The prophet spoke to King Ahab and told him that since the Arameans had thought that the Lord is a God of the hills, and not a God of the valleys, they will see how God gives you victory over them. By this two things are accomplished:
1- Ahab and the people of Israel will know that God has authority over the whole world, so they will believe in Him and abandon idol worship.
2- The Arameans will know that the God of Israel is the only God, above all their gods, so that they may believe in Him.
Footmen: a soldier of the infantry and not a horseman.
The two armies met at Aphek, but they remained for seven days without either of them moving, for the following reasons:
1- The army of the Arameans was in fear as a result of its first defeat, so it was observing the points of weakness and strength in the army of Israel and drawing up its plans to destroy them.

2- The army of Israel trusted in God's power and awaited His intervention, as He intervened in the days of Jericho, which fell after seven days (Josh 6:15-21). It did not know how it would be victorious, but it trusted in the victory.

And after seven days the two armies engaged, and God's power was with His people, so they won a crushing victory over the Arameans and killed a huge number of them, one hundred thousand footmen, which was most of the Aramean army, for the following reasons:
1- The trust of the people of Israel in God's power made them attack the army of the Arameans with force and courage.
2- God cast terror into the hearts of the army of the Arameans, so they tried to defend themselves but in weakness, and so this huge number of them fell.
3- Perhaps the army of the Arameans, in their fear and confusion as they tried to flee, killed one another, as happened with the army of the Midianites in the days of Gideon (Judg 7:22).

After the crushing defeat of the army of the Arameans and the death of most of them, only twenty-seven thousand soldiers were left of them, and they all fled to the city of Aphek to take refuge inside its walls. And here God intervenes to give the Arameans their due, who had overstepped against Him and claimed that He was a God of the hills only, so He stretched out His hand and allowed the walls of the city of Aphek, with the buildings connected to them, to fall upon them. Perhaps this was by an earthquake that occurred in that region, and they all died, and so what they tried to take shelter in, the wall, fell on them, for who can stand before God? He alone is the source of protection. As for King Ben-hadad, in his terror he fled from house to house and from room to room, for fear of the buildings falling on him. And what the army of Israel had expected came about, that God would give them victory as He gave victory to His people in the days of Jericho, so the walls fell to kill the rest of the Aramean army. The king was followed by a few of his counselors and servants, who survived the falling of the walls and buildings upon them.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: Sackcloth on our loins: coarse clothing worn on the waist and below, a sign of humbling oneself.

Ben-hadad and his servants, shut up inside the city of Aphek, felt that they were in the hand of the king of Israel and that he would surely seize them and kill them. So in fear Ben-hadad's servants proposed to the king a proposal that might save him and save them with him. They said to him: we know from the history of the kings of the children of Israel that they are forgiving and kind, so we propose that all of us put sackcloth on our loins as a sign of our humbling ourselves before King Ahab, and tie ropes on our heads as a declaration that we deserve to die by hanging with these ropes, and that we beg the king, that he may forgive you and let you live, and so we shall live with you. For Ben-hadad's servants knew from the history of the children of Israel the forgiveness of King Saul toward Agag (1 Sam 15:9) and the forgiveness of David toward Saul and toward Absalom his son.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: Ben-hadad agreed to his servants' proposal, so they girded on the sackcloth and the ropes and went to King Ahab and begged him to forgive Ben-hadad their king. Ahab marveled that he was still alive, and when he made sure of that he declared his pardon of him, and even said respectfully, "He is my brother", that is, a king of standing like me.
Ahab's pardon may seem a kind of mercy and magnanimity, but it was very wrong, for the following reasons:

1- Because it was against God's commandments to destroy the wicked; for he had blasphemed the name of God and said that He was a God of the hills and not a God of the valleys. And Ahab did not take warning from what Saul did when he spared Agag, and God rebuked him by the mouth of Samuel the prophet (1 Sam 15:19).

2- Perhaps the humiliation Ahab tasted before Ben-hadad's threats, before fighting him, found in this situation an opportunity to regain his dignity at the expense of God's word and to forgive his opponent.
3- He made a covenant with Ben-hadad and broke his covenant with God, because he still believed in idol worship such as Baal and did not submit to God, the only God.
4- He did not seek God's counsel, nor did he ask the prophet who had given him the good news what to do with Ben-hadad.

5- His action was against his people. He thought he was being merciful to Ben-hadad, but he was unmerciful to his people, whom Ben-hadad had humiliated and who would return after three years to fight them; so he wronged his people.

6- He did not rebuke Ben-hadad for his blasphemy against God, nor that the cause of his defeat was his defying God, and he did not benefit from the situation by taking compensation for the war losses that Ben-hadad had caused, but was content with Ben-hadad's promise to return to him afterward the cities that his father had taken from Omri, Ahab's father, and to allow him to trade in Damascus.

7- Perhaps he thought that sparing Ben-hadad would make him ally with him against Assyria, which was beginning to grow strong as a state to dominate the world. And he did not rely on God, who protects him.

8- Ahab pretended mercy, but his heart was wicked, for he did not believe in God who gave him victory, did not obey His word, and did not thank Him in any way, and by this he angered God greatly, because God searches the hearts and reins and does not care for appearances.
Be merciful to the weak, but do not pretend mercy for purposes in your heart. Do mercy for God's sake and not for any personal purpose, or to please people.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: They pressed: from persistence, that is, they pressed.
Whether it were his: Ben-hadad's servants asked one another whether Ahab truly meant these words, that Ben-hadad was his brother.

Ben-hadad's servants were gladdened and rejoiced greatly when they heard Ahab's words that Ben-hadad was his brother, that is, that he had pardoned him. So they caught this word from him and confirmed it, saying to Ahab: "Thy brother Ben-hadad", relying on the fact that kings do not go back on their word. And of course this pardon would include Ben-hadad's servants standing before Ahab, so their joy was great that they would not die.

And Ahab commanded that they bring Ben-hadad to him, that is, take him from the city of Aphek and bring him to Ahab. When he came to him, Ahab greeted him and took him by the hand and caused him to come up into his royal chariot, that is, he gave him the honor due to a king.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: In the face of this great pardon from Ahab and the excessive honor, Ben-hadad declared that he would restore the cities which his father, who was also called Ben-hadad (ch. 15:18), had taken from Omri, Ahab's father, and that he would allow the Jews to trade in Damascus, which was a great commercial city and the capital of Aram.
