This may imply that they would build houses and quarters for themselves in Damascus, called the quarters of the Jews, to establish their trade.
Ahab rejoiced at these promises and made a covenant with Ben-hadad, since he thought this was to the benefit of the Jews, as we mentioned at (v. 32).

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: After Elijah killed the prophets of Baal, Jezebel grew weaker to some extent, so the sons of the prophets began to appear, who gather in the schools of the prophets that the prophet Samuel founded, and one of the most important rules of these schools was obedience to God. So one of these prophets came forward and said to another prophet, his companion, that God commanded him to strike him. But the prophet's friend was ashamed, or took pity on his fellow prophet who was commanding him from God to strike him, and refused to obey God's word and strike the prophet.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: When this friend refused to obey God's command, the prophet told him a message from God, that because he refused to obey God, when he left the place where he was and went on his way a lion would meet him and kill him, and this actually happened.
All this is so that God may confirm to us the importance of obedience, because Ahab's sin in sparing Ben-hadad was refusing to obey God.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: This prophet continued on his way and met another man and asked him the same request that God wanted, which was that he strike him. When the man learned that this was a command from God, he obeyed and struck him hard until he wounded him, and this is what the prophet wanted, that signs should appear on him showing that he was a soldier who had been struck and wounded in the war.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: Bandage: a long piece of cloth tied on the head over the cap or tied on wounds.

The prophet bound the wound on his head with a large bandage, so that it covered most of his eyes and therefore concealed to a great extent the features of his face, so that Ahab would not know that he was a prophet, because he fears the prophets, since they represent God and make him hear His voice rebuking him for his mistakes. Then he waited for King Ahab on his return from Aphek, after he had bidden farewell to King Ben-hadad king of Aram, to make him hear a message from God.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: After a while the king reached the place where the prophet was, and the prophet called out to him, asking for his guidance and judgment. The king stopped with his chariot and the disguised prophet came forward, as if he were a soldier wounded in the war, and told the king that when he was in the battle, one man, probably a commander, came to him and asked him to keep a certain prisoner with all care and attention, and threatened him that if he did not keep him or he got lost, he would be seized in his place, or would pay a large sum of money, a talent of silver, which equals about three thousand shekels. And the price of a slave, as we know from the sale of Christ by Judas, is thirty pieces of silver, that is, this prisoner was very important and his price a hundred times that of an ordinary slave. The prophet intended by this story, to which God guided him, to alert the king so that he would understand the truth of what he had done, since he had released a very precious prisoner, Ben-hadad, but the king did not understand the meaning of the parable.

Then the prophet continued his speech and said that during the battle he moved right and left and was not careful in guarding the prisoner, so he escaped from him; that is, he was busy with the business of war, but the result was the loss of the prisoner. Then he asked the king's judgment, perhaps to rescue him from this predicament, but the king in all harshness said to him: you have judged yourself by your promise and agreement to keep this prisoner, so you must be seized in his place.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: After the prophet told the king this story, he lifted the bandage that was on his head and covered his eyes, and the mark that the prophets used to put on their foreheads, declaring their identity, appeared, so that people would know them and accept God's word from their mouths. And here Ahab discovered that he was one of the prophets, and he was afraid, since he expected a message from God, because he was wicked and greatly angered God.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: The prophet declared God's message plainly to Ahab and rebuked him for releasing the wicked Ben-hadad, who had blasphemed God and whom God in His Law had commanded to be killed, so Ahab deserved to have done to him what ought to have been done to Ben-hadad, that is, to die. And here only Ahab understood the meaning of the parable; indeed perhaps the prophet told him what had happened to his companion who did not obey God's command and was killed by the lion, so Ahab understood that since he had not obeyed God's word he deserved death.

And the message carried not only punishment of death for Ahab, but also that his people would die in place of Aram, because the people also shared in the fault with Ahab in the worship of Baal and had not returned with all their hearts to God.

entries.section: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

paragraphs.text: When Ahab heard God's judgment by the mouth of the prophet, he was very sad and went on his way to his house in Samaria, the capital of his kingdom, but he did not return to God by repentance, because his heart was far from God, although before him was a practical example, namely Ben-hadad's seeking Ahab's mercy and Ahab's forgiving him (v. 31). How much more, then, will the tender God forgive His children if they take refuge in Him, and as He forgave the great David for his fault.

Beware of the sorrow without hope, which is sorrow over what you lose of the things of this world. And if you meet any trouble, or err in any matter, take refuge in God, confident of His mercies and forgiveness.
Naboth the Jezreelite

Jezreel: a city lying in the plain of Jezreel, which extends from the Mediterranean Sea in the west to the Jordan River in the east. Its climate is pleasant and suited to the winter season, and it is 32 km from Samaria.

After Israel's victory over Aram, Ahab's release of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him, he became depressed and went to his palace in Jezreel to rest, and tried to cheer himself up. He looked beside his palace and found a field owned by Naboth the Jezreelite, a man who believed in God and held fast to the Law, as will appear from (v. 4), and who was one of the seven thousand knees that had not bowed to Baal (19:18). Ahab wished to take this field and make it a garden belonging to his palace.

Ahab called Naboth and asked him to give up his field to him, because he wanted to make it a private garden for himself and plant some vegetables in it. Perhaps Ahab wanted to cheer himself with this garden so as to get out of his depression. He offered Naboth two proposals:
The Second Book of Kings
1- To give him another vineyard from the king's possessions in place of this vineyard, and he was even ready to give him a better vineyard than this one.
2- To give him the price of this vineyard in an amount of silver.

In all this Ahab forgot that the Law ordains that no one should give up his field, the inheritance of his fathers, and if he is forced to mortgage it because he needs money, it returns to him in the year of Jubilee (Lev 25:23-24). This offer seems fair, but it does not agree with God's Law, because Ahab did not care about God or His Law. By this request he broke the tenth commandment, which says, "Thou shalt not covet ... any thing that is thy neighbour's" (Ex 20:17).
Naboth was very distressed when he heard King Ahab's request and refused to give him his vineyard, for the following reasons:

1- Because Naboth was a godly man who held fast to God's Law, which stipulates that a person must hold fast to the inheritance of his fathers in the land, because it is a gift from God that cannot be squandered, and it is a type of the new earth, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven.
2- The land bears the memories of the fathers and forefathers who toiled in it and took care of it.

3- Naboth refused Ahab's words because he understood that the king would take the land and would not return it to him again, for it was not like other lands that can be mortgaged and then recovered after a while. Therefore Naboth's refusal was decisive, and this shows not only Naboth's faith but also his courage.

Be strong in holding fast to your spiritual practices and your relationship with the Church, however much circumstances press upon you or others try to distract you from them, however logical your justifications. Your relationship with God and the salvation of your soul are more important than anything. Be courageous in holding fast to your right to life with God.

If Ahab had been depressed by the words of the prophet, who told him that he would die because he released Ben-hadad, and had tried to cheer himself and rejoice in the desire to own Naboth's vineyard, now he returns to his depression a second time because Naboth refused his request. So Ahab went into his chamber and lay down on his bed in sorrow with his face to the wall, and refused to eat. This shows the following:
1- The weakness of Ahab's character and his agitation over any small matter, which is not fitting for a king.

2- The mastermind of the kingdom was his wife Jezebel, as will appear from the following verses, and this shows that the cause of the spread of idol worship in the kingdom was Jezebel, using Ahab's weakness and indifference.

3- Material desires give only a temporary pleasure, then they pass away, and losing them brings sorrow upon a person. They are not the means that give joy and peace, but a temporary deception by which a person thinks he can make himself rejoice. Ahab was a man of pleasure who tried to delight himself with possessions and buildings, as he built a house of ivory (ch. 22:39), and at the same time he quickly became depressed, but did no useful work and did not return to God.

Jezebel learned from the king's servants that he had refused to eat and had gone into his bedchamber sad, and perhaps some of them told her what they had heard of his conversation with Naboth. So she hurried to his chamber and found him sunk in his sorrow, and she asked him in astonishment why he was sad, because with her strong personality these small matters did not affect her, in addition to the fact that she used her wicked means to reach her ends, so these small problems did not stand in her way. This shows the strength of her personality and that she in truth was the one running this kingdom and not Ahab.

Ahab expressed the depression that he had stored up in his heart and told his wife the reason for his sorrow, which was Naboth's refusal to give him his vineyard. Of course he did not mention that this was contrary to the Law, because Naboth had said, "The LORD forbid it me ...", and this is because Ahab did not care about God's commandments or His Law.

Jezebel rebuked her husband for his weakness and slackness in using his authority as king to get what he wanted, since she believed that the king's authority is absolute and is not subject to any god or law. By this she stirred up Ahab's pride, then reassured him that she would give him Naboth's vineyard, so let him arise, eat and rejoice, for what he desired was sure to be obtained. This shows:
1- How strong Jezebel's personality was, for she carried out what she wanted in the whole kingdom.
2- How great Jezebel's wickedness was, for she used any means, however wicked, to achieve her ends, as will appear in the following verses, since she respected no law; what she wanted had to be done.

3- How weak Ahab was, since he could not argue with her and accepted her rebuke cowardly, and did not even ask her how she would give him the vineyard, for he was completely subject to her and left to her the management of the kingdom as she wished.
Belial: a Hebrew word meaning without profit, or worthless, and it is also used to express Satan, so the sons of Belial are the sons of evil and of worthlessness and of Satan.

Jezebel used the king's seal, which was in her hand because the king was subject to her. She sent letters to the elders and nobles of Naboth's city and sealed them with the king's seal, that is, they were royal orders, in which she asked them to proclaim a fast in the city, meaning that a great problem had befallen the city and its solution was to take refuge in God by fasting, that He might lift from the city what had befallen it. So she deceives and plays the hypocrite and appears as if she were religious, calling for a fast, and as if she also cared for the cities of the kingdom and solved their problems. Then she demanded with all impudence that they bring two wicked men to bear false witness against Naboth that he had blasphemed God and the king, who is God's deputy and the executor of His commands (Ex 22:28). Blasphemy means that he spoke wicked words against God and the king. This was to be in a public council gathering the elders and great men of the city, and they were to seat Naboth in a prominent place, visible, to be tried, that is, it would be a lawful court, and they would accuse Naboth in it of blasphemy and sentence him to death by stoning (Lev 24:16, Jn 10:33). Jezebel's cruelty appears in that she also commanded the killing of Naboth's sons (2 Kgs 9:26), so that he would have no heir, and his property would pass to the state, that is, the king, in addition to the fact that he was considered a servant of the king, so his property would be given to the king (2 Sam 16:4). And of course she arranged an accusation against them, that they shared with him in the blasphemy, so they also deserved death.
Jezebel's action here shows:
1- That she had studied the Law, so she was careful to bring two witnesses, for one witness is not sufficient (Deut 17:6).
2- That she was wicked and very cruel, regarding the killing of people as permissible.
3- That she was deceitful, adorning herself in the garb of spirituality and of holding fast to the worship of God and caring for her people, while she was as far from this as could be.
The elders and nobles of the city of Jezreel, that is, the leaders of the city, carried out Jezebel's words exactly and stoned Naboth, and this shows the following:
1- Their great fear of the cruel, violent Jezebel.
2- Perhaps they were hoping for her favor or for some gains from her.
And Naboth here is a type of Christ, who was wronged, and they bore false witness against Him and killed Him, although He was completely innocent. The Second Book of Kings

The elders of the city informed Jezebel that they had carried out her words and killed Naboth, and she rejoiced because she had completed her plan, and went to Ahab to tell him of Naboth's death and to give him the good news that he had become the owner of the vineyard without paying anything; that is, she had easily achieved his desire for him. This shows how little she regarded people's lives, and her violent wickedness and selfishness.

Ahab rejoiced that Naboth's vineyard had become his, and in his joy he went down himself to inspect this vineyard and see what he wanted to make of it, to enjoy himself with the pleasures of life. This shows his immersion in his pleasures and his joy and submission to his wife, that is, his conviction that she was running the kingdom well, because she had fulfilled his desire. It also shows that he was selfish, not caring about what had happened to Naboth, but the important thing was that he had come to own the vineyard.

Do not rejoice in obtaining your desires unless it is in a sound way that does not violate God's commandments, because every pleasure is temporary and passing, and you cannot gain happiness on earth except by following God's commandments, and afterward you gain the joys of the Kingdom.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of Ahab and Jezebel

paragraphs.text: God was greatly angered by the injustice of Jezebel and Ahab and their killing of Naboth and his family, so He spoke to Elijah the Tishbite, to leave the wilderness and go down to Jezreel, to Naboth's vineyard, to meet Ahab, who reigns in his capital Samaria.
And we notice two things in this:

1- That God summons Elijah to service more than five years after his weakness and his flight from the face of Jezebel, after he killed the prophets of Baal. After he spent a period of seclusion in the wilderness and regained his spiritual and psychological strength, God renews his vigor and calls him to service, and this shows God's pleasure with him. Therefore He calls him as He called him at the beginning of his ministry (1 Kgs 17:1), as Elijah the Tishbite, that is, he starts anew, for God had forgiven him his weakness and called him to a new service. Elijah's virtues appear in that he obeyed at once and did not fear Ahab or Jezebel and did not flee from Jezebel as the first time, although the message was very difficult, for he informs the king that he, his wife and all his descendants will die.

2- That God is jealous for His believing children, that is, Naboth, and sends the greatest of the prophets at that time, Elijah, and not an ordinary prophet as He sent to Ahab during his war with Ben-hadad.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of Ahab and Jezebel

paragraphs.text: When Elijah met Ahab, fear covered Ahab's face, because he had not seen Elijah for more than five years, since the time he killed the prophets of Baal who followed him, and because Ahab felt that he had erred in taking possession of Naboth's vineyard, even if he and Jezebel tried to forget their fault. In front of Elijah, who of course represented God, Ahab was afraid.

Elijah declared to Ahab the grounds of the sentence against him, that is, the reasons for the divine punishment of him. These reasons are his killing of Naboth, then his seizing his vineyard, that is, his inheriting his vineyard without right. Although Ahab did not himself order Naboth to be killed, he is responsible for his killing, because he left authority to his wicked wife to do what she wanted. The divine punishment included two things:
The Second Book of Kings
1- That as Ahab killed, Ahab too will be killed.

2- As the dogs licked the blood of Naboth in Jezreel, the dogs will lick the blood of Ahab. And this is what actually happened, for Ahab was killed in his war with Aram and the dogs licked his blood in the same place where Naboth died, that is, in Jezreel (ch. 22:38). Licking the blood is a kind of contempt, and this signifies what will happen in the eternal torment of the wicked, where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.
And we see how Elijah regained his strength to deliver to Ahab a severe message of rebuke, than which there is none harder, for with courage he told him that he would die a shameful death.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of Ahab and Jezebel

paragraphs.text: After Ahab heard God's judgment upon him, his fear and agitation increased, and in weakness he said to Elijah:

"Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" For he feels that he is walking in evil and rejecting God by his worship of idols, so God is against him and his enemy, and God's representative is Elijah; and whoever befriends Satan of course has God as his enemy, because the worship of idols is the worship of demons, just as the thief says to the police officer, "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?", since he knows that he is a criminal who deserves punishment.

But Elijah made clear to him that the problem was within him, for he had sold himself to evil, that is, he had made sin permissible and his heart was no longer moved to repent, so he became sold, that is, enslaved to evil. Ahab sold himself by himself, for he chose evil and rejected God. And Elijah represents the conscience, that is, the voice of God that alerted Ahab to his sin, for as soon as Ahab saw Elijah he was alarmed and remembered his sin. On the other hand, whoever declares the truth to those who err is hated by them, but he declares it for God's sake and in obedience to Him.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of Ahab and Jezebel

paragraphs.text: Him that pisseth against the wall: a male, whether a child or an adult.
Shut up: an old man unable to go out or bound in one of the prisons.
Left: a young man who goes out and moves about much, or a free person who is not bound.

Elijah paid no attention to Ahab's objection but continued God's punishment of him, that perhaps he would take notice and repent. He said to him that God would bring evil upon you and all your descendants would be destroyed, especially the males, whether adults or children, who could succeed you in the kingship, that is, He would cut the kingship off from your house.

This total destruction proclaims God's great anger at Ahab's persistence in evil. And strangely, this destruction was carried out by King Jehu, who was one of Ahab's military commanders and was present when Ahab took possession of Naboth's field (2 Kgs 9:25), and when he became king he was extremely violent in destroying Ahab's descendants. Perhaps Jehu heard God's sentence on Ahab from the mouth of Elijah, because he was one of those close to King Ahab.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of Ahab and Jezebel

paragraphs.text: God confirms through Elijah's mouth that the total destruction of all Ahab's descendants will be like the destruction of the descendants of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, the first king of Israel, who introduced idol worship into the kingdom by making the two golden calves. Then Baasha reigned after that, who destroyed the descendants of Jeroboam, not out of love for God or to stop idol worship, but so that he would have no rival, and he left idol worship as it was; therefore God destroyed his descendants by the hand of King Zimri (ch. 14:10, 11, 16:3-4). These are historical events that Ahab knew well, and Elijah declared them to him, that perhaps he would repent and leave idol worship and remove it from the kingdom, otherwise God would not go back on His word and would destroy his descendants, because he encouraged the worship of Baal and Ashtaroth, and in addition to that he killed God's prophets.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of Ahab and Jezebel

paragraphs.text: Rampart (wall): a wall built outside the city for fortification, that is, set at the border of the city. God's punishment also included the source of corruption in the kingdom, the pagan Jezebel, who encouraged idol worship and killed God's prophets, using the name of her husband Ahab to do every evil. God said that she would die at the border of Jezreel and the dogs would eat her corpse in the same region in which Naboth was killed. This actually happened by the hand of King Jehu, and the dogs left of her nothing but the skull, the feet and the palms of her hands (2 Kgs 9:35).

Whoever seizes another's right, or covets what is not his, will have a terrible result like Ahab and Jezebel. So set limits to your looks, your thoughts and your words, and do not covet what belongs to another, because God's punishment is stern, and it is eternal torment. And if you have fallen into these desires, set your affairs right by repentance, and if you have taken anything from anyone, you must return it to him.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of Ahab and Jezebel

paragraphs.text: God makes clear that Ahab's descendants will die without honor, although they are of royal seed. No funerals or lamentations will be made for them, but they will be thrown on the ground, and the wild dogs in the city will eat them, and whoever is killed in the field will be eaten by the birds of prey.
The Second Book of Kings

entries.section: (3) The punishment of Ahab and Jezebel

paragraphs.text: Ahab was the most wicked of the kings of Israel, for the following reasons:
1- He encouraged idol worship and injustice, knowing that this was wrong.
2- He regarded this evil as permissible, defying God, and did it before the eyes of the LORD.
3- He was not excusable, but sold himself of his own will and enslaved himself to this evil, that Satan might do with him what he wished.

4- He was led along and convinced to submit to his wicked wife Jezebel, who seduced him to do all evils; he was weak in character yet at the same time completely given over to her, so his evil increased.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of Ahab and Jezebel

paragraphs.text: Did abominably: that is, became filthy; this is the linguistic origin of the word, but with time what was meant by it was that he was immersed in uncleanness and evil.

Ahab imitated the Amorites, the original inhabitants of the Promised Land, who were the strongest of the Canaanite tribes and lived in the mountains, as the inhabitants of Samaria and what belonged to it lived in the mountains. So Ahab worshiped idols and spread this worship in his kingdom, with all the debauchery and unclean desires connected with it, imitating the Amorites, and so he became very unclean. And as God destroyed the Amorites from the land of Canaan because of their abomination, God destroys Ahab's descendants because he imitated them.
When Ahab heard from Elijah God's punishment of him, he was deeply moved, and this appeared in a number of things:
1- He rent his clothes, as a sign of the dreadfulness of the news he had heard and of his great sorrow and remorse.
2- He changed his splendid royal garments and put on sackcloth, that is, coarse clothing, which suits austerity and humbling oneself before God.
3- He fasted, as a declaration of his rejection of the pleasures of the world and evil desires and of his drawing near to God.

4- He lay in sackcloth, that is, he continued wearing sackcloth even while sleeping, as a sign of his continuing to humble himself before God. Perhaps the sackcloth prevented him from sleeping, so he prayed, asking God's forgiveness.

5- He went softly, from his fear of God and his remorse and his deep sorrow over his sins that had caused him all this punishment. Perhaps he was reviewing himself about all that he had done. This great emotion is a sign of clear repentance.
But sadly it was a temporary repentance and a passing emotion, as is proved by:
1- That he did not return Naboth's vineyard to one of his relatives, or give it to God, because it was seized and stolen, and it was not his right to keep it.
2- His greed to own cities of the Arameans, for he stirred up war against them without reason (ch. 22:3).
3- He consulted the false prophets, the prophets of Baal, to enter the war with Aram (ch. 22:6).

4- He rejected God's word by the mouth of the prophet Micaiah, not to enter the war with Aram, but was angry with Micaiah and put him in prison (ch. 22:27). This confirms that sin was rooted in his life and that his remorse was temporary.

Do not let your repentance be a mere emotion, but make resolutions for repentance and try to carry them out carefully, so that the fruits of repentance appear in your life as a sign of God's acceptance of your repentance.

When Ahab did all these signs of repentance, God said to Elijah: since Ahab has shown his repentance, even though it is a temporary emotion, I will reward him by postponing the punishment to the days of his son. So Ahab died a shameful death in his war with the Arameans after three years (ch. 22), then all of Ahab's descendants were destroyed in the days of his son Jehoram by Jehu (2 Kgs 9, 10). And so we see God's mercies, which take into account even any signs of repentance, however temporary, to give Ahab an opportunity to complete his repentance. But sadly he learned nothing.
And by God's foreknowledge that Jehoram, Ahab's son, would be wicked, He allowed the destruction of all Ahab's descendants in his days. The death of Ahab

entries.section: (1) Ahab allies himself with Jehoshaphat to recover Ramoth-gilead

paragraphs.text: Because of Ahab's humbling himself and his repentance before God, God caused Ben-hadad king of Aram and all the countries surrounding Israel not to fight it, so it lived in peace for three years.

Be sure that the shortest way to God's heart is humility and repentance, and you will receive His mercies and tenderness. This humility is not only before God in prayer but is confirmed before others, so that you bear with them and are distinguished by fellowship with God and His love.

entries.section: (1) Ahab allies himself with Jehoshaphat to recover Ramoth-gilead

paragraphs.text: Jehoshaphat had become related by marriage to Ahab, in that he took Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, as wife for his son Jehoram (2 Chr 18:1, 2), and this was a spiritual concession, because Jehoshaphat worshiped God in His temple in Jerusalem, while Ahab and his family worshiped idols. So Jehoshaphat, who lived in Jerusalem, built on the mountains, went down to Samaria, which is lower than it geographically by about three hundred meters, and at the same time it was a spiritual descent, as we mentioned. He visited Ahab either to show affection, since they were relatives, or perhaps for political and military purposes, for Aram had taken Ramoth-gilead, which is near Jerusalem, at a distance of forty miles, and so represented a danger to the kingdom of Judah, as it could also threaten the kingdom of Israel. Also the kingdom of Assyria had begun to grow strong and could represent a danger to the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah, so the alliance of the two kingdoms, Judah and Israel, is logically useful but spiritually a mistake, because the One who protects Jerusalem is God, who is able to defend it against any human power, as will appear in the days of King Hezekiah (Isa 36, 37).

entries.section: (1) Ahab allies himself with Jehoshaphat to recover Ramoth-gilead

paragraphs.text: Ramoth-gilead: a city of the Amorites (Deut 4:43), meaning the heights of Gilead. The children of Israel took it and it was given to the tribe of Gad, then it was assigned to the Levites and was one of the cities of refuge. It lies east of the Jordan at a distance of twenty-five miles.

Ahab gathered with his servants and counselors and said to them: Ben-hadad king of Aram promised me, when I defeated him, to restore to me the cities which his father Ben-hadad had taken from the children of Israel (ch. 20:34). Since three years have passed and he has not fulfilled his promise, it is certain that he has gone back on it. So Ramoth is our right, and we are negligent in recovering it. Ahab may have been slack in demanding these cities because he was occupied with resisting Assyria, allied with Aram and the Hittites.

entries.section: (1) Ahab allies himself with Jehoshaphat to recover Ramoth-gilead

paragraphs.text: After Ahab honored Jehoshaphat greatly (2 Chr 18:2), he seduced him and encouraged him to ally with him by fighting Aram, so that they could recover Ramoth-gilead from it. Ahab may have pressed Jehoshaphat and shown him the danger of not recovering it, because it is near Jerusalem. So Jehoshaphat agreed to this alliance, and even confirmed it, saying that the peoples of Judah and Israel are originally one people, and he promised to give him a number of the people and horses equal to the number of people and horses that Israel would send out to war. The army of the kingdom of Judah at that time was large, one million one hundred and sixty thousand. Jehoshaphat erred in his sympathy and his taking part with Ahab in the war, in saying "I am as thou art", for he forgot that Ahab worshiped idols, so how could he unite with one who defies God? This is not sound love, but a concession of the faith and fellowship with the enemies of God. On the other hand, Ahab thought with human logic that Aram was a great power, so he allied with Jehoshaphat to have a larger army, and forgot that victory is from God, and because he was far from God, He did not support him in the war. Perhaps he did not understand that the victory he first achieved over Aram was, as the prophet told him, so that Aram might understand God's power, which is stronger than the pagan gods, and was not because of Ahab's godliness; on the contrary, when Ahab sinned Elijah rebuked him and declared to him God's punishment. He neglected repentance and thought only of relying on human strength; therefore he was defeated in the war and killed, as we shall see in the following verses.
Jehoshaphat neglected to ask God before going out with Ahab to war against Aram, but he remembered this after this promise and asked Ahab to inquire of God by means of a prophet, and this shows:
1- Jehoshaphat's godliness and his concern to inquire of God.

2- His entanglement in the alliance with Ahab, because he had become related to him by marriage and made relations of affection with him, although he was wicked, against God, and an idol worshiper. And his going down to Samaria, the place of idol worship, took him away from Jerusalem, where God's temple was, in which he could have inquired through the priests by means of the Urim and Thummim, through which God declares His voice, and they are two stones, one of which had written on it yes and the other no, so one of them lights up to declare the voice of God.

Learn to ask God before you enter into any work, and not after you have entered into it and become bound to it and it is hard for you to get out of it, and God may not answer you because of the uprightness of your heart, if you relied on yourself and neglected Him. And know that God loves you, but you too must love Him and want Him, so that He may guide you and keep you from all evil. Put Him before everything and submit to Him, and you will hear His voice.

When Ahab heard Jehoshaphat's request, he took refuge with those nearest to him, the prophets of the idols, that is, the false prophets, who were probably the four hundred prophets of Ashtaroth, whom Jezebel sustains. This shows how attached Ahab was to idol worship and his rejection of God, forgetting that his first and second victories over Aram were by God's power and not Baal's, as is clear from the words of God's prophet.

And when Ahab asked the four hundred prophets, they thought by human logic that since Ahab had won twice over Aram with a small army, then all the more, when he gathers all his army and allies with Jehoshaphat, he would of course win. So they said to him: be at ease, you will win and recover Ramoth-gilead. In this they forgot that God is the cause of the victory over Aram, as is clear in the words of His prophet.

The crookedness of these prophets' words is to be noticed, for they said that the Lord says to you that He will deliver Ramoth-gilead into your hand, and they did not say "the LORD", so that Jehoshaphat would understand that what is meant by "the Lord" is the LORD, and Ahab would understand that what is meant by "the Lord" is Baal. But Jehoshaphat understood that they were false prophets because they did not mention the name of the LORD; and perhaps he noticed the hypocrisy, pretense and flattery in their words.
It is understood from the above that the gathering of four hundred on one opinion is not proof of its soundness, for it may be an agreement on evil, as happened here.

Since Jehoshaphat realized that these prophets were false, as was mentioned before in (v. 6), he did not believe their words, especially since the words of the wicked do not give peace, and he did not feel at ease. So he asked Ahab about a true prophet of God, to learn from him whether he should enter the war or not.

Micaiah the son of Imlah: a prophet of God who appeared in the days of Ahab, and he is different from Micah the writer of the book in the Holy Bible, who appeared about a hundred years after this time.
Ahab answered Jehoshaphat that there was a prophet of God, but he did not like him because he always spoke evil about him, and this shows:
1- That God had sent Micaiah to Ahab more than once before to rebuke him for his evil.
2- That Ahab was troubled by Micaiah so that he put him in prison, as appears from (v. 26), when he asked that he be returned to the prison where he had been.
3- That Ahab persisted in evil and in not repenting, for he gathers false prophets who agree with him in his evil and rejects God's word by the mouth of Micaiah.

But Jehoshaphat rebuked Ahab for rejecting the word of Micaiah the prophet of God, and in this he shows himself to be a godly man who worships God. But sadly, his mixing with the wicked Ahab made him give up God's guidance, so he entered the war with him, as we shall see, despite God's clear warning by the mouth of Micaiah.

Do not refuse to hear the voice of God that comes to you through those around you, if he is reproaching you or rebuking you, but review yourself and repent. And beware of gathering around you a group of hypocrites who falsely make you believe that you are righteous, and others do not frighten you, so that they refrain from declaring the truth to you because you attack, and by this you deprive yourself of hearing the voice of God.

Ahab was compelled, to honor his friend Jehoshaphat, to summon Micaiah the prophet quickly, because he was imprisoned and Ahab knew his place, to hear God's voice from his tongue, and he sent a eunuch to bring him. This means that the kings of the children of Israel used eunuchs, like the kings of the nations, and they were probably non-Jews, because the Law did not allow anyone to be made a eunuch.
And we notice that Ahab's response to Jehoshaphat's request did not change his heart, because he did not obey the prophet's word, as will appear in the following verses.

All these conversations took place between the two kings Ahab and Jehoshaphat while they sat, each on his throne, wearing his royal garments, and these thrones were portable, carried where the king needed them. They were sitting in the large open space of the city of Samaria beside the gate of the city, for it was the custom to set up a large square beside the gate of the city for the people to gather in it for any important matter, and this square was so large that it held the four hundred prophets as well as the people, to decide in it important matters such as whether to enter war or not. This means that this conversation took place before the people and the false prophets, and this shows Jehoshaphat's courage and his holding fast to God. He did not fear to ask for a prophet of God in a city that worshiped Baal. It also shows Ahab's and his people's persistence in idol worship, since none of the leaders of the people or the king's servants objected to Ahab for his refusal to hear the word of the prophet of God.

Before the prophet Micaiah arrived, one of the prophets of Baal came forward, called Zedekiah, who was perhaps one of their chiefs, and he was wearing two horns on his head. In ancient wars they used to wear such horns as a sign of strength and in anticipation of victory. Zedekiah said that Ahab would win and push the Arameans, as an animal pushes other animals with its horns and destroys them.
And Zedekiah's hypocrisy appears in the following:
1- That he spoke his words in the name of the LORD, as if God had told him this prophecy.
2- He made two horns symbolizing the two kings, to confirm their victory over Aram.

3- Zedekiah imitated God's true prophets, for he made a visual aid of these horns, to make the king and the people believe that this prophecy was from God. The true prophets such as Elisha and Isaiah used visual aids as God commanded them (2 Kgs 13:15, Isa 20:2).
Of course all the false prophets agreed with Zedekiah in his false prophecy and cried out, saying to Ahab: go up to Ramoth-gilead, for you will take it and defeat the Arameans.

When the eunuch, Ahab's messenger, reached Micaiah to bring him from the prison to the king, he told him that all the prophets had encouraged the king to go to Ramoth-gilead and fight the Arameans, so his victory over them was assured, and he asked him to say the same to the king, so that his words might be for the king's good. This shows:
1- The eunuch's conviction that the agreement of many on one opinion shows that their opinion is sound.
2- That the king's agreement with his purposes is a comfortable thing, so he encourages Micaiah to this for the king's comfort.
3- Perhaps if Micaiah said words agreeing with the king's purposes, he would release him, so the eunuch is giving Micaiah loving advice to be freed from prison.
4- In the eyes of this eunuch and the people in general, good is agreeing with the king and not obeying God.
Micaiah swore by the LORD to declare to the eunuch that he stood before the living LORD and that he would say nothing except what the LORD says to him, and this shows:
1- Micaiah's courage and his holding fast to God's word and obeying it.
2- His readiness to bear suffering for the sake of God's word.
3- His not being affected by the words of people such as the eunuch and the king, for the most important thing is the word of God.

When Micaiah arrived before Ahab, Ahab asked him, before all who were present, "Shall we go up to Ramoth-gilead to recover it?" Micaiah answered him with clear sarcasm: go up and you will defeat the Arameans and take Ramoth-gilead. By this he meant: since you insist on going up, go up, and since you want to hear that you will win, I tell you that you will win. Micaiah's words were sarcasm that Ahab and all who were present understood; that is, Ahab understood that he had not told him the truth, but that what he said was a repetition of Ahab's wish.

Ahab understood that Micaiah was mocking him and not telling him the truth, but agreeing with his opinions and ridiculing him. Ahab may have asked Micaiah before this about other matters and Micaiah mocked him, or he may have asked him in this situation more than once and Micaiah repeated the same words of sarcasm. Therefore Ahab implored him for God's sake to tell him the truth, for Ahab was afraid of the Arameans, so he adjured him in the name of the LORD. Ahab wants to carry out his wish but at the same time is afraid, so he begged Micaiah to tell him God's word.

When Ahab declared his readiness and concern to hear God's word, Micaiah began to declare the prophecy that God had shown him. He said: I saw a vision in which God's people were scattered and spread on the mountains without a shepherd, that is, without a leader, because the leader, who is Ahab, would have been killed in the war, and God said, "let them return every man to his house in peace". For Ben-hadad king of Aram, as we shall see in the coming verses, had as his aim the killing of Ahab, and when he achieved that he stopped the war, so God's people returned in peace.
This prophecy includes two things:
1- The killing of Ahab in the war.
2- The scattering of the people on the mountains, without leadership.

The meaning of this prophecy is clear, which is that they should not enter the war, because Ahab would die and the people would not achieve victory, but God would have compassion on them and bring them back in peace, and perhaps this was for the sake of Jehoshaphat's righteousness. Sadly, Ahab did not benefit from this prophecy and did not obey God, so he died in the war. Likewise Jehoshaphat felt embarrassed to withdraw from the war, so he went out with him and did not obey God's word, which he had sought with concern; but after he heard Micaiah he neglected his word.

When God declares His voice to you, whether through your father of confession, or in the Holy Bible, or by the mouth of those around you, or in any way, do not neglect it, because your judgment will become greater and you will meet a dark future, as Ahab did not obey and died with his sin upon him.

Ahab was angry when he heard the word of Micaiah the prophet and considered it ill feeling from Micaiah toward him, and refused to accept his words as a prophecy from God. Perhaps he was influenced by the four hundred prophets who encouraged him to go to war. On the other hand, Ahab bore hatred toward God and His prophets, so he thought that they hated him, although the hatred was in his heart to begin with.
Here Jehoshaphat's weakness appears, that he was influenced by Ahab's words and did not answer him and call him to obey God, so that in the end he rejected God's word and entered the war with him.
Micaiah did not care to defend himself against Ahab's accusation that he speaks evil about him, because Micaiah was occupied with declaring the voice of God.

So Micaiah completed the second part of the vision he had seen, for he saw the LORD sitting on His throne in heaven with His angels around Him on the right and on the left. This produced in his heart:
1- Reverence and joy at being in the presence of God.
2- Not being disturbed by Ahab's anger, or the prison into which Ahab had thrown him.
3- His trust in God's word that he declares, and in the falsehood of its opponents from among the prophets of Baal.
4- His faith that everything is in God's hand, so He allows victories, or defeat, or leaves the wicked to fall into their sins.

5- God is the Controller of all; perhaps what is meant by the angels on the right is the angels appointed by God to convey His blessings to mankind, and those on the left are the angels appointed to discipline sinners.

The vision that God showed Micaiah was in the form of a dialogue, so that he might understand the reality of the matters and declare them in a way understandable to human beings, although in heaven the matter does not need all these dialogues, for the movement of thought takes place in less than a moment and God declares His command at once.

God showed in the vision that He asks before His angels: who can incite Ahab to evil and to disobeying God? Of course God does not want any human being to walk in evil, but He allows Satan to tempt all in the proper measure, and sometimes gives up the wicked if they persist in sin, that perhaps they, and those around them, may feel the seriousness of sin, so that they turn back from it. In Ahab's case, he persisted in rejecting God, so He gave him up, to be an example of evil before his people, that they might repent. When God asked, His angels replied with different opinions or suggestions according to their understanding. All this, as we mentioned, is so that Ahab and the people may understand what is taking place in heaven.

Then God allowed Satan, that is, the evil spirit, to stand before Him, and Satan declared that he was able to seduce Ahab. God asked him how he would seduce him. Satan said that he would enter the prophets of Baal and speak lying words through their tongues to deceive Ahab. God said to him that you are indeed able to do so, for Satan is full of evil and wicked tricks, and God allowed him to go out and seduce Ahab because Ahab had sold himself and surrendered to evil.

This vision reminds us of what happened at the beginning of the book of Job, for all these are portrayals by God of what takes place in heaven, that we may understand God's righteousness and Satan's evil. By this God gave Ahab a last warning, that he might know that Satan, or the Baal whom he worships, will lead him and his prophets to destruction, that perhaps he might take notice and repent, for God seeks the salvation of all, however great their evil.
Micaiah summed up God's voice in the vision for Ahab in two things:
1- That the words of the prophets of Baal are all falsehood.
2- God allowed the evil that befell Ahab, that is, his destruction in the war. And this is the end of the most wicked of the kings of Israel.

entries.section: (4) The striking and imprisonment of Micaiah

paragraphs.text: With insolence and wickedness Zedekiah, who was probably the chief of the prophets of Baal, came forward and struck Micaiah on the cheek, and did not ask Ahab's permission for it, but he knew well that Ahab supported his prophets, that is, the prophets of Baal. As for Jehoshaphat, as a guest with no authority, he did nothing, although in truth he could at least have declared that this was wrong, but he was weak and slack, despite his confidence that Micaiah was the true prophet and all the other prophets were false, and Jehoshaphat, as a believer in God, is able to distinguish the true prophet from the false.
Then Zedekiah said to Micaiah in astonishment and mockery: how did you dare, Micaiah, and claim that the Spirit of God who is upon me has passed by and come to you?
Zedekiah's action shows two things:
1- The boldness of evil and its assault on the children of God.

2- The lie and sophistry by which Satan, through his children, tries to deceive people, for although Micaiah is the true prophet and Zedekiah and those with him are all liars, the lying Zedekiah claims that the Spirit of God is with him only and not with Micaiah. Of course the Spirit of God does not harm others, as Zedekiah struck Micaiah, for the Spirit of God is gentle and firm but not violent and harsh.

entries.section: (4) The striking and imprisonment of Micaiah

paragraphs.text: Micaiah bore the blow for God's sake and did not defend himself, but was occupied with confirming God's voice to Zedekiah. He said to him: you will understand and know God's word when it comes to pass and God's people are defeated before Aram and flee from it, and you, Zedekiah, will flee from house to house and from room to room, either for fear of the Arameans or of Jezebel, who will be disturbed by the death of her husband and will try to kill Zedekiah, who lied and led her husband astray, so that he died.

Let your aim be to declare the voice of God even if the wicked rise against you and insult you. Bear it for God's sake, confident that God appreciates your labor and will support you, and prepares for you a great crown in heaven.

entries.section: (4) The striking and imprisonment of Micaiah

paragraphs.text: In anger and pride Ahab commanded the eunuch who had brought Micaiah to return him to the prison under the authority and responsibility of Amon, the governor of the city of Samaria, and Joash, Ahab's son, who apparently was in charge of the prison.

And in going further in his pride Ahab commanded that they afflict Micaiah in the prison, giving him only the barest amount of water and the worst food, to humiliate him because of the lie he had told and the evil words he had spoken against Ahab. So Ahab believed, and added that they should do this until Ahab returns in peace. This shows that evil blinds the eyes of its owner, so that he does not see the truth, however clear.

entries.section: (4) The striking and imprisonment of Micaiah

paragraphs.text: Micaiah was not disturbed by Ahab's arbitrary orders of imprisonment and ill treatment within it, but continued to confirm God's voice before all the people, declaring to Ahab that he would surely not return from the war, because he would die, and if he returned, then God had not spoken. For Micaiah was sure of God's vision and commands, and declared them to all the people, so that when they see Ahab killed they will repent and return to God.

entries.section: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

paragraphs.text: Despite all of God's clear declarations by the mouth of Micaiah that they should not enter, Ahab went up with his army, and with him Jehoshaphat with the army of Judah, to Ramoth-gilead to recover it from the Arameans. While Ahab persisted in harm because of his distance from God, Jehoshaphat's position is the strange one, in entering the war despite all these warnings, and this appears to be for the following reasons:

1- Jehoshaphat's previous promise to Ahab to go with him to the war, and kings do not go back on their word; but of course it is possible to go back if God has commanded the opposite of the king's word.
2- Jehoshaphat's weakness before his relative by marriage Ahab, for he found himself embarrassed to leave him alone, because Ahab insisted on entering the war, completely despising God's word.

3- Perhaps he understood that only Ahab would die, but he and all the people would return in peace, as Micaiah said, so he took courage and went with Ahab. But this is a great mistake, since in it there is opposition to God's word, and he did not heed Micaiah's word.

4- Jehoshaphat's doubt of God's word through Micaiah, and what may have helped him in this was Ahab's anger and his and his prophets' accusation of Micaiah that he speaks evil. And this is a natural result of mixing with the wicked, that a person goes astray and his faith in God weakens.

entries.section: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

paragraphs.text: Ahab felt that he was the target of Ben-hadad in this war, especially after hearing Micaiah's prophecy of his death, so he was even more afraid and decided to enter the war in disguise, as an ordinary soldier. But can he disguise himself before God? Since God had decided that he would be killed, there was no solution except that he repent and believe in God, and He would have mercy on him. Perhaps Ahab's disguise came from what he had heard from Micaiah, that God's people would be scattered on the mountains, so he decided to disguise himself so as not to be killed and to remain leader of his people, so that they would not be defeated or scattered. By this he is trying to stop God's judgment, which, as we said, cannot be stopped except by repentance.

Ahab announced to Jehoshaphat that he would disguise himself, but proposed to Jehoshaphat that he put on his royal garments, and this was a great evil from Ahab, to expose his friend, who had come to ally with him, to die in the war in his place. Ahab disguised himself, while Jehoshaphat put on the royal garments, although it was unwise of Jehoshaphat to agree to this. Why, then, did Jehoshaphat agree?
1- Perhaps he felt pride in being the sole commander of the armies in his royal garments.

2- His trust in God's word by the mouth of Micaiah, that the one who would die was Ahab, because God had spoken evil about him, and Micaiah had not directed a rebuke or divine judgment to Jehoshaphat.

entries.section: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

paragraphs.text: Ben-hadad king of Aram organized his army, made up of thirty-two divisions, each led by a commander who was one of the vassal kings, who are the heads of the provinces mentioned in (ch. 20:1). He commanded these commanders to concentrate on killing Ahab, in order to reduce the number of the dead in his army, because he knew that if the commander of the army of Israel, who was Ahab, were killed, the army would scatter at once and the victory would be Aram's.

entries.section: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

paragraphs.text: The captains of the chariots searched for the king of Israel, and saw from afar a person wearing the royal garments, and they thought he was Ahab and attacked him. Here Jehoshaphat cried out at once and they left him, and this cry means the following:
1- A cry to God to save him from death, and this shows his faith in the hour of danger, so God drew the soldiers of Aram away from him, as appears in (2 Chr 18:31).

2- He cried out declaring before the soldiers that he was not Ahab, so they left him, with God's help, for God made them leave him to search for Ahab, as Ben-hadad had commanded them. Perhaps some of them knew Ahab's appearance and voice from the former wars, since they accompanied Ben-hadad during the treaty that Ahab made with him (ch. 20:31-34).

3- Because Jehoshaphat believed Micaiah's prophecy that the one who would meet evil was Ahab (v. 23,), he hurried to declare to the Aramean soldiers that he was not Ahab, so that they would leave him.
Jehoshaphat was exposed to death, and God allowed this because of the mistakes he made, which are:
1- His mixing with the wicked, even becoming related to them by marriage, that is, mixing with Ahab and the marriage of his son to Ahab's daughter.
2- His not obeying God's word by the mouth of Micaiah, which was clear, not to enter the war, because its result was defeat.
3- His love of leadership and of appearing as commander of all the armies of God's people; but God saved him from death because of his faith in Him and his return to Him in the hour of danger.

entries.section: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

paragraphs.text: Drew a bow: he pulled his bow back, so the arrow that was in the bow was released.

The joints of the harness: the area between the armor that protects the chest and the armor that protects the thighs, and the two pieces of armor are joined by linen connections, so it is the region of the belly.
Turn thine hand: stop the chariot's moving forward and turn the chariot to go in the opposite direction, that is, to leave the battle.

An Aramean soldier was holding his bow with an arrow in it, and perhaps he was trying to fix it, or test it, so the arrow was released without intent, and struck the disguised Ahab in the belly with a deep wound whose seriousness Ahab felt, so he asked the driver of his chariot to turn the chariot and take him out of the battle.

We notice that the disguised Ahab was struck by a stray arrow with a deep wound that killed him, while Jehoshaphat, who wore the royal garments, was protected by God from death because he cried out to Him. For God's judgment must be carried out, however much the wicked man tries to protect himself, and the righteous save themselves by faith and prayer.
God allowed Ahab to die and not be taken by Ben-hadad alive, because he might pardon him in return for Ahab's earlier kindness; for God's judgment was Ahab's destruction because of his many evils.

You cannot escape from the hand of God, so do not commit sin in secret, because He sees you, and the wages of sin is death, and the only solution is to return to God by repentance, for He is a tender Father ready to forgive you everything, and the Church always opens her arms with forgiveness in the sacraments of confession and Communion.

entries.section: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

paragraphs.text: The driver of the king's chariot and the commanders around his chariot did not approve of Ahab leaving the battle, lest his army scatter if they learned that he had been seriously wounded. So they supported him and kept him standing in his chariot, although his blood was flowing abundantly and ran onto the floor of the chariot, and even one who noticed his wound would think it a slight one. The fighting continued fiercely with the Arameans until evening, when King Ahab died.

entries.section: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

paragraphs.text: The news spread quickly among the soldiers of Israel that their king Ahab had died, so their commanders called for withdrawal and for every soldier to return to his home, whether the soldiers of Israel or of Judah, for the following reasons:
1- The death of the commander leaves the army without leadership, so it is impossible to continue the war, and this shows the importance of the commander, especially in ancient times.
2- Perhaps some of them remembered Micaiah's prophecy that Ahab would die and the soldiers would be spread on the mountains, fleeing and scattered, so they hurried to withdraw.

3- The Arameans heard of Ahab's death and saw the army's withdrawal, so they stopped the fighting and withdrew too, since their aim was to kill Ahab and thereby keep Ramoth-gilead subject to them. So the Arameans withdrew also, and thus the war lasted only one day and ended.

entries.section: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

paragraphs.text: The soldiers of Israel returned with their dead king to Samaria, his capital, which his father Omri had built, and buried him there.

entries.section: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

paragraphs.text: Here details are explained about the transport of the dead Ahab and his chariot and how his blood was washed. They passed through the city of Jezreel on their way to Samaria; there they washed his chariot and weapons in a pool outside Jezreel, called the pool of Samaria, then they carried him to Samaria. By this the word of Elijah the prophet to Ahab was fulfilled after his killing of Naboth the Jezreelite and seizing his field: the dogs licked the blood of Naboth, since Elijah said that the dogs would lick your blood, Ahab, in the same place where they licked the blood of the wronged Naboth (ch. 21:19). There is another opinion, that the soldiers washed the chariot in the pool of Samaria, which lies beside the city of Samaria, and the dogs licked Ahab's blood there, as the dogs licked Naboth's blood outside Jezreel, but the first opinion is the more likely.

The place where Ahab's chariot was washed, in the pool of Samaria, is the place where the harlots who were dedicated to harlotry in the temples of Baal, which Ahab encouraged, used to wash; that is, in the end Ahab's blood was washed in an unclean place, because he defiled himself by the worship of Baal throughout his life, and so he died a shameful, unclean death.
And so the great royal chariot was washed for another king to use, and Ahab died and took nothing, as all die; and if he had remembered that, he would have repented and returned to God.

entries.section: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

paragraphs.text: Ahab was concerned with building palaces and cities, especially a great house that he adorned with ivory, which is taken from the tusks of elephants, and it was called the ivory house. So all his concern was material, far from spiritual things. All these matters and the account of his death are mentioned in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel, which is different from the Book of Chronicles in the Holy Bible. And after his death his son Ahaziah reigned in his place.

entries.section: (6) Jehoshaphat king of Judah and his most important works

paragraphs.text: In the fourth year of Ahab's reign over Israel, Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over the kingdom of Judah, and he was at that time thirty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-five years over Judah. Jehoshaphat's mother was called Azubah the daughter of Shilhi, and it seems that she was a godly person, for her husband Asa was righteous and did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, and likewise her son Jehoshaphat walked like his father with uprightness of heart. The Holy Bible mentions some mothers to show their holy role, or on the contrary the evil one, which appears in husbands and sons, like the wicked Jezebel, the wife of Ahab and the mother of Ahaziah and Athaliah, all of whom were wicked. The details of the life and works of Jehoshaphat are mentioned in (2 Chr 17-20).

entries.section: (6) Jehoshaphat king of Judah and his most important works

paragraphs.text: The Holy Bible gives us a summary of the life of Jehoshaphat and his most important works.

If Asa was upright in the eyes of the LORD, indeed perfect (ch. 15:14), then Jehoshaphat his son walked in the upright way of his father before God, that is, he cared for the worship of God in His temple and rejected idol worship in all its forms.
The offering of sacrifices on the high places and the burning of incense was personal worship, while public worship remained in the temple.

But the mistake that Jehoshaphat did not correct was that he allowed sacrificing on the high places to God and not to the idols, although God commanded that the offering of sacrifices be in His temple only and forbade that it be on the high places (Deut 12:13, 14), because these high places turned in time into idol worship.

entries.section: (6) Jehoshaphat king of Judah and his most important works

paragraphs.text: The greatest mistake Jehoshaphat fell into was his reconciliation, alliance and association with the king of Israel, who was wicked, Ahab, and then his son Ahaziah. Although understanding and reconciliation between neighboring states is useful, in addition to the fact that the kingdoms of Israel and Judah are originally one nation, God's people, yet on the other hand alliance with the wicked has many harms, and this is what Jehoshaphat fell into. The reconciliation and alliance appeared in the following:
1- His alliance with Ahab in the war against Aram to recover Ramoth-gilead (v. 32).
2- The marrying of his son Joram to Athaliah the daughter of Ahab.
3- His going out to war with Ahaziah the son of Ahab against Moab (2 Kgs 3:7).

4- His partnership with Ahaziah in building a fleet of trading ships (2 Chr 20:36). This reconciliation with the kings of Israel brought many troubles on Jehoshaphat, because of the LORD's anger with him. The most important of these troubles:-
1- His exposure to death in his war with Ahab against Aram, and God saved him at the last moment (v. 32).

2- His causing his son Joram to stumble by marrying him to Athaliah, who introduced the worship of Baal into Judah and dominated the kingdom, for she killed her grandchildren and sat on the throne of Judah (2 Kgs 11:1).

3- The breaking of the trading fleet at Ezion-geber, and Jehoshaphat lost much, because he angered the LORD, and God declared this to him by Eliezer the prophet (2 Chr 20:37). It is noticed that Jehoshaphat did not quickly learn the danger of mixing with the wicked, for what befell him from his mixing with Ahab did not make him keep away from Ahaziah, his wicked son; therefore God was angry with him and his ships were broken, but finally he learned obedience to God, so he refused Ahaziah's offer to share in the trade by ships (v. 49). But the love of Christ, the Redeemer of sinners, appears in that He came from the descendants of Joram the son of Jehoshaphat and Athaliah his wife (Mt 1:8, 9), for He seeks the salvation of everyone who believed and tried to obey God, like Jehoshaphat.

It is good to be at peace with all, as far as you can, but beware of mixing with the wicked, or sharing in their works by your own choice, lest you be defiled by their thoughts and behavior, and so anger the LORD and He abandons you. Let your heart be open with love toward all, but be careful about whom you choose as friends and those close to you.

entries.section: (6) Jehoshaphat king of Judah and his most important works

paragraphs.text: Jehoshaphat was strong in facing idol worship, so he removed it and all the corruption connected with it. On the other hand, his superiority in wars against the surrounding nations appeared, such as the Ammonites and the Moabites (2 Chr 20:1). The details of Jehoshaphat's works are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, which is a historical book concerning the kings of Judah, and is different from the Book of Chronicles in the Holy Bible.

entries.section: (6) Jehoshaphat king of Judah and his most important works

paragraphs.text: The sodomites: the men who gave themselves to the pagan gods, to practice homosexual acts with them, and who live in houses beside the temples so that males may lie with them, and by this they please the gods according to their belief.

Asa destroyed idol worship and all the adultery and perversion connected with it, but it seems that some sodomites were able to flee and continued their sexual practice, so Jehoshaphat completed what his father Asa had done and destroyed the remainder of these sodomites, that is, he removed the corruption from the land, so as not to put a stumbling block before his people, that they might worship the LORD in purity.

entries.section: (6) Jehoshaphat king of Judah and his most important works

paragraphs.text: The kingdom of Edom lived in the mountains of Seir and extended south and east of the kingdom of Judah, from the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. Edom was subjected to many attacks from the kings of the children of Israel, among them Saul (1 Sam 14:47), then David, who destroyed all the males. Edom grew strong in part in the days of Solomon, and it seems that it was weak in the days of Jehoshaphat, so he set over it a deputy from himself, that is, a representative of Jehoshaphat, and he may have been from the Edomites themselves; that is, Edom was under the control of Judah.

entries.section: (6) Jehoshaphat king of Judah and his most important works

paragraphs.text: Tarshish: a famous trading city in the south of Spain on the Mediterranean coast. Gold and many goods were imported from it.

Ophir: a city lying in the south of the Arabian Peninsula in the present state of Yemen, famous for producing the purest kinds of gold (Sir 7:20), and it was named Ophir after one of the descendants of Shem (Gen 10:29). Ezion-geber: a famous ancient port on the Gulf of Aqaba, lying west of the present city of Eilat. Jehoshaphat built huge trading ships able to go to the farthest country known at that time, which was Tarshish, lying at the end of the Mediterranean Sea, the end of the ancient world, in order to send them to Tarshish, joining in this with Ahaziah king of Israel, but the ships were broken, because of God's anger with Jehoshaphat for his partnership with the wicked, that is, Ahaziah (2 Chr 20:37). Then Jehoshaphat built other strong ships like the first, and Ahaziah asked him to join him in the trade, but Jehoshaphat refused, for he had finally learned to obey God and not to share in work with the wicked.

entries.section: (6) Jehoshaphat king of Judah and his most important works

paragraphs.text: After twenty-five years of reign, Jehoshaphat, the righteous king, finally died. And his firstborn son Jehoram reigned after him (2 Chr 21:3), and sadly he was not righteous like his father, because of his marriage to the wicked Athaliah the daughter of Ahab, and this shows the importance of choosing a righteous wife.

After the death of Ahab in the battle of Ramoth-gilead, his son Ahaziah reigned over the kingdom of Israel, and because of his evils and his worship of idols the LORD allowed illnesses upon him and he died quickly, so he reigned only two years in his capital Samaria.

The details of Ahaziah's evils are that he continued in the worship of the golden calves that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up in Bethel and Dan, and also continued in the worship of the idols that his father and mother introduced, such as Baal and Ashtaroth. By this he defied God and provoked Him by his persistence in idol worship, because he not only allowed it, but himself led the people in bowing down to the idols and worshiping them. And he did not learn from the danger of disobeying God in the days of his father, who did not obey Elijah, who withheld the rain and brought down fire from heaven and killed the prophets of Baal, and yet Ahab did not return to God, and he did not obey Micaiah either, who warned Ahab not to enter the war with Aram, but he obeyed the false prophets and died.

Be careful in all your actions, whether you are a father, or a leader, or responsible anywhere; indeed, since you are a Christian you are the light of the world, so do not be lax in your words or actions, lest you cause others to stumble. You are the image of God, even if all around you are wicked.

We see that this book began with the greatest of the kings of the children of Israel, David, when the kingdom was united, and ends with the most wicked of the kings of the kingdom of Israel, Ahab, after the division of the kingdom. Why did it begin with a joyful beginning and end with a shameful end? The reason is clear: the relation between the king and the people was strong in the days of David, but at the end of the book we find how they left God and worshiped idols and walked in many evils and uncleanness, so they were defeated before their enemies the Arameans, and Ahab died, as a punishment for his evils, a shameful death in the war.
A comparison between the false prophets and the prophets of God; serial; the false prophets; the prophets of God
1- They speak false messages of their own composition and not true messages, because they do not speak from God. Except what God says to them.

2- They have personal purposes. They speak God's word even if it exposes them to many troubles, as the prophet who spoke against the altar before Jeroboam was exposed to death, but God rescued him when Jeroboam's hand dried up (ch. 13:4).
3- They hold political positions because they please rejected by the wicked kings and do not seek the kings. to the positions.
4- Rich, they care about their material gains. Poor, detached, they live for God and are content with food and clothing.

5- The kings love them because they agree with them, but they are merely, even if one prophet before the followers of the kings, and the kings rely on the multitude of many, like Elijah, who stands before four hundred in number, since they have no awe. of the prophets of Baal and four hundred and fifty of the prophets of the groves (ch. 18:19)

6- They try to flatter the kings and the people, so they say what pleases them, and they rely on their minds in; and the people as a rebuke; or divine punishment for them, such as deducing the future (ch. 22:5-12); they speak God's word even if it troubles the kings. The prophet's word to Ahab that he would die instead of Ben-hadad king of Aram, whom he released (ch. 20:42)

7- They were an obstacle in the way of the people's repentance. They used to call the people to repent and return to God, like Elijah when he called the people to choose the worship of God or Baal (ch. 18:21).
